title: Tenant Property After Eviction
bodyText: In the District, a tenant's belongings are handled through the eviction process, not a stand-alone abandoned-property procedure. For an eviction from a covered unit, at least 21 days before the scheduled date you must send the tenant a final notice by phone or electronic message, first-class mail and posting, warning that property left behind is deemed abandoned 7 days after the eviction (not counting Sundays and federal holidays). At the eviction you change the locks in the Marshals' presence at your expense; that day you post a notice at the unit, and mail it first-class to the tenant's emergency contact if one was provided, naming an agent who can grant access. For 7 days you must store the property in the unit with reasonable care and give the tenant at least 16 hours of access between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. over up to 2 days (including a Saturday if asked), charging no rent or fees. Then you may dispose of what remains, but never by leaving it outdoors except while hauling it to a lawful disposal site, and you are immune for lawful disposal. For tenancies outside the Rental Housing Act, property is deemed abandoned at ejectment and any sale proceeds go to the tenant's account. No statute lets you declare a unit or belongings abandoned on your own; get a written surrender or a court finding first.

title: Renting an Accessory Unit: License, Registration and Coverage
bodyText: Whether you may build or rent an accessory unit is a zoning question for the District's zoning regulations (DCMR Title 11). Renting an English basement, converted basement apartment or carriage house in a single-family home, where the main house is occupied by the owner or another tenant, needs a two-family rental business license, which in turn requires a certificate of occupancy; each rental unit must also be registered with the Rental Accommodations Division unless the small-owner exemption is claimed. Once rented, the accessory unit is a rental unit with the same just-cause eviction, entry, deposit and fee protections as any other. For the purchase-right law, a house with one accessory unit counts as a single-family accommodation, so its sale needs only the 3-day notice of purchase offers to tenants, not a full offer of sale (with an exception for some elderly or disabled tenants). Practical step: confirm zoning approval and the certificate of occupancy before advertising the unit, and license and register it before the first lease.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText: In the District the owner of every new and existing occupied dwelling unit is responsible for installing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors in accordance with the District's Construction Codes. The statutory definition of owner excludes a lessee or anyone who merely has the right to occupy, so the installation duty cannot be shifted to the tenant. The older detailed Smoke Detector Act sections on locations, equipment, maintenance, installation by tenants, notices and civil penalties have been repealed, so look to Title 12 for those rules. The housing regulations also require each owner or operator of a housing business to install smoke detectors, and the operator of each housing business to keep required fire alarm systems operable and post signs explaining how the local alarm works. The District runs a program that can supply and install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. A lease may require tenants not to disable or remove detectors and to report problems promptly. These duties do not differ between fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Relocation and Alternate Housing Duties
bodyText: District law has no general rule that a landlord must provide alternate housing whenever a unit becomes uninhabitable or on a tenant's request; instead, specific duties arise from government action or your own plans. If the Mayor orders lead-hazard work, you must make temporary comparable relocation arrangements for an at-risk tenant (unless the risk assessment says relocation is unnecessary), pay all reasonable temporary relocation expenses until the unit passes clearance, give at least 14 days' written notice unless the Mayor orders or you and the tenant agree to less, try to keep the household in the same building, ward or school district, and let the tenant return on the same terms; the tenant may choose its own arrangements instead. If a District agency closes a unit and the Office of the Tenant Advocate houses the tenants, you must reimburse hotel stays up to 180 days, moving and storage, deposits and first month's rent when the conditions arose from circumstances within your control, such as failed maintenance or cutting utilities, and the debt becomes a lien. Substantial rehabilitation, demolition or discontinuing housing use requires notice and relocation assistance payments. These duties apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: No Work That Makes a Unit Uninhabitable After a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: After you give a notice to vacate, and until the tenant actually moves out, you may not alter the building's structure, plumbing or electrical systems in a way that puts the tenant's unit in substantial violation of the housing regulations (or in worse violation) for more than 24 hours. It is no defense that the notice to vacate was invalid, and a violation is a crime (up to 10 days in jail, a $300 fine, or both). There are only two ways around this: the affected tenants agree in writing after you give them written notice of the work and its effect on their units, or the Mayor inspects and finds the work necessary for the immediate safety of the residents. Applies to every rental unit covered by the Rental Housing Act. Practical step: schedule renovation work that affects occupied units after they are vacated, or get each affected tenant's written agreement first.

title: Tenant Alterations and Disability Modifications
bodyText:
District law has no general statute on tenant alterations, so the lease decides whether a tenant may paint, install fixtures or make other changes, and a clause requiring your prior written consent is lawful. Two limits apply.

First, under the District's Human Rights Act you may not refuse a tenant with a disability permission to make reasonable modifications of the unit, at the tenant's own expense, when they may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises; where it is reasonable, you may condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. District law does not shift the cost of these modifications to larger or subsidized landlords. The Act does not reach certain small owner-occupied buildings or some single-family rentals by owners of three or fewer homes who rent without a broker or discriminatory advertising, so check those exceptions before relying on them.

Second, a tenant's promise to leave the unit in good repair does not oblige the tenant to make substantial repairs, replace obsolete materials or fix defects that are not the tenant's fault. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

Practical step: require written requests and give written approvals that say whether removal and restoration will be required.

title: Owner-Furnished Appliances Must Be Maintained
bodyText: District law has no presumption about who supplied appliances found in a unit, but it ties maintenance to what you furnish. If you furnish any facilities for cooking, storage or refrigeration of food, such as a stove or refrigerator, you must keep them in safe and good working condition; if you provide air conditioning, through window units or a central system, you must keep it able to cool at least 15 degrees below the outside temperature and have it inspected every year. Facilities the housing regulations require, including the kitchen sink, bathroom fixtures, hot and cold water, water heating, heating and entrance locks, must be provided and maintained by you and cannot be excluded. So a lease term saying you will not repair a stove, refrigerator or air conditioner you leave in the unit is unlikely to hold; if you do not want that duty, remove the item before the tenancy or let the tenant bring its own. An exclusion is safer only for non-required extras, such as a washer or dryer, stated clearly in the lease. In a rent-stabilized unit, taking away an appliance or service you provided can be challenged as a reduction in services. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Listing Included Appliances
bodyText:
Listing the appliances and equipment you provide is a good idea in the District, because what you furnish determines what you must maintain. Any stove, refrigerator or other facility for cooking, storage or refrigeration of food that you furnish must be kept in safe and good working condition, and air conditioning you provide must cool at least 15 degrees below the outside temperature and be inspected each year.

Required facilities, such as the kitchen sink, bathroom fixtures, water heater, heating equipment and entrance locks, are your responsibility whether or not they are listed. A lease cannot shift these duties to the tenant. In a rent-stabilized unit, the listed appliances and services are part of what the rent pays for, and removing them without approval can be challenged as a reduction in related services. See the appliances-excluded row for detail. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Screening Notices and the Application Disclosure Form With the Tenant Bill of Rights
bodyText:
Before screening or taking fees, give or post the screening notice: each fee and deposit and whether refundable, information checked, denial criteria, the consumer reporting agency, unit availability, decision time, and dispute, refund and complaint rights. Unless you own and live in a building with 3 or fewer rental units, also give the written eligibility criteria (financial, employment, criminal, rental history) and a statement that the applicant may show record errors or rehabilitation before accepting an application fee.

At application (every covered unit): give the Rent Administrator's disclosure form with supporting documents: the rent; rent-controlled or exempt status with business license and registration or claim of exemption; how often rent may rise; housing code violation reports from the last 12 months or still unabated; the application fee; the deposit amount, interest rate and how it is returned; any pending condominium, cooperative or non-housing conversion; ownership information; known indoor mold in the last 3 years unless professionally remediated; the Board of Elections voter registration packet; and the Tenant Advocate's Tenant Bill of Rights.

The statute also lists pending petitions, surcharges and the Rent Administrator's pamphlet for every unit; the regulation lists them only for rent-stabilized units, so the cautious course for an exempt unit too is to give the pamphlet and list any pending petition or surcharge (or state that there is none). The Tenant Advocate published a revised Bill of Rights (form dated September 25, 2026); use the version the agency currently publishes. Keep a compilation for tenants and update it within 30 days of changes.

title: Application Fee Cap, Screening Notice and Refund
bodyText: For every covered rental unit, an application fee may not exceed $50 adjusted for inflation; the Rental Housing Commission publishes each year's limit before February 1. Before signing the lease, the application fee is the only fee you may charge (a holding deposit is allowed, but not from an applicant paying with a government housing voucher). Before asking for any information or fee, give or post the written screening notice: each fee and deposit with amount, purpose and refundability, what you will check, denial criteria, the consumer reporting agency, your decision time, and the applicant's rights to dispute, to a refund of an unused fee, and to complain to the Office of Human Rights or sue. Before accepting the fee, also give your written eligibility criteria (financial, employment, criminal and rental history) and a statement that the applicant may show record errors or rehabilitation; this criminal-screening step does not apply to an owner who lives in a building with 3 or fewer rental units. Give the Rent Administrator's disclosure form when the application is filed. Refund the fee within 14 days if you do not screen, and charge only one fee for applications to your units within 30 days unless a new screening is needed.

title: Late Fees Cannot Be Taken From Rent Payments
bodyText:
District law sets no complete order for applying a tenant's payments, but one rule controls the most common question: you may not take a late fee out of a later rent payment. A payment made as rent must be applied to rent; an unpaid late fee is collected separately. After the grace period you may send an invoice giving the tenant 30 days to pay a lawful late fee, and if it is still unpaid you may deduct it from the security deposit at the end of the tenancy.

You may not charge interest on a late fee or evict for an unpaid late fee. This applies to every covered rental unit, month-to-month or fixed-term. Your written receipts must show any amount still owed for late charges, court costs or other charges beyond rent, including when the tenant pays by personal check.

Practical step: apply each payment to current or oldest rent first and track late fees on a separate invoice.

title: Asbestos: Licensed Abatement and Occupant Notice Rules
bodyText: The District has no asbestos disclosure rule for leases: no District statute or housing regulation requires you to tell applicants or tenants about asbestos-containing materials. What District law does regulate is removal. No business may abate asbestos or asbestos-containing material without a District permit and license, and every person working on an abatement project must be a licensed asbestos worker; removal of resilient floor coverings (sheet vinyl, tile and adhesives) done by manufacturers' work practices is exempt, with 10 days' written notice to the District for jobs over 18 square feet. The statute directed the Mayor to adopt rules protecting occupants of buildings affected by an abatement project, including notice and education of occupants at least 30 days before work begins, alternate accommodations and protection of belongings, and certification that units are safe to reoccupy. Those rules are in the District's environmental regulations, so check them before any project. Practical step: before renovating, or if a tenant reports damaged pipe insulation, ceiling or flooring material, have it assessed and use a licensed abatement contractor; plan tenant notice well ahead of the work.

title: Assigned Parking Spaces
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation deals with assigned parking spaces as such. Assigning a specific space and reserving the right to move the tenant to a comparable space is a matter for the lease. Three District rules frame it.

First, parking provided with the unit is a "related facility" under the Rental Housing Act. In a rent-stabilized unit, a substantial reduction in related facilities can lead the Rent Administrator to reduce the rent, a change in registered facilities must be reported, and you may not impose an unapproved mandatory charge for a facility.

Second, a tenant with a disability may ask for an accessible or closer space as a reasonable accommodation under the Human Rights Act.

Third, because a lease term may not be changed without the tenant's agreement, reassigning to a space that is not comparable, or taking the space away, is a change you may not make by notice. Applies to all District rental units; the rent-stabilization points apply only to rent-stabilized units.

Practical step: identify the space in the lease, keep any reassignment to a comparable space, and document accommodation requests.

title: Service and Assistance Animals in District Rentals
bodyText:
Two District laws apply, with different reach. Service animals (D.C. Code chapter 7-10): a person with a physical or mental disability who has a trained service animal is entitled to full and equal access to every rental housing accommodation in the District, may not be charged extra for the animal, and is liable for damage it does. An animal that serves only as a companion is not a service animal under this law.

To confirm eligibility you may ask only for a physician's or other licensed healthcare professional's verification that the person meets the definition, plus a showing of the link between the disability and what the animal does; you may not ask about the nature or severity of the disability or demand a description of it, and you must allow at least 30 days to produce documentation. This law has no small-landlord exemption and its text has no direct-threat exception.

Other assistance animals, including emotional-support animals: the Human Rights Act requires reasonable accommodations in rules and policies, such as a no-pets rule; it does not reach a tenancy that would be a direct threat or cause substantial damage, and it exempts some small owner-occupied buildings and certain single-family rentals.

Practical step: treat assistance animals as non-pets, charge no pet fees, and keep documentation requests within these limits.

title: Association Rules Bind Tenants Through the Lease; Antenna and Cable Access Rules
bodyText:
No District statute makes a condominium or homeowners association's rules binding on a tenant, requires the owner to deliver those rules at lease signing, or lets an association collect rent from a tenant. A lease term requiring the tenant to follow the association rules is how they become the tenant's obligation. Two District rules make that term worthwhile: the condominium instruments may have common expenses caused by occupants or their guests specially assessed against the owner's unit, and any failure to comply with lawful provisions of the instruments can support an association suit against an aggrieved person.

Antennas and satellite dishes: District cable law bars a landlord from interfering with cable installation (subject to reasonable conditions) or taking payment from a tenant or cable operator for cable access except as the cable office's compensation rules allow, and bars a cable operator from making agreements with a landlord that interfere with a tenant's right to choose satellite or other video service or use antenna equipment; the housing code bars antenna parts on fire escapes and sets an 8-foot roof clearance.

Federal rules on over-the-air antennas also apply. Practical step: attach the current association rules to the lease, have the tenant sign for them, and enforce a breach only through the 30-day notice to correct; passing fines to a tenant should be limited to fines the tenant's own violation caused.

title: No Lease Fee-Shifting to Tenants
bodyText: A District residential lease may not include a clause requiring the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees, whether written one-way or as a prevailing-party term; including or demanding one is prohibited, and a bad-faith violation exposes you to treble damages. Fees and costs can still be awarded by a court or agency where the law allows. In a landlord-and-tenant case the prevailing party is awarded taxable costs as a matter of course (filing fee, notary, postage, up to $10 per defendant for a special process server, and writ fees). Reasonable attorney's fees may be awarded to the prevailing party in actions under the Rental Housing Act, but not in eviction cases under the eviction statute. Other statutes give tenants fee awards in particular claims (for example mold violations and cable-access violations). There is no District rule requiring a reciprocal fee sentence, because the lease may not shift your fees to the tenant at all. Practical step: leave fee-shifting out of the lease and use the District default clause ("Default by Tenant" clause).

title: Automatic Renewal: 30-Day Tenant Notice Cap and Renewal-Disclosure Law
bodyText: Two District rules shape a lease clause that automatically renews a fixed term. First, the tenant's notice: a lease may not require more than 30 days' notice of the tenant's intent to leave at the end of the initial term unless it says that requirement ends with the initial term and that the tenant may then leave on 30 days' notice while month to month, and in any event may not require more than 30 days' notice to vacate unless you must give rent-increase notices at least 30 days longer than that period. An auto-renewal clause needing 60 or 90 days' objection runs into these limits. Second, the District's Automatic Renewal Protections Act requires a seller of goods or services under a contract that automatically renews at the end of a definite term to disclose the renewal and cancellation terms clearly and conspicuously, and, for a contract of 12 months or more renewing for a month or more, to send a renewal reminder 30 to 60 days before the cancellation deadline; a violation voids the renewal provision. Whether a residential lease is a sale of a service under that Act is not settled by its text. Practical step: keep any opt-out notice at 30 days, display renewal terms conspicuously, and send a reminder 30 to 60 days ahead.

title: Marijuana Rules in District Rentals
bodyText:
District law lets adults 21 and older possess up to 2 ounces of marijuana, and lets them grow up to 6 plants (3 mature) inside the house or rental unit that is their principal residence, with a household limit of 12 plants (6 mature). Selling it remains unlawful. That law expressly does not stop anyone who owns or controls real property from prohibiting or regulating the possession, use, display or growing of marijuana on or in that property, so a District lease may ban smoking, vaping, growing or possession of marijuana anywhere on the property, including inside the unit.

Medical cannabis may be administered at a qualifying patient's residence only "if permitted", and the medical cannabis law gives patients no housing protection against a lease restriction, so a lease ban can reach medical use too; a tenant with a disability may still ask for a reasonable accommodation, decided case by case. Lawful home use is not an "illegal act" eviction ground, so enforce a lease ban as an ordinary lease violation (written 30-day notice to correct).

Federal law, which still treats marijuana as illegal and matters for federally assisted housing, is outside this summary. Applies to all District rental units.

Practical step: use the optional marijuana clause if you want a ban, and apply it evenly.

title: Federal 30-Day Notice and District Notices
bodyText: The federal row explains the CARES Act 30-day notice to vacate for properties with a federally backed mortgage or in covered federal housing programs. Here is how it fits District notices. For nonpayment, District law requires a notice of intent to file, with prescribed wording and a rent ledger, delivered by tracked certified mail and by hand delivery or door posting at least 10 days before filing (and none if less than $600 is owed); the prescribed wording itself tells the tenant it has 30 days to pay. Whether that notice, which tells the tenant it may stay by paying, also counts as a federal notice to vacate is not settled, so on a covered property wait at least 30 days after the notice before filing. District notices for other grounds are already 30 days or longer (30 days to cure a lease violation, 30 days after a court finds an illegal act, 90 to 180 days for owner use, sale, renovation or demolition), except the 10-day notice for certain violent-crime cases, which on a covered property should be extended to 30 days. No District statute or court rule requires a CARES Act statement when filing.

title: No Professional Cleaning Charges or Deductions
bodyText: In the District you may not charge a tenant or former tenant a fee, or withhold any part of the security deposit, for professional cleaning, which includes professional carpet cleaning, or for other expenses caused by ordinary wear and tear. So a lease term authorizing a professional-cleaning charge or deposit deduction at move-out should not be used for District units, even if the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy. District law does not expressly address a term requiring the tenant to hire a cleaner directly, but because it would reach the same result and courts may void unconscionable lease provisions, we recommend against it. What you can do: tenants must keep the part of the premises they occupy clean and sanitary, and floor coverings must be kept clean; and you may deduct the actual, itemized cost of repairing damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, such as stains or burns caused by the tenant's negligence or abuse, if you follow the 45-day notice and itemization rules and keep photos or other documentation. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Casualty and Mitigation: What a Lease Can and Cannot Change
bodyText: Casualty: the District has no casualty statute for private residential leases, so there is no statutory casualty right to waive. Two rules still control and cannot be waived by the lease, because the housing regulations void any lease term contrary to their landlord-tenant chapter: a lease is void if the unit is unsafe or unsanitary from code violations at the start, or becomes so later from violations the tenant did not cause that you do not correct in time. And you cannot end a tenancy because of fire or other damage, since eviction is allowed only on the statutory grounds (renovation, demolition and similar routes need their own notices). A clause giving the landlord a casualty termination option is not lawful; any rent abatement should be written as a tenant benefit. Mitigation: if a tenant leaves early or refuses in bad faith to take possession, your damages are subject to your duty to mitigate. The statute does not say whether a lease can waive that duty, and the Rental Housing Act has no general anti-waiver section; the regulations' anti-waiver rule does not reach it. Whether a waiver would hold is for the courts. Do not include one; the District early-termination clause sets an agreed fee instead. A month-to-month tenant simply gives 30 days' notice.

title: Children and Occupancy: Notice of Limit, No Family Discrimination
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation requires a lease to address occupancy by children. What District law requires instead: tell each tenant in writing (in the lease or otherwise) the maximum number of occupants allowed in the unit under the housing regulations' floor-area standards, and do not discriminate against families with children.

The Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms, or advertise a preference because a person has children living with them, or because of familial status or family responsibilities. Occupancy limits stricter than 2 persons in an efficiency, or 2 per bedroom plus one in larger units, are presumed discriminatory against a family with children (rebuttable); District or federal maximum-occupancy rules still apply, and housing for older persons is excepted.

The Rental Housing Act separately bans discrimination against families with children when renting, with fines up to $5,000 per violation. These rules apply to every rental and do not differ between fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

Practical step: use the District occupancy clause ("Permitted Occupants and Maximum Occupancy" clause), set the limit from the floor-area standard, and never write a no-children or adults-only term unless the property qualifies as housing for older persons.

title: Collection Fees Need Express Lease Authority
bodyText:
Under the District's debt-collection law, rent or other money owed under a residential lease that is more than 30 days past due is a consumer debt, and a landlord collecting its own debt counts as a debt collector. You (or an agency) may not collect any interest, fee, charge or expense added to that debt unless the lease expressly authorizes it and it is legally chargeable, or a law authorizes it, and you may not pass on a collector's own fee unless the law or the lease provides for it. So a collection fee must be written into the lease.

The library's optional clause applies only to amounts still owed after move-out and caps the fee at what the agency actually charges and a percentage you state; keep that percentage modest and take advice, because no District statute or regulation says what percentage is reasonable. But a residential lease may not require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees; only a court can award those.

After move-out, send the written notice of unpaid amounts within 45 days and keep proof it was served for at least 60 days before you send any balance to a collector. The same law limits calls, texts and home visits and sets a 3-year deadline to sue on consumer debt.

title: Common-Area Lighting Is the Owner's Duty
bodyText: Hallways, stairways and other common space used by the occupants of more than one unit must have adequate lighting facilities kept in good condition at all times, and in a licensed housing business stairs and hallways must be lit from sunset to sunrise and whenever daylight falls below six foot-candles at floor level. Common space is your responsibility as owner, not a tenant's. District law has no rule, like some places have for small buildings, letting a lease make a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric service. Avoid that arrangement: since August 14, 2026 you may not charge tenants fees for services you must provide, including utility-related services, and beginning January 1, 2027 you may not separately charge tenants, other than through rent, for utility charges accrued by the building's common spaces. If existing wiring puts a hallway or entry light on a tenant's meter, rewire it or account for it in the rent. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Common-Area Rules and Tenant Organizing
bodyText:
A District lease may set reasonable rules for common areas, balconies, wall fastenings, heavy items such as waterbeds or pianos, candles, and signs visible from outside. No District statute or housing regulation protects a tenant's waterbed, clothesline, drying rack or flag display, or limits sign rules for private rentals. One District statute does limit common-area rules in multifamily buildings: tenants and tenant organizers have a protected right to organize, and the owner and its agents may not interfere with distributing literature in common areas and lobbies, placing literature at or under tenants' doors, posting information on building bulletin boards, or holding tenant meetings at reasonable times in community rooms, lobbies, other common areas or a tenant's unit, and may not attend or record those meetings without permission.

Canvassing rules depend on whether the building has a consistently enforced written policy against canvassing. A knowing violation can bring civil penalties of up to $10,000 (inflation-adjusted), damages, injunctions, license consequences and attorney's fees. The Human Rights Act's reasonable-accommodation duty also applies to common-area rules. Applies to all District rental units; the organizing rules apply to multifamily housing accommodations.

Practical step: write common-area rules so they do not reach tenant-organizing activity.

title: Placarded Units: Rent Suspended During Administrative Displacement
bodyText: No District statute expressly bars rent after a unit is condemned or ordered vacated, but the Rental Housing Act regulations do: for a covered unit, displacement of a tenant by administrative order due to unsafe premises suspends the tenant's obligation to pay rent, and the tenancy continues until the unit is offered back and the tenant waives that right (14 DCMR § 4300.19). Several other rules point the same way. The housing code director may placard a non-compliant unit as unfit for human habitation, and for apartments it becomes unlawful for you to permit, or anyone to continue, occupancy 30 days after placarding until the placard is removed. A placarding for life, health or safety violations does not end the tenancy: it continues until the unit is offered back to the tenant. Separately, a lease is void if the unit was unsafe or unsanitary from code violations at the start of the tenancy that you knew or should have known of, or becomes so later through violations the tenant did not cause that are not corrected in time. If a court appoints a tenant receiver for serious violations, you are barred from collecting rent during the receivership. If tenants must be relocated under a closure order caused by conditions within your control, you may have to reimburse the District's relocation costs. Practical step: stop billing for a placarded unit and offer it back once repaired. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Move-Out Inspection Notice; No Move-In Checklist Required
bodyText:
District law does not require a move-in inspection, inventory or condition checklist for private rentals, but it does regulate the move-out inspection. To decide how much of the deposit to return, you may inspect the unit within 3 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays) before or after the tenancy ends. If you do, you must notify the tenant in writing of the date and time, delivered to the tenant or at the unit at least 10 days before the inspection, and hold it at the time and place in the notice.

Since August 14, 2026, any claim for unpaid amounts after move-out, including damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, must be sent within 45 days with photographs or other documentation, so a dated move-in record with photos is the practical way to prove what changed. No fee or deposit deduction is allowed for ordinary wear and tear or professional cleaning. Housing Authority programs (for example converted public housing) require joint move-in and move-out inspections under their own rules.

title: Condo and Co-op Conversion Rules
bodyText: Converting an occupied District rental building to a condominium or cooperative is tightly controlled. You may not convert until the Mayor certifies compliance, and certification generally requires a tenant election in which more than half of the qualified heads of household approve (or no election is held within 60 days of your written request, which must go to every tenant and the Mayor and be posted in common areas). Coercing votes is prohibited. For a condominium, after registration is approved you must give each tenant at least 120 days' notice of conversion before any notice to vacate, and tenants get an exclusive 60-day right to contract to buy their unit on terms at least as good as the public's. For a cooperative, you must give 120 days' written notice of intent to convert and a bona fide offer of shares, with at least 60 days to contract. Low- and moderate-income elderly tenants and tenants with disabilities may stay as tenants after conversion. Tenants who leave get a relocation payment of $125 to $1,000. If a building is registered as or converting to a condominium or cooperative, the application-stage disclosure form must say so.

title: Written Notice Before Occupancy That a Unit Is in a Condominium or Cooperative
bodyText:
District law does not require a lease of a condominium, cooperative or homeowners-association unit to list the association's obligations or attach its documents. Three related rules apply. Condominium or cooperative notice before occupancy: when renting a unit in a building already converted to (or built as) a condominium or cooperative, give the tenant written notice, before the tenant moves in, that the unit is part of a condominium or cooperative. That notice (or the tenant's written waiver) is what lets the owner avoid having to comply anew with the District's conversion requirements.

Application disclosure: the Rent Administrator's disclosure form you give each applicant states whether the building is registered as, or converting to, a condominium or cooperative. Cooperative units: an owner registering a cooperative unit as a rental must show the cooperative association has authorized renting it.

Practical point: the condominium instruments can make the unit specially assessed for common expenses caused by occupants or their guests, so landlords commonly attach the association rules to the lease and make tenant compliance a lease term (see the association-rules entries).

title: Condominium Leasing Limits Spare Existing Tenancies; No Association Rent-Collection Statute
bodyText: Condominium associations: unless the condominium instruments prohibit it, a unit owners' association may reasonably restrict the leasing of residential units. A new restriction does not apply to a unit that is leased when the association acts until the owner later occupies the unit or ownership transfers, so an existing tenancy is protected. Condominium instruments entered into, amended or recorded after November 11, 2023 may not prohibit a licensed child development facility in a unit (the association may require insurance, retrofit costs and a share of jointly metered utilities). Cooperatives: an owner who registers a cooperative unit as a rental must file evidence that the cooperative association has authorized renting it. No District statute caps association lease-approval fees, regulates association deposits from tenants, limits what tenant information an association may require, or lets an association collect rent directly from a tenant when the owner is delinquent. Those questions turn on the recorded condominium or cooperative documents. For landlords: before leasing, check the instruments for leasing limits and approval steps, build approval into the timeline before the tenant moves in, and remember that once a tenant takes possession, the District's just-cause rules apply; failing association approval is not itself a ground to evict.

title: No Confession-of-Judgment Clauses
bodyText: A District residential lease may not contain a confession-of-judgment clause. The housing regulations forbid an owner to put in a lease or rental agreement any provision authorizing someone other than the tenant to confess judgment against the tenant, and forbid including such a term or demanding that a tenant sign a lease containing one. A bad-faith violation can make you liable to the tenant for treble damages. The court rules point the same way. A judgment for possession or money in a landlord-tenant case may rest on the tenant's own confession of liability before the court or a consent judgment, but not on a pre-signed authorization. In civil and small-claims cases, a judgment by confession or consent can be entered only after a complaint is filed, and where any party has no lawyer a judge must first hold a hearing to make sure the party understands the judgment. This applies to every residential tenancy, fixed-term or month-to-month. Practical step: leave confession-of-judgment and cognovit language out of the lease and any guaranty or payment-plan form given to a tenant; settle cases through a consent agreement entered by the court.

title: No District Rule on Double Letting, Detector Shielding or Application Fraud
bodyText: Three rules found in some other jurisdictions do not exist in District statutes, housing regulations or court rules. (1) No double-letting rule: nothing specifically bans renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; general contract, consumer-protection and fraud law apply. (2) No smoke-detector liability shield: District law makes the owner of each occupied dwelling unit responsible for installing smoke and carbon monoxide detectors under the construction codes, but nothing makes compliance or noncompliance inadmissible in an injury case or bars insurers from reducing payment because of it. Detector requirements beyond the duty to install sit in the District's construction codes (Title 12 of the municipal regulations). (3) No statutory right to end a tenancy for a false rental application: a misstatement can be acted on only as a violation of a substantial lease obligation, with a 30-day notice to correct or vacate served within 6 months of the violation (see the rental-application-accuracy row). Practical step: avoid overlapping lease commitments, install and maintain detectors under the construction codes, and keep application questions within District screening limits.

title: Receipts and Registration Required; No Squatter Fast Track
bodyText: Three things landlords ask about. (1) Rent receipts: present. You must give a written receipt for every payment of rent, deposit or other money unless the tenant pays by personal check, showing the exact amount, the date and the purpose, and any amounts still due for late charges, court costs or similar charges; even for a personal check, give a receipt if such charges remain due. (2) Registration and licensing before eviction: present. You cannot file a possession complaint without a valid rental registration or claim of exemption and a current rental housing business license, certified at filing (the court may waive the license for extenuating circumstances, and subtenant cases are excepted), and no writ of restitution issues without proof of a current license. Two business-registration laws can also block the case: an out-of-state corporation or limited liability company doing business in the District may not maintain an action until it registers with the Mayor (whether renting out property is doing business is a case-law question), and anyone doing business under a trade name may not maintain any suit in a District court until the trade name is properly registered (D.C. Code §§ 29-105.02(b) and 47-2855.03(d)). (3) Squatter or unauthorized-occupant remedy: absent. There is no special fast-track removal process; an occupant without right is removed through the ordinary Superior Court possession case, and unlawful entry is a misdemeanor (see the unauthorized-occupant row). Practical step: keep your registration and license current before any eviction filing, and give receipts for every non-check payment.

title: Construction Liens for Tenant Work
bodyText:
Under the District's mechanics' lien law, a contractor's lien attaches to a building improved or repaired at the direction of the owner or the owner's authorized agent, and only to the extent of that owner's interest. A lessee who contracts for work counts as an owner of a lesser estate, and when a building is erected or repaired by a lessee or tenant, the lien extends only to the tenant's own interest or estate, not to yours. No recorded lease or special notice is needed for that protection.

The risk is that a tenant is treated as your authorized agent, or that you direct the work yourself. A contractor must record a notice of intent during construction or within 90 days after the project ends and send you a copy by certified mail within 5 business days.

Practical step: if you consent to tenant work, say in writing that the tenant is not your agent and that your consent is not an agreement to pay; you may require the tenant to clear any lien, but the lease may not make the tenant pay your court costs or legal fees. These rules do not differ between fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Consumer Protection Procedures Act and Leasing
bodyText: The District's Consumer Protection Procedures Act covers leasing: its definitions of consumer and merchant include leasing, its goods and services include real estate transactions, and it speaks expressly of its application to landlord-tenant relations. The Attorney General may enforce it against landlords; the consumer protection agency may not use its administrative complaint process for landlord-tenant matters. A tenant (or a qualifying nonprofit or public-interest group) may sue in Superior Court for treble damages or $1,500 per violation, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, punitive damages and an injunction. Listed unfair practices that bear on leasing include: misrepresenting or leaving out a material fact; claiming a lease gives rights or remedies it does not, or that the law prohibits; failing to give the consumer a copy of a lease the consumer signs; making or enforcing unconscionable lease terms; and advertising a price that leaves out mandatory fees (other than government taxes or fees). Violating another District law in a consumer transaction is also a listed practice. The Act does not list leaving blank spaces at signing. How far courts apply the Act to residential tenancies is case law, not reviewed. Practical step: quote rent with all mandatory fees, deliver a signed copy, and keep lease terms within District law.

title: Illegal Acts: Court Finding First
bodyText:
In the District, criminal activity is a ground for eviction only through a court. You may recover possession after a court determines that the tenant, or someone occupying the unit, performed an illegal act within the unit or the building; you must then serve a 30-day notice to vacate. If the person was an occupant rather than the tenant, the tenant can be evicted only if the tenant knew or should have known of the illegal act.

For cases filed after December 31, 2025 involving a dangerous crime or crime of violence (not self-defense), you must first consider in good faith alternatives that keep non-offending occupants housed, such as barring the offender or transferring the lease, then serve a 10-day notice; the court holds an expedited hearing. A District regulation adopted before the 10-day rule still bars filing until 30 days after an illegal-act notice, so the cautious course is to wait 30 days before filing.

A tenant who is the victim of an intrafamily offense that is the basis of the notice has a defense, and the court may not enter judgment if the tenant has a protective order ordering the abuser out. Drug-haven cases follow a separate expedited statute. No District law requires you to evict for crime, and a lease clause cannot let you end the tenancy without a court. Use the optional District illegal-act clause ("Illegal Acts" clause).

title: Criminal Record Screening: Conditional Offer First
bodyText: The Fair Criminal Record Screening for Housing law governs criminal history for every housing provider except an owner who lives in a building with 3 or fewer rental units, and except where other law requires or allows criminal-history denials. Before accepting an application fee, give written eligibility criteria and a statement that the applicant may show inaccuracies or rehabilitation. You may never ask about or consider an arrest that did not lead to a conviction. Before a conditional offer you may not ask about pending charges or convictions (you may collect signed authorizations). After a conditional offer you may consider only pending charges or convictions within the past 7 years for listed serious offenses. You may withdraw the offer only if, on balance, withdrawal serves a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, weighing the statutory factors (offense severity, age then, time elapsed, rehabilitation, risk to others, link to rented property). Give written reasons and notice of the right to complain to the Office of Human Rights; on a request within 20 days, provide the records relied on free within 10 days. Never ask about minors' records. The remedy is an OHR complaint (fines up to $5,000 by portfolio size), and you are immune from claims based on knowledge gained through a lawful inquiry once the applicant becomes a tenant.

title: Eviction Grounds and the 30-Day Cure
bodyText:
The District has a closed list of eviction grounds, and the end of the lease term is not one of them: a tenant who keeps paying rent cannot be evicted except on a listed ground after the required written notice. Two tracks matter most. For nonpayment, you give a prescribed notice of intent to file at least 10 days before filing (no filing at all for less than $600), and the tenant can avoid eviction by paying; a late fee alone is never a ground.

For any other violation of a tenancy obligation, you must give written notice and the tenant has 30 days after receiving it to correct the violation; only an uncorrected violation supports a case. Other grounds are a court-determined illegal act (30-day notice, or a 10-day notice for certain violent crimes, though a regulation still says to wait 30 days before filing), personal use by a natural-person owner or a sale for a buyer's personal use (90 days), and approved renovation, rehabilitation, demolition, discontinuance or conversion (120 to 180 days).

Notices other than for nonpayment go to both the tenant and the Rent Administrator; posted notices need a timestamped photo, and a notice must be in a covered non-English language you know the tenant speaks. Use the District default clause ("Default by Tenant" clause).

title: Tenant Default: Court Process Only
bodyText:
A tenant default in the District does not let you end the tenancy or retake the unit yourself. You may recover possession only on a ground District law allows, after the written notice and cure time it requires, and only through the Superior Court. For unpaid rent, give the prescribed notice of intent to file at least 10 days before filing (none for less than $600); even after a judgment for possession, the tenant can usually redeem the tenancy by paying the amount the court states, and you must file the court's notice of the payment needed within 7 days.

For other violations, the tenant gets 30 days after written notice to correct. The lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney's fees or court costs (only a court can award them), may not waive a jury trial or allow confession of judgment, and nonpayment of a late fee is never grounds for eviction. If the tenant leaves early, your damages are limited to actual damages subject to your duty to mitigate. Use the District default clause ("Default by Tenant" clause).

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds Go to the District
bodyText: If you cannot return a security deposit refund because the former tenant cannot be found or never cashes the check, the money does not become yours. Under the District's Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, you are the holder of the unclaimed refund. The Act does not list deposit refunds by name, so they fall under the general rule (or, for a landlord that is a business association, the rule for a debt of a business association): presumed abandoned 3 years after the obligation to pay arises. Before reporting, if you have a usable address and the refund is $50 or more, mail the former tenant a notice by first-class mail 60 to 180 days before the report (and by email too if the tenant agreed to email). Then report the property to the Administrator before November 1 for the 12 months ending the prior July 1, and pay it over. A dormancy charge may be deducted only if a valid contract authorizes it and you regularly impose it, and only in a reasonable amount. A lease term letting you keep an unclaimed refund is not supported by District law. Keep proof of your refund attempts.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: The District's security deposit rules cannot be waived in a lease. They sit in chapter 3 of the housing regulations, and any lease or agreement provision contrary to that chapter, or providing for a waiver of it, is void and unenforceable. You also may not put such a provision in a lease or demand that anyone sign a lease containing one, and a housing provider found to have violated that ban in bad faith is liable to the tenant for treble damages. So clauses that raise the cap above one month's rent, skip the escrow account, waive interest, extend the 45-day and 30-day return deadlines, allow deductions for ordinary wear and tear or professional cleaning, or make the deposit nonrefundable have no effect. The statutory ban on withholding for ordinary wear and tear applies regardless of the lease as well. This applies to month-to-month and fixed-term leases alike.

title: Refund Does Not Depend on a Forwarding Address
bodyText:
District law does not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving a forwarding address, a notice of surrender or a demand. The duty runs the other way. When the tenancy ends, you must ask the tenant for a forwarding mailing address or email address. Within 45 days after the tenancy ends you must, without any demand, either pay back the deposit with any interest due, or notify the tenant in writing, personally or by certified mail to the last known address, that you intend to withhold.

If you fail to do one or the other, that is prima facie evidence the tenant is entitled to the full deposit and interest. If you make a good-faith effort but cannot serve the tenant personally or by certified mail, that alone is not a failure to comply. Within the same 45 days, send any notice of unpaid amounts personally, by email or by certified mail to the forwarding address. A lease clause conditioning the refund on a forwarding address or surrender notice would conflict with these rules.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: The District's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful discrimination to refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, and to refuse a tenant with a disability permission to make reasonable modifications of the premises at the tenant's own expense. Where reasonable, you may condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at move-out, reasonable wear and tear excepted. District law does not require that restoration condition to appear in the lease, and it has no rule on an interest-bearing account for restoration funds. Disability is also a protected trait for every term and condition of a rental, and in screening you may not base a denial on an alleged lease breach related to an applicant's or household member's disability. The Act does not reach some small owner-occupied buildings and certain single-family rentals by owners of three or fewer homes. The District's own regulation on accommodation requests to the housing-code agency concerns its rules, not yours. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Drug, Firearm and Prostitution Nuisance Abatement and Drug-Haven Evictions
bodyText: Two District statutes reach rental property used for illegal drug activity. First, the U.S. Attorney, the District, or a neighborhood community group (supported by an affidavit of someone living or owning property within 3,000 feet) may sue the owner to abate a drug-, firearm- or prostitution-related nuisance. After a reasonable attempt to notify the owner at least 14 days before filing, the owner is presumed to know of the nuisance. The court can order repairs, locks, lighting, security or camera surveillance, put all rent into a court escrow for up to 90 days or into the hands of a trustee, order the property vacated, sealed or demolished, award fees, and impose damages for each day the nuisance continued after notice. Second, a housing provider (or the Mayor) may bring a fast possession case against a tenant or occupant of a rental unit that is a drug haven, outside the normal just-cause notice rules; affected tenants and resident associations can start one by petition to the Mayor. The court may order eviction within 72 hours or closure of the unit, but not against a tenant who shows the activity could not reasonably have been known, was not a pattern, or was reported to police. Practical step: respond promptly to any nuisance notice and document what you do to stop the activity.

title: What You May Collect Before and at Signing
bodyText:
Until the lease is signed, the only charge you may collect is the application fee, plus a holding deposit (never from an applicant using a government housing voucher); a holding deposit becomes part of the first month's rent or the security deposit. At signing, District law does not cap how much rent may be collected, but it does cap security: every deposit or other payment held as security for the tenant's performance, together, may not exceed the first full month's rent and may be charged only once.

A pet deposit or a prepayment you hold as security (for example a so-called last month's rent you would keep against damage) counts toward that one-month cap. You may not charge any fee, at signing or later, for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable, and in a rent-stabilized unit no mandatory fee for an unapproved service or facility. Write the deposit's terms in the lease or on the receipt, and give a written receipt for every payment not made by personal check.

title: Domestic Violence Information: Address Confidentiality and Screening Limits
bodyText: District law has no landlord-specific rule requiring you to keep a tenant's domestic-violence documentation confidential, and no rule on how you store the protective order or third-party statement a tenant gives you to end a lease early or get locks changed. Two District rules still limit what you do with that information. First, the Address Confidentiality Program: a crime victim certified in the program uses a substitute address with District agencies, and no person may intentionally obtain a participant's actual address from a District agency, or disclose it, knowing the person is a participant, unless the law requires it; the civil fine is up to $10,000. The program does not oblige a private landlord to accept the substitute address on a lease. Second, in screening you may not ask about or rely on a lease-breach allegation that stemmed from an incident the applicant shows may be a domestic-violence defense, including protection-order records, and the Human Rights Act bars treating someone worse because they are a victim of an intrafamily offense. Housing Authority public housing follows federal VAWA confidentiality rules. Practical step: keep any DV documentation in a restricted file, share it only as needed to act on the request, and never disclose a known program participant's address.

title: Domestic-Violence Release: Normal Deposit Deadlines
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of an intrafamily offense (or the parent or guardian of a minor victim) may be released from the lease by giving written notice with a copy of a civil protection order or documentation signed by a qualified third party, within 90 days of the reported incident. The release takes effect 14 days after you receive the notice and documentation, or earlier if a new tenancy begins, and the tenant owes rent only prorated to the earlier of re-renting or 14 days after the request. District law does not create a special deposit timeline for these releases: the release law expressly leaves the ordinary security deposit rules unchanged, and it also leaves in place the tenant's liability for rent or other sums already owed before the release. So the usual deadlines apply from the end of the tenancy: return the deposit with interest due, or send a written notice of intent to withhold, within 45 days, then refund the balance with an itemized statement within 30 days of that notice. District law does not tie the deposit clock to other occupants leaving.

title: Eviction Protections for Abuse Victims
bodyText: District law protects tenants who are victims of intrafamily offenses (crimes against an intimate partner, family member or household member) from losing their housing because of the abuse. In an eviction for a lease violation or an illegal act, it is a defense that the tenant, or a minor in the tenant's care, is the victim and the offense is the basis for the notice to vacate; if the tenant has a protective order ordering the abuser out, the court may not enter judgment, and with a recent police report or a pending order request the court may decline to. The Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to refuse, end or change a tenancy because someone is, or has a record of being, such a victim, to refuse reasonable security accommodations (which the tenant may be charged for), to refuse an early lease release under the District's domestic-violence release law, or to bar or penalize calling police or emergency help (a right that cannot be waived). In screening, you may not consider lease-breach allegations that stem from such an incident. Victims can also require a lock change and an early lease release (see those rows).

title: Intrafamily-Offense Citations Current; Two Stale Cross-References
bodyText: The District's intrafamily-offense (domestic violence) protections for tenants rest on cross-references that are still current: the definition of an intrafamily offense in the intrafamily-proceedings chapter of Title 16 (an offense against an intimate partner, family member or household member, including certain animal cruelty), and civil protection orders issued under that chapter's hearing section. A tenant can use either a copy of such a protection order or documentation signed by a qualified third party to be released from a lease or to raise a defense in an eviction: a Metropolitan Police officer, a sworn officer of the District Housing Authority police, a licensed health professional, or a domestic violence counselor as defined in the District's counselor-confidentiality statute. Two cross-references are out of date. The Human Rights Act's definition of a record for intrafamily-offense discrimination points to the wrong paragraph of the police-definitions section (it now cites the definition of a kinship caregiver rather than a law enforcement officer), and the housing regulation listing what an illegal-act notice to vacate must say refers to a nonexistent section number. Neither changes what you must do. Practical step: accept a protection order or qualified third-party documentation as described and do not demand more; use current forms and notices.

title: Early Lease Release for Abuse Victims
bodyText:
A tenant who is the victim of an intrafamily offense (or the parent or guardian of a minor victim) may end the lease early. The tenant gives you written notice plus either a copy of a civil protection order issued on the tenant's petition, or documentation signed by a qualified third party (a police officer, a Housing Authority public-safety officer, a health professional or a domestic violence counselor) showing the tenant reported the offense.

The request must come within 90 days of the reported incident. The release takes effect 14 days after you receive the notice and documentation, or earlier if a new tenancy for the unit begins. Whatever the lease says about penalties, the tenant owes rent only up to the earlier of the date you re-rent the unit or 14 days after the request, plus any rent or other sums already owed.

Security-deposit rules apply as usual. The statute releases the requesting tenant; it does not say whether co-tenants are also released, so treat their obligations under the lease and general law. Refusing a lawful release is also a Human Rights Act violation. The District early-termination clause does not override this right.

title: Lock Change for Intrafamily Offense Victims
bodyText: If a tenant who is the victim of an intrafamily offense (a crime against an intimate partner, family member or household member) asks in writing, you must change the locks on every entrance door to the tenant's unit within 5 business days. If the offender is not, or is no longer, a tenant of the same unit, you may not ask for any proof. If the offender is a co-tenant in the same unit, the requesting tenant must give you a copy of a civil protection order directing the offender to stay away from the tenant, another household member or the unit. You pay for the lock change first. The lock-change statute lets you recover the cost (plus any fee no higher than you charge other tenants for lock changes) within 45 days after you give the tenant documentation, but since August 14, 2026 the District's ban on fees for services you must provide names locks, and whether it now bars this reimbursement is unsettled; the District keys clause ("Keys and Locks" clause) waives it, so the cautious course is not to charge. Once you receive the court order, do not give the offender keys or access unless the court allows it; you are not liable to the offender for complying, and the offender stays liable under the lease. These rules apply to all covered rental units, whatever the lease says, and the keys clause ("Keys and Locks" clause) addresses them.

title: Documents Abuse Victims Must Provide
bodyText: What a victim of an intrafamily offense must give you depends on the right being used. Early lease release: written notice plus either a copy of a civil protection order (or other order under the District's intrafamily-offense law) issued on the tenant's petition, or documentation signed by a qualified third party acting officially, meaning a sworn Metropolitan Police officer, a sworn Housing Authority public-safety officer, a District-licensed health professional or a trained domestic violence counselor, showing the tenant reported the offense. Lock change: a written request only; you may ask for a protective order (stay-away or vacate order against the offender) only if the offender is a tenant of the same unit, and otherwise may require no documentation at all. Eviction defense: a temporary or civil protection order ordering the abuser to vacate bars judgment; a police report written within the preceding 60 days, or a pending request for such an order, lets the court decline judgment. Do not demand more than the statute requires, and keep the documents confidential. Basing housing decisions on a person's record of being a victim is unlawful discrimination.

title: Early Termination by the Tenant
bodyText:
District law gives tenants no general right to end a fixed-term lease early, with one statutory exception: a victim of an intrafamily offense may obtain an early release on notice and documentation, owing at most rent up to 14 days after the request (see the domestic-violence lease release row). Federal law may give servicemembers a separate right.

If a tenant simply leaves early, you may recover only actual damages, subject to your duty to mitigate by trying to re-rent. A lease may offer an optional early-termination right for a fee, as the District clause does, but the fee should be a reasonable, clearly optional price for ending liability early, not a penalty on top of full rent; courts may refuse to enforce unconscionable terms.

Notice rules also limit how much notice you can demand: no more than 30 days to vacate at the end of the initial term unless the lease includes the statutory month-to-month statement, and month-to-month tenants end by 30 days' written notice expiring on the first of a month. Remember that you, the landlord, cannot end the tenancy early except on a District eviction ground through the court.

title: Electronic Leases and Signatures Valid With Consent; Notice Methods Still Control
bodyText:
The District has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. When both parties have agreed to do business electronically, a lease or other record may not be denied legal effect just because it is electronic, an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature. Agreement can be shown by the parties' conduct.

The District's version excludes only wills and testamentary trusts and most of the Uniform Commercial Code; unlike some jurisdictions, it does not exclude eviction, default or cure notices. Two limits matter. An electronic record satisfies a duty to deliver information in writing only if the tenant can save or print it, and a record you block from being saved or printed is not enforceable against the tenant. And where another law requires a notice to be sent by a specific method (such as certified mail and posting for a nonpayment notice, or a paper copy of an entry notice when the tenant does not acknowledge an electronic one), that method still controls.

Practical step: get each tenant's written consent to electronic signing and delivery, give a downloadable copy of every signed document, and keep using the statutory delivery methods for eviction and other prescribed notices.

title: Right to Call Police or Emergency Help (Intrafamily-Offense Victims)
bodyText: The District protects the right to call police or emergency help in one setting: where a person living in the unit, or intending to live there, is (or has a record of being) a victim of an intrafamily offense (domestic, dating or family violence). As to that person, it is unlawful under the Human Rights Act to bar or limit the right to call for police or emergency assistance, or to impose any penalty for making such a call, and the statute says that right cannot be waived. The District has no broader statute giving every tenant a non-waivable right to summon police or emergency services or voiding all lease terms that penalize such calls. Even so, because you cannot know in advance which tenant or guest may be a victim, and because eviction for criminal activity requires a court finding and the statutory notice, lease terms that count 911 or police calls against a tenant, charge fees for them, or treat them as a lease violation are risky for every tenancy. Practical step: do not use nuisance-call or crime-free clauses that penalize calls for help; address actual criminal conduct through the District illegal-act route (see the law-enforcement-cooperation and criminal-activity rows).

title: Eminent Domain: Court Sets Possession and Rent
bodyText: District law has no landlord-tenant statute saying whether a lease ends, or rent stops, when the rented property is taken by eminent domain. The condemnation statutes leave it to the court: once the District (or the United States) files a declaration of taking and deposits estimated compensation, title passes, and the court may fix when and on what terms the people in possession must surrender it and may make just and equitable orders about rents and other charges. Compensation is paid to the persons entitled to it, with the court deciding how the deposit is distributed among those with interests in the property. A transfer by eminent domain, or under threat of it, is excluded from the tenant opportunity-to-purchase rules. Because the statute is silent on the lease itself, an express condemnation clause (for example, that the lease ends on the taking date and rent is prorated, with each party keeping its own claim to the award) is a matter of contract. Practical step: if a taking is threatened, tell tenants promptly and follow the court's possession and rent orders.

title: Energy Benchmarking and Tenant Utility-Data Consent
bodyText:
Owners of privately owned buildings must benchmark the building's energy performance every year using the ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager tool and report it to the District; the benchmarking rule has been phased in down to buildings of 10,000 square feet of gross floor area or more since January 1, 2025 (the section's general scope line still says 50,000 square feet, so owners of buildings between 10,000 and 50,000 square feet should assume the duty applies).

Where residential tenants pay their own utilities, getting their usage data is limited by District utility-privacy law: unless the customer consents in writing, the electric company or an electricity supplier may not disclose information about a customer that the customer supplied, and natural gas suppliers face the same limit through their licensing rules. Two exceptions help owners. Disclosures to a building owner about the energy use of a non-residential tenant are allowed. And aggregated consumption data may be released to the building owner if at least 5 accounts are combined and no single account is more than 80% of the total; for electricity, customer-identifying information may be included only if the owner requesting the data supplied it.

Beyond that, a residential tenant's written consent, which may be given in the lease, allows release. Practical step: if you must benchmark a large building and aggregated data is not enough, include the optional District energy-data consent clause and use the data only for benchmarking.

title: Entity Landlords Need a D.C. Lawyer in Court
bodyText: If your rental is owned by a corporation or partnership, it must appear in the Superior Court's Landlord and Tenant Branch through a member in good standing of the District of Columbia Bar; a property manager or other non-lawyer may not file or try the eviction case for it, beyond securing a continuance. The same is true when such an entity sues as plaintiff in Small Claims (for example, for unpaid rent or damages after move-out). An individual owner may represent himself or herself. The court rules name corporations and partnerships; they do not mention limited liability companies by name. Treat an LLC like a corporation and use a lawyer. Practical step: if you hold property through an entity, retain District counsel before filing any landlord-tenant or small-claims case.

title: Tenant EV Charging: Enacted but Not in Effect
bodyText: No District law now in force gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger, and none bars a lease from prohibiting one. A tenant's installation is an alteration that needs your consent, and you may agree to it on your own terms. Watch item: the Council enacted a tenant charging right in the Comprehensive Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Access, Readiness, and Sustainability Amendment Act of 2024, but it applies only after funding, which has not occurred (the Code section reads "Not Funded"). Once in effect, it would override contrary lease terms and require you to allow a tenant to install a charger at the tenant's expense with your written approval, subject to safety, registration, aesthetic and licensed-electrician conditions and proof of insurance; you could charge only for actual electricity and, in shared areas, a reasonable space-reservation fee, and you would have to adopt installation and removal procedures. Willful violations would draw fines of up to $1,000 per 30 days. In force now: new or substantially improved multi-unit buildings with 3 or more off-street spaces (permits after January 1, 2022) must be built charger-ready for at least 20% of spaces. Practical step: handle charger requests by written agreement and monitor funding of the 2024 Act.

title: EV Make-Ready Building Requirements
bodyText: One District charging-infrastructure rule is in force, and it is a building rule, not a lease rule: for building permits issued after January 1, 2022, new construction or substantial improvement of a multi-unit (or commercial) building with 3 or more off-street parking spaces must include electric vehicle make-ready infrastructure for at least 20% of the spaces, under technical rules the Mayor issues, with a hardship waiver. The 2024 electric vehicle act would tighten this (for multi-unit buildings with 6 or more spaces, at least 25% of spaces EV-ready for permits after January 1, 2027, rising to 29% after 2031 and 33% after 2034, with "EV-READY" labels), add EV-ready rules for new single-family homes, and give tenants charging rights. Those amendments apply only after funding, which has not occurred. No District statute, housing regulation or court rule requires a landlord to provide chargers to tenants in an existing building or sets standards for tenant-installed equipment beyond ordinary electrical permitting. Practical step: if you are building or substantially improving, confirm the make-ready requirement with the permit reviewer; otherwise treat chargers as an optional amenity and handle tenant installations by written agreement.

title: Weather, Assistance and Court Stays
bodyText: District law and court rules give tenants several ways to delay an eviction. Weather: no eviction may be carried out on a day the National Weather Service predicts at 8 a.m. a temperature below 32 degrees F or above 95 degrees F at National Airport, or while precipitation is falling at the unit (except after a court finding of an illegal act, undue hardship to neighbors, or abandonment). Rental assistance: in a nonpayment case the court may stay the case once while an Emergency Rental Assistance application is pending; if the tenant tells you at least 48 hours before the scheduled eviction that an approved application will pay the full redemption amount, you must cancel the eviction and may not reschedule it sooner than 3 weeks later. Failing for more than 45 days to give an assistance provider requested payment information can lead the court to waive that rent. Notice failures: missing the 21-day pre-eviction notice can lead to an injunction staying the eviction. Court stays: a tenant may ask the court to stay execution of the writ; if the writ is executable the court may stay it up to 3 business days pending a hearing. A tenant who pays the full redemption amount before the eviction keeps the tenancy.

title: Eviction Process Step by Step
bodyText: District evictions run only through the Superior Court's Landlord and Tenant Branch. 1. Notice: serve the written notice the eviction statute requires for your ground (nonpayment: prescribed notice at least 10 days before filing; most other grounds: a notice also sent to the Rent Administrator). 2. Filing: you may not file for nonpayment under $600, and you must certify a valid rental registration or claim of exemption and a current rental housing license (the court may waive the license in extenuating circumstances). 3. Service: the summons, in English and Spanish, must be served at least 14 days before the initial hearing; if posted, mail a copy within 3 days and file a timestamped photo. 4. Hearing: bring rent ledgers back to the last zero balance to every hearing; the court may order rent paid into its registry. 5. Judgment and redemption: in nonpayment cases the tenant can usually pay the stated amount and keep the tenancy. 6. Eviction: show your license to get the writ, give the tenant the 21-day final notice, and have the Marshals execute it (not in extreme weather), then follow the 7-day property rules. Self-help lockouts are never allowed.

title: Eviction Record Sealing and Screening
bodyText: The Superior Court seals District eviction case records automatically: 30 days after the case ends if you did not obtain a judgment for possession, and 3 years after the case ends if you did. A tenant can also move to seal at any time, and the court must seal if the tenant shows, for example, that the case was over $600 or less, the tenant was in a subsidized housing program, the filing was retaliatory or discriminatory, you failed to abate housing-code violations in the unit, the case stemmed from domestic violence, or a settlement did not give you possession. Landlords have no statutory right to object to automatic sealing.
