For screening: you may not ask about, or base a decision on, an eviction case that did not end in a judgment for you or that was filed 3 or more years ago; a sealed eviction record is a protected trait under the Human Rights Act; and if you intentionally deny an applicant, or offer worse terms, based on a record you know is sealed, the applicant can sue within a year for fees, damages and equitable relief. Practical step: tell screening vendors to exclude sealed and older eviction records.

title: No Clauses Excusing the Owner From Its Own Negligence
bodyText: A District residential lease may not exempt you from, or limit, your liability for injury to people or damage to property caused by your own negligence (or that of your agents, employees or servants) in operating, caring for or maintaining the leased unit or any part of the property. The housing regulations forbid placing such a provision in a lease, forbid demanding that a tenant sign one, and make any lease term that waives the landlord-tenant chapter of the regulations void. A bad-faith violation can make you liable to the tenant for treble damages. The rule is aimed at your own negligence. It does not stop a lease from making the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household or guests cause, or from requiring renters insurance where otherwise lawful. No District statute separately addresses tenant indemnification or hold-harmless clauses; a broad clause that makes the tenant indemnify you for your own negligence would collide with this rule, and courts may also refuse to enforce unconscionable terms. This applies to every residential tenancy. Practical step: limit any release or indemnity to losses caused by the tenant's side, and add an express carve-out for your own negligence.

title: Exempt Units Need Pre-Lease Notice That Rent Increases Are Unregulated
bodyText: District law has no rule requiring every lease or renewal to say whether the unit is covered by just-cause eviction protection; nearly every rental unit is covered, whether or not it is rent-stabilized, so there is no coverage line to disclose. District law does require coverage notices about rent stabilization: Exempt units: before a lease is signed, a prospective tenant of a unit exempt from rent stabilization (for example, buildings permitted after 1975, qualifying small-owner properties with a claim of exemption on file, or subsidized units) must receive written notice that rent increases for the unit are not regulated by the rent stabilization program. Housing Finance Agency-assisted projects have a similar pre-lease notice. All covered units: the disclosure form given at application gives the building's rent-controlled or exempt status, its business license and registration or claim of exemption, and includes the Tenant Advocate's Tenant Bill of Rights, which explains just-cause eviction. Practical step: put the exempt-unit statement in writing before signing (a lease clause signed before occupancy works) and keep the signed application disclosures. Any later notice to vacate must give a lawful ground under District law.

title: Rent When a Rent-Stabilization Exemption Ends
bodyText: If your unit was exempt from rent stabilization because it was subsidized, because it is in a cooperative, or because you were a small owner with a filed claim of exemption, and the exemption ends (for example the subsidy ends, or the owners come to hold other District rental units), the unit comes under rent stabilization and its rent is capped. For a formerly subsidized or cooperative unit, an occupied unit's rent may not exceed the rent charged when the unit became exempt plus each later general adjustment; a vacant unit may go to 110% of that figure, or to the rent of a substantially identical unit in the building but no more than 30% above it. If you cannot prove the rent charged when the exemption began (a stamped copy of the original filing), the cap is the lowest of the last rent on file plus later adjustments, HUD's Small Area Fair Market Rent for the unit, or the average rent of the last 6 months of the exemption. For a former small-owner unit the cap is 105% of the average rent charged during the last 6 months of the exemption. Within 30 days after the event that ends any exemption, file a Registration/Claim of Exemption Form with the Rent Administrator stating the lawful rent. Any increase still needs the 60-day notice and the usual rent-stabilization procedure. Practical step: keep a stamped copy of every exemption filing and a record of the rent charged when it was filed.

title: Condition of the Unit at Move-In
bodyText:
District law does not require a move-in inspection or a signed condition checklist, but it makes the unit's condition at the start of the tenancy your responsibility. Every lease carries an implied warranty that you will keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations. If the unit or common space is unsafe or unsanitary at the beginning of the tenancy because of housing-code violations you knew or reasonably should have known about, the lease is void.

At application you must give the disclosure form with copies of housing and property-maintenance code violation reports issued for the building or unit in the last 12 months (or older ones not yet abated) and information about indoor mold contamination in the past three years unless professionally remediated; pre-1978 units also need the lead disclosure.

A tenant's signed acknowledgment that the unit is in good condition is useful evidence, but it cannot waive the implied warranty or the housing regulations; lease terms that do so are void and may not be included.

Practical step: do a dated, photographed walk-through signed by both sides, fix code issues before move-in, and keep the record for the deposit return. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Expedited Eviction for Violent Crime and Drug Havens
bodyText:
The District has two faster tracks for crime-related evictions, both through the court. Violent crime: in cases filed after December 31, 2025 where the illegal act would be a dangerous crime or crime of violence (not self-defense), you must first consider in good faith ways to keep non-offending occupants housed, such as barring the offender or transferring the lease, then serve a 10-day notice to vacate (a District regulation adopted before the 10-day rule still bars filing until 30 days after the notice, so the cautious course is to wait 30 days before filing); the court holds an expedited hearing within 20 days of filing, and if it finds the crime proved it must enter judgment and order the eviction.

Tenants who did not know, took reasonable steps to prevent the crime, or were victims have defenses. Drug havens: you, the Mayor, the U.S. Attorney, or a civic or community association (and tenants, after review by the Mayor) can sue to evict from a unit used to store, make, use or sell illegal drugs, with at least 5 days' notice before a hearing. A preliminary injunction is available; the full hearing follows within 10 business days, and an order can require eviction within 72 hours or closure of the unit, executed within 5 business days. A tenant who could not reasonably have known, or who reported the activity to police, may avoid eviction.

title: District Fair Housing: Protected Traits and Enforcement
bodyText: The District's Human Rights Act goes well beyond federal fair housing law. In any rental transaction you may not refuse, end, set different terms, restrict services or repairs, or advertise a preference based on actual or perceived race, color, religion, national origin, sex, age, marital status, personal appearance, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, familial status, family responsibilities, disability, matriculation (being a student), political affiliation, source of income (including housing vouchers), a sealed eviction record, status as a victim of an intrafamily offense, place of residence or business, or homeless status. Discrimination against families with children, including occupancy limits stricter than 2 per bedroom plus one, is presumed unlawful. Voucher holders get extra screening protections, and you must make reasonable accommodations and allow reasonable modifications for disability. The business-necessity defense does not apply to residential rentals. Complaints go to the Office of Human Rights within 1 year, or to court within 2 years. In a housing case, either the complainant or the respondent landlord may elect to have the case decided in a civil action, which the Attorney General then files. Practical step: use written, uniform screening criteria and train anyone who shows units or answers inquiries.

title: Fair Housing Exemptions: Owner-Occupied Buildings and Single-Family Homes
bodyText: The Human Rights Act has two rental exemptions, and they work differently. Owner-occupied small buildings: the Act does not apply to renting units in a building where you or your family live in one unit and the building has, or will have, units for no more than two families living independently, or for no more than four families where the tenant would share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner-occupant. This exemption takes the rental outside the whole Act, including its advertising ban, though federal fair housing advertising rules still apply. Single-family homes: the Act does not apply to renting a single-family home by an owner who owns no more than 3 such homes, but only if no broker, agent or other rental professional is used and no discriminatory advertisement is published, posted or mailed. Here the advertising ban survives. The same exemptions cover source of income; neither statute gives voucher holders separate exemption rules. The Rental Housing Act's own ban on discriminating against families with children, elderly tenants and families receiving tenant assistance has no owner-occupancy exemption, and the exemptions never permit a rental that another law prohibits. Religious organizations and private clubs have narrow non-commercial exceptions. Practical step: do not rely on an exemption when using a property manager or listing service.

title: Fee Disclosure and All-In Pricing
bodyText: District law requires fee disclosure at three points. First, before you request any information or fee from an applicant, give or post a written notice of the amount and purpose of every fee and deposit, mandatory or optional, that may be charged, when it is charged, and whether and when it is refundable. Second, when the application is filed, give the Rent Administrator's disclosure form, which includes the rent, any rent surcharges, any nonrefundable application fee, and the deposit amount, interest rate and return method. Third, under the consumer protection law, any price you advertise, display or offer must include all mandatory fees and charges except government taxes or fees; quoting a base rent and adding required fees later risks a violation. In a rent-stabilized unit, no mandatory fee may be charged for any service or facility that has not been approved, so required charges belong in the approved rent. District law does not require a fee schedule on the lease's first page. Practical step: quote one all-in monthly figure for every non-optional charge and keep the screening notice and disclosure form current.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: District law has no single rule worded as a ban on fees for services not provided, but several rules reach the same result. For every covered unit, you may not charge any fee for services you are already required to provide to keep the unit habitable, including utilities, trash, locks and third-party billing administration. Under the consumer protection law it is an unfair practice to offer a service you do not intend to provide as offered, or to represent that something was supplied as promised when it was not. In a rent-stabilized unit, any service or facility carrying a mandatory fee must be approved by the Rent Administrator and is then treated as a related service that you may not reduce or eliminate without approval; if a related service lapses through accident or neglect and is not promptly restored, you must reduce the rent by its monthly value until it is restored, and a tenant can petition for a refund or rollback. Practical step: charge only for optional services the tenant actually receives, and stop billing as soon as a service stops.

title: All Required Charges Are Rent Under the Act
bodyText: Under the Rental Housing Act, rent means the entire amount of money or other value you demand or receive as a condition of occupying the unit or using its related services and facilities, so a mandatory charge for parking, amenities or similar services included with the unit is generally rent for the Act's purposes whatever the lease calls it. Three limits apply. A late fee is never a ground for eviction, so labelling it rent does not change that. A lease may not require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees, so calling them additional rent does not make them collectable; only a court may award them. And in a rent-stabilized unit, a mandatory fee for an unapproved service or facility is barred outright, and all rent counts toward the stabilization limits. For eviction, you must give the 10-day nonpayment notice before filing, and you may not file for possession or send that notice when the unpaid rent is under $600. These rules apply to month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike.

title: Fire Code: District Construction Codes and Housing-Regulation Duties
bodyText: The District's fire code is part of its Construction Codes: the most recent International Code Council codes (or comparable national codes) as adopted and amended by the District's supplement and published in DCMR Title 12. The Mayor adopts new editions and amendments by rulemaking, which takes effect only after a 45-day Council review. The housing regulations add owner and operator duties for every rental: occupancy limits never override fire-safety and egress limits; required fire alarm systems must be kept operable with signs explaining how to use them; fire signs must be posted; smoke detectors must be installed; and fire escapes, stairways, exits and fire doors must be kept in repair and unobstructed. The owner of every dwelling unit must install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in accordance with the Construction Codes. Practical step: check the current Title 12 Fire Code and Property Maintenance Code for your building type before leasing, and keep inspection records.

title: Just Cause Required: Eviction Grounds and Notice Periods
bodyText: District law requires just cause to evict. For essentially every rental unit, whether rent-stabilized or exempt, a tenant who keeps paying the lawful rent cannot be evicted, even after the lease term ends. Only the tenant can end a residential tenancy with a 30-day notice, so a fixed term simply continues. The only grounds, each needing a written notice and a minimum wait before filing: unpaid rent of at least $600 (notice of intent to file; the statute says 10 days, the regulation still says 30, so wait 30); a substantial lease or housing-code obligation not corrected within 30 days of a notice to correct or vacate; an illegal act a court has finally found (30 days, or a 10-day notice for certain violent crimes, though a regulation still says to wait 30 days before filing); a natural-person owner's own residence (90 days); a sale under written contract to a buyer who will live there, after the tenant purchase offer (90 days); Rent Administrator-approved renovation (120 days); demolition with a permit (180 days); approved substantial rehabilitation (120 days); and permanently ending housing use (180 days). Condominium or co-op conversion and drug-haven cases follow their own statutes. Serve notices in English and Spanish, and file every non-rent notice with the Rent Administrator within 5 business days.

title: Foreclosure Does Not End a Tenancy
bodyText: Foreclosure is not one of the District's eviction grounds, so it does not end a residential tenancy by itself. Whoever takes title and receives the rent becomes the housing provider and takes the tenancy subject to the just-cause eviction rules: a tenant who keeps paying rent can be removed only on a listed ground with the required notice (for example, a natural-person owner who will live in the unit, after a 90-day notice). A buyer at a foreclosure or other auction may not serve a notice to quit, sue for possession, or charge rent or use-and-occupancy against a current occupant until a deed to the buyer has been recorded at the Recorder of Deeds. District statutes and housing regulations do not require a landlord to tell tenants that the mortgage is in default or that a foreclosure sale is scheduled; the statutory foreclosure notices go to the borrower, the record owner and the Mayor. Practical step: if a property you own or manage is in foreclosure, keep accepting, receipting and accounting for rent as usual; if you buy at auction, record the deed before contacting occupants about rent or possession, and then follow the eviction-ground rules. Federal foreclosure-tenant rules may also apply.

title: Nonpayment Judgments Can Be Redeemed Until Eviction
bodyText: In the District a lease clause or notice cannot forfeit a tenancy for unpaid rent. You must give the notice of intent to file, sue, and win a judgment for possession, and even that judgment can be redeemed. After a trial the court states on the record the amount the tenant must pay to redeem the tenancy and avoid eviction, an amount that grows as new rent and costs come due. For other nonpayment judgments, including defaults, you must file the court's notice to tenant of payment required to avoid eviction (L&T Form 6) within 7 days unless the court rules otherwise; no writ can issue on a nonpayment judgment until the court has set the amount or you have filed that notice. If the tenant pays the full redemption amount at any time before the eviction is completed, the judgment is permanently stayed by law and the tenancy continues. The redemption amount may not include late fees, and the right ends when the U.S. Marshals execute the writ. In the rarely used ejectment action for half a year's unpaid rent, paying the arrears and costs before trial ends the case, and the tenant may seek equitable relief within six months after execution. Practical step: file the notice on time and accept a full redemption payment tendered before the eviction.

title: Which Code Edition Applies: Adopted Editions Only
bodyText: District building and fire standards follow a moving-but-adopted model. By statute, the Construction Codes are the most recent edition of the International Code Council codes (or comparable national codes) as adopted and amended by the District, and all future amendments, supplements and editions take effect only when the Mayor adopts them by rule after a 45-day Council review. So a new national edition does not apply in the District until it is adopted, and work allowed to finish under an earlier edition stays under that edition. The adopted editions are listed in DCMR Title 12. Some older housing regulations still point to specific historic codes: natural-light rules refer to the 1941 and 1961 Building Codes, the heating-control rule refers to a 1951 engineering guide, and fire-sign rules refer to the Fire Prevention Code of 1986. The Human Rights Act lets accessible-design compliance be shown by meeting the American National Standard for accessible buildings, without naming an edition. The smoke and carbon monoxide detector law points to the Construction Codes generally. Practical step: when a question turns on a code edition, check the current Title 12 adoption and the date of your building permit rather than the latest national code.

title: Furnished Rentals: Same Deposit Cap and Wear-and-Tear Rules
bodyText:
District law treats a furnished rental mostly like any other. Points to know: there is no separate or higher security deposit for furniture; all money held as security, together, may not exceed the first full month's rent. You may not withhold any deposit money for the replacement value of furnishings or other apartment items damaged by ordinary wear and tear, meaning deterioration from intended use, age or deteriorated condition, but you may for damage from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, family or guests.

In a rent-stabilized unit, furnishings and equipment provided with the rent are related facilities, so you may not remove or substantially reduce them without Rent Administrator approval, and a mandatory furniture fee needs approval. If you sue for possession of a unit leased with furniture, the court may also give judgment for recovery of the furniture.

Practical step: attach a dated inventory with photos so you can document any claim within the 45-day post-move-out notice.

title: Governing Law in the District
bodyText:
A lease of a District rental unit is governed by District law and by federal law. The District is one jurisdiction: the Council legislates for the whole city, there is no separate county or municipal code to name, and Congress keeps power to legislate for the District directly. That is why the District lease uses its own governing-law clause instead of the shared clause, whose jurisdiction wording does not fit the District.

No District statute regulates choice-of-law or forum clauses in residential leases. In practice the clause cannot move a possession case: an action to recover a District rental unit is brought in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, and the lease may not waive the tenant's jury-trial right or make the tenant pay the owner's court costs or legal fees. Applies to all District rental units, whether month-to-month or fixed-term.

Practical step: use "Governing Law" clause and do not add a clause choosing another jurisdiction's law or courts.

title: Government Fines: Tenant Liability and Snow Fines
bodyText: District law has no general rule on whether a landlord may pass a government fine on to a tenant. Two specific rules apply instead. First, a tenant who causes a housing code violation is personally subject to the same penalties as an owner, and a tenant whose action or neglect causes an insanitary condition that leads to condemnation commits a misdemeanor; the government can pursue the tenant directly. Second, the owner of property fronting a paved sidewalk must clear snow and sleet within the first 8 hours of daylight after it stops falling. The owner may delegate that duty to a tenant only by written agreement, and the owner stays liable for the fine (up to $25 for a residential property); with a written delegation, the owner may seek reimbursement of the fine from the tenant. Practical step: if you want tenants of a house to handle sidewalk snow, say so in the lease and include the reimbursement term; do not bill tenants for fines that result from your own maintenance failures.

title: Substantial Housing-Code Violations
bodyText: The District's materiality test is the "substantial violation": a housing condition that violates the housing regulations or another law on residential conditions and may endanger or materially impair the health and safety of any tenant or occupant. For rent-stabilized units it has teeth: you may not raise the rent above base rent unless the unit and common elements are in substantial compliance (unless the problem is the tenant's doing), a failure to promptly abate a substantial violation counts as a reduction in related services that can support a rent reduction, and the regulations list examples, including frequent lack of water, hot water or heat, hazardous wiring, roof or wall leaks, defective plumbing, insect or rodent infestation, deteriorated lead paint, blocked exits, missing locks, inoperable elevators, professional-level mold and failure to supply utilities under your control, plus many minor violations together. Unsuccessful efforts to fix are not a defense. For every covered unit, rent-stabilized or exempt, a lease is void if the unit is unsafe or unsanitary from code violations at the start of the tenancy that you knew or should have known about, or becomes so and is not corrected in time. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived by Lease
bodyText: In the District the habitability duty cannot be modified or waived by the lease. Every lease or rental agreement is deemed to include an implied warranty that you will maintain the premises in compliance with the housing regulations, and any lease or agreement provision contrary to, or providing for a waiver of, the housing-code chapter that contains that warranty is void and unenforceable; no one may include such a provision in a lease or demand that a tenant sign one. A bad-faith violation can make you liable for treble damages. Courts may also strike other lease provisions as contrary to public policy or unconscionable. There is no District exception, as some places have, allowing a separate signed agreement or a situation-specific waiver (for example, for water service) to shift your code duties to the tenant; the owner must provide and maintain the facilities, utilities and services the regulations require. A tenant may still agree to specific minor tasks that do not displace your code duties, and the tenant keeps its own duties for areas under its exclusive control. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: District law has two habitability presumptions. First, mold: in a tenant's lawsuit, claim or defense for violation of the property maintenance or housing code, a professional indoor mold assessment finding mold contamination in the unit or a common area creates a rebuttable presumption that you violated your duty to keep the property free of defective surface conditions, if the tenant shows you received the assessment in written or electronic form. The court may then award assessment costs, attorney fees and court costs, and treble damages if you did not remediate within 60 days and acted in bad faith. Second, for rent-stabilized units, you get a rebuttable presumption of substantial compliance when seeking a rent adjustment that needs prior approval if every unit was inspected at your request within 30 days before filing and any substantial violation cited was abated and certified within the allowed time, with tenants given notice and 10 days to object. Separately, actions taken within six months after a tenant's repair request or code complaint are presumed retaliatory unless rebutted by clear and convincing evidence. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Habitability Cannot Be Waived by Agreement
bodyText: No written agreement can remove a District habitability requirement. Every lease or rental agreement is deemed to include your implied warranty to keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations, and the sentence that does the work is the regulations' own anti-waiver rule: any provision of any lease or agreement contrary to, or providing for a waiver of, the landlord-tenant chapter of the regulations (or its civil-enforcement and tenant-notice sections) is void and unenforceable. Including or demanding such a term is itself prohibited, with treble damages for bad faith. The same chapter makes a lease void if the unit is unsafe or unsanitary at the start, or later becomes so through violations you do not correct in time. The District has no mechanism for a tenant to accept specified defects in exchange for a stated rent reduction, and no separate-document rule for heat: where the tenant does not control the heat, you must keep the unit at 68 degrees F by day and 65 degrees F at night regardless of what the lease says. What remains non-waivable is therefore everything in the regulations. Only who does minor tasks can be agreed (see the tenant-repair agreement clause, "Tenant Task Agreement" clause). This applies equally to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Housing-Code Materials Tenants Must Receive
bodyText: The District has no local health districts with their own rental rules; housing standards come from the District-wide housing regulations in Title 14 of the DCMR, enforced by the Department of Buildings. The closest District counterpart to a duty to give tenants the health rules is broader: you must give every tenant, at the start of the tenancy and to each existing tenant, a copy of the housing-code chapter on leases and tenant rights (14 DCMR chapter 3) plus the sections on civil enforcement (§ 101) and notification of tenants about violations (§ 106). When an inspector issues a violation notice to you after inspecting a unit, the tenant receives a copy for information, and where a violation affects more than one unit the notice is posted in the building; no one may tamper with a posted notice. Tenants can report conditions to the District government, and a written or witnessed oral complaint triggers the six-month retaliation presumption. See the habitability-statement row for the delivery duty. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Heat Requirements
bodyText: Every residential building in the District must have adequate heating facilities, meaning a central system, a non-portable flue-connected heater or an electric heating facility, kept in good repair and capable of keeping habitable areas at 70 degrees Fahrenheit. If the heating equipment for a unit or bathroom is not under the tenant's control, you must supply enough heat to keep it at least 68 degrees from 6:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. and 65 degrees overnight. If the tenant controls the equipment (for example, an individually metered furnace or electric heat), the lease may make the tenant pay for the fuel or electricity, but you still must provide and maintain the equipment, and any utility that is your responsibility or under your control must be furnished as normal occupancy requires. In buildings with two or more units the central heating system must be inspected by a licensed qualified person each year between March 1 and September 1, including for carbon monoxide, with defects fixed and certified by October 1; a rented single-family home needs the same inspection after a heating violation notice. For rent-stabilized units, frequent lack of heat between October 1 and May 1 is a substantial violation. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Holding Deposits: After Approval, Never From Voucher Holders
bodyText:
A holding deposit is money you require after approving an application to take the unit off the market temporarily; if the applicant takes the unit, it becomes part of the first month's rent or the security deposit. It is the one payment besides the application fee you may require before the lease is signed, and you may not require one from an applicant who will pay rent with a government-funded housing voucher.

Ask for it only after approval, not with the application. Disclose it in the written screening notice you give or post before requesting any information or fee, with its amount, purpose, timing and whether and when it is refundable. District law does not cap the amount or say what happens if the applicant backs out, so write the refund terms down; if it is credited to the security deposit, the combined deposit still may not exceed one month's rent. Give a written receipt unless paid by personal check.

title: No Holdover at Term End; Double Rent Only After Tenant Notice
bodyText:
In the District, a tenant who stays after the lease term ends is not a wrongful holdover as long as the tenant keeps paying the rent you are entitled to: the end of the term does not end the tenancy, and you cannot charge holdover damages or a holdover rate just because the term has expired. You can recover possession only on a just-cause ground, after the required notice, through the court.

The one statutory holdover penalty runs the other way: if the tenant gives you written notice of the tenant's intention to quit and then, without reasonable excuse, refuses to give up possession on that notice, the tenant owes rent at double the lease rate for the whole time of the wrongful holding over, collectible like ordinary rent and claimable in a possession or ejectment suit up to judgment. Neither party can take back a notice to quit without the other's consent.

Practical step: do not use a lease clause that treats the end of the term as requiring the tenant to leave or that charges holdover damages for staying; use the District holdover clause ("Staying After the Term Ends" clause), which keeps the tenancy going on the same terms and repeats the double-rent rule for a tenant who gives notice and then stays.

title: No Converting Rental Housing to Hotel or Transient Use
bodyText: District law forbids converting a rental unit or housing accommodation into a hotel, motel, inn or other transient residential occupancy, and forbids demolishing rental housing to build or expand a hotel or other transient accommodation. So you may not take a unit out of the long-term rental market by turning it into transient lodging. This is separate from the condominium and cooperative conversion rules, and from the separate short-term rental licensing rules for hosts. Applies to every rental unit and housing accommodation in the District. Practical step: before offering a former rental unit for stays to transient guests, get advice on whether the change is a prohibited conversion.

title: Dispute Resolution Clauses and the District Conciliation Service
bodyText:
No District statute requires or forbids a lease term asking the parties to try to settle a dispute informally before going to court, so a non-binding meet-and-confer clause that leaves possession actions, statutory notices and deadlines untouched is lawful. Two District rules limit what such a clause may add.

First, a standardized lease that requires binding arbitration of later disputes with an individual renting a home is a consumer arbitration agreement, and its mandatory binding-arbitration provision is void except to the extent federal law makes it enforceable.

Second, the lease may not waive the tenant's jury-trial right. The District also runs a free, voluntary conciliation and arbitration service at the Rental Accommodations Division: either side may start a proceeding, no one can be made to attend, results bind only if the parties agree, and arbitration needs both parties' consent; an agreement reached under the panel's recommendation and approved by the Rent Administrator binds the parties. Applies to all District rental units.

Practical step: keep any dispute-resolution clause voluntary and non-binding, and do not add mandatory arbitration.

title: Periodic and Move-Out Inspections
bodyText:
Inspecting the premises is one of the listed reasonable purposes for which you may enter a District rental during the tenancy. Outside an emergency, you must give written notice at least 48 hours before the entry (or a shorter period the tenant agrees to in writing); email or text counts only if the tenant acknowledges it in writing, otherwise give paper notice. Enter between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., not on a Sunday or federal holiday, unless the tenant agrees to another time.

No District law caps how often you may inspect, but repeated unreasonable demands for entry let a court enjoin you and award the tenant damages. Move-out inspection follows its own rule: to set the security deposit refund you may inspect within 3 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays) before or after the tenancy ends, at a time and date you give the tenant in writing at least 10 days ahead. A tenant who reports a housing-code violation must give you access to assess and fix it within 48 hours of your written request. Use the District entry clause ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause) for the notice terms.

title: No Jury-Trial Waivers in Residential Leases
bodyText: A District residential lease may not waive the tenant's right to a jury trial. The housing regulations forbid an owner to place such a provision in a lease or rental agreement, forbid demanding that a tenant sign a lease containing one, and make any such term void. A bad-faith violation can make you liable to the tenant for treble damages. In an eviction or other landlord-tenant case, any party entitled to a jury may demand one by filing a jury demand by the initial hearing date (or the next hearing date if the first is continued, or a date the court sets), with the filing fee unless waived, and a defendant tenant must attach a verified answer setting out the defense. The case then moves to the Civil Actions Branch for an expedited trial. The District has no general standard-form contract statute making jury or class-action waivers presumptively unconscionable, and no statute-of-frauds rule for waivers of constitutional rights; for residential leases the specific prohibition above settles the jury question, and courts may refuse to enforce other unconscionable terms. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike. Practical step: delete jury-waiver and class-action-waiver language from District leases (see also the arbitration row).

title: Owner Supplies Working Locks and Keys; No Lock Fees; Intrafamily-Offense Lock Change
bodyText:
Every covered rental: when a tenant first takes possession, you must supply an adequate lock and key for each door that is or could be used as an entrance or exit, keep each lock in good repair, and make each lock lockable from inside and outside. Since August 14, 2026, you may not charge a fee before move-in, during the tenancy or after move-out for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable and code-compliant, and the law names locks expressly. So lease terms that charge for keys, re-keying or lock changes are risky; the law still lets you withhold from the security deposit to replace items the tenant damaged beyond ordinary wear and tear.

Intrafamily-offense victims: on a tenant's written request you must change the entrance locks within 5 business days (a protective order is required only if the abuser lives in the same unit), and you may not give the abuser keys after receiving the order. You pay for the change first; the lock-change statute lets you recover the cost (plus any fee no higher than you charge other tenants for lock changes) within 45 days after you give the tenant documentation, but whether the newer no-lock-fee rule now bars that reimbursement is unsettled, and the District key clause ("Keys and Locks" clause) waives it, so the cautious course is not to charge. Use the District key clause rather than a generic re-key charge clause.

title: Penalties for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: The District does attach money consequences to using prohibited lease terms. A housing provider found to have violated the housing regulations' prohibited-terms section (waivers of the landlord-tenant chapter, owner-negligence exculpation, jury-trial waivers, fee shifting, confessions of judgment), or the statutory rules on tenant notice to vacate and on sublet bans, is liable to the tenant for treble damages if it acted in bad faith. That section itself prohibits including such terms or demanding that a tenant sign them, so the violation can occur when the lease is used, not only when the term is enforced. Separately, anyone who willfully violates the Rental Housing Act faces a civil fine of up to $5,000 per violation, and knowing or willful late-fee violations carry excess or treble recovery plus a $100 to $5,000 fine per violation. Including a discriminatory clause in a rental transaction is itself an unlawful practice under the Human Rights Act, and the Consumer Protection Procedures Act lists making or enforcing unconscionable lease terms. Each rule's voidness provision works alongside these penalties; none displaces the treble-damages remedy. Practical step: remove prohibited terms from all District lease forms in use, including older forms still circulating.

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Fails to Maintain
bodyText: When a landlord fails to maintain a unit, District tenants have several statutory routes, on top of court remedies for breach of the implied warranty of habitability. A lease is void if the unit becomes unsafe or unsanitary from code violations the tenant did not cause that are not corrected in time. Tenants of rent-stabilized units can petition the Rent Administrator for a rent reduction or rollback when services are reduced or substantial violations persist, and rent cannot be raised while substantial violations exist. For mold, a professional assessment creates a presumption of violation, with fees, costs and possible treble damages. A tenant who legally withholds rent after notice of a code violation, complains to the District or requests repairs is protected by a six-month retaliation presumption. When a building has cited violations posing a serious threat to health, safety or security that you fail to abate, or a 30-day pattern of serious neglect, the Attorney General or a majority of tenants can seek a court-appointed receiver to collect the rents, and you may not collect rent during the receivership. Repeated improper entry can be enjoined with damages. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Entry: 48-Hour Written Notice Rule
bodyText:
In the District, entry turns on notice, purpose and time, not on the tenant's consent. Except in an emergency to protect the premises or people, you may enter only for a reasonable purpose (keeping the property safe, inspecting, agreed or necessary repairs, improvements, services or maintenance, showing the unit to buyers, lenders, tenants or contractors, or government-ordered work), at a reasonable time (9 a.m. to 5 p.m., not Sundays or federal holidays, unless the tenant agrees to another time) and after reasonable notice: written notice at least 48 hours ahead, or a shorter period the tenant agrees to in writing.

Email or text works only if the tenant acknowledges it in writing; otherwise deliver paper notice. Showings follow the same rule; the District has no separate end-of-lease showing exception. If you enter unlawfully or keep making unreasonable demands, a court may enjoin you and award damages for breach of quiet enjoyment.

A tenant who alleges a code violation must allow access within 48 hours of your written request; other refusals are lease violations you can address only by notice to cure and the courts. Use the District entry clause ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause).

title: Statutory Rent Lien on Non-Exempt Goods, Court-Enforced Only
bodyText: District law still gives a landlord a statutory (tacit) lien for rent on the tenant's personal property kept on the premises, but only on property that could be taken on execution for a debt, so exempt items such as household goods within the exemption limits, health aids and family pictures are outside it. The lien starts with the tenancy and lasts until 3 months after the rent falls due, and longer if you sue for that rent within the 3 months. It is enforced through the court: by attachment on an affidavit that rent is due and unpaid (or that the tenant is about to remove or sell the goods), by judgment and execution against the goods, or by suit against a buyer who knew of the lien. A tenant or helper who fraudulently removes or hides goods to defeat the lien owes double their value. Other creditors executing on goods on the premises must first pay up to 3 months' rent arrears. Practical step: never seize, lock up or hold a tenant's belongings yourself; use the court process, and remember that after an eviction a tenant's belongings must be handled under the District's 7-day post-eviction rules. Do not add a lease clause creating a contractual lien or confessed judgment.

title: Landlord Maintenance Duties
bodyText:
Every District lease carries an implied warranty that you will maintain the premises in compliance with the housing regulations, and it cannot be waived. You may not rent a unit that is not clean, safe, sanitary, in repair and free of rodents and vermin; you must provide and maintain the facilities, utilities and services the regulations require in safe, good working condition, including heat, hot water, plumbing, lighting, locks and any cooking or refrigeration appliances or air conditioning you furnish; you are responsible for common areas and for extermination when two or more units are infested; and mold reported in writing or electronically must be inspected within 7 days and remediated within 30 days.

If the unit is unsafe or unsanitary from code violations at the start of the tenancy that you knew or should have known about, the lease is void, and later uncorrected violations the tenant did not cause also void it. Persistent serious violations can lead to rent reductions for rent-stabilized units, a court-appointed receiver collecting the rents, and fines.

A lease may ask tenants to report problems in writing, but retaliation protection also covers witnessed oral repair requests. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Rental License and Rental Unit Registration
bodyText: The District has two landlord registrations, and both apply before you rent. First, every dwelling or rooming unit offered for rent, including a room or basement unit in a home the owner lives in, needs a basic business license (Housing: Residential endorsement) before it is rented. Post the license at the property and name a property or resident manager on the application. Second, every rental unit covered by the Rental Housing Act, including units exempt from rent stabilization, must be registered with the Rental Accommodations Division, with a claim of exemption where one applies; a new housing provider files within 30 days. Within 15 days after the registration or exemption number issues, post a copy at a multi-unit building or serve it on the tenant of a single unit. Consequences: a housing provider who fails to register may owe $100 per unit (the statute imposes this from 91 days after the District's online rent-control registration database is completed) and may not raise the rent, reduce services or rely on an exemption until 90 days after registering, and no possession case may be filed without a valid registration or claim of exemption and a current rental license (the court may waive the license in extenuating circumstances; neither applies to complaints against subtenants). Non-resident owners must also keep a District registered agent (see the non-resident owner row). Two general business filings can matter too: an out-of-state company doing business here must register with the Mayor and cannot maintain an action until it does, and if you rent under a trade name you must register it with the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection and cannot maintain a suit until you do (D.C. Code §§ 29-105.02, 47-2855.02 and 47-2855.03(d)).

title: Possession, Rent and Damages Remedies Run Through Court
bodyText: When a District tenant defaults, your remedies run through the Superior Court's Landlord and Tenant Branch. A complaint for possession (on a just-cause ground, after the required notice) may also ask for a money judgment for rent in arrears and lawful late fees, but a money judgment can be entered only against a tenant who was personally served or who files a money counterclaim, and it cannot be enforced until 14 days after entry. A nonpayment possession case cannot be filed for less than $600 owed, but you may still sue to collect any smaller amount. You may also sue separately for rent or damages without seeking possession, and an ejectment action can combine possession with rent arrears, double rent where the tenant gave notice and held over, and damages for waste. If a tenant leaves before the term ends, your recovery is limited to actual damages that you could not avoid by reasonable mitigation, such as re-renting. The prevailing party recovers taxable court costs, but a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney's fees or court costs, and fees are not available in eviction cases under the Rental Housing Act. Practical step: plan to seek possession and money in one case where the tenant can be personally served, and document your re-renting efforts.

title: Late Fees: 5% Cap, 5-Day Grace, Lease Must State Both
bodyText:
For every unit covered by the Rental Housing Act, month-to-month or fixed-term, you may charge a late fee only if the written lease states the grace period and the maximum late fee, and only if the full rent is still unpaid more than 5 days after the due date (or any longer grace period in the lease). The fee may not exceed 5% of the full rent due. You may charge it only once per late payment, may not charge interest on it, may not deduct it from a later rent payment, and may not charge it on any portion of the rent a subsidy provider is responsible for paying.

Nonpayment of a late fee is never a ground for eviction. After the grace period you may send an invoice payable within 30 days; an unpaid lawful late fee may then be deducted from the security deposit at the end of the tenancy. Knowingly or willfully charging an unlawful late fee makes you liable for the excess (trebled for bad faith) plus a civil fine of $100 to $5,000 per fee. District law has no rule that accepting late rent waives the late fee or other rights.

title: Late Fee Cap: 5% of Rent Due
bodyText: The District caps residential late fees at 5% of the full amount of rent due for that payment, for every unit covered by the Rental Housing Act, whether the tenancy is month-to-month or for a fixed term and whether or not the unit is rent-stabilized. No lease may provide for a larger late fee, and a fee is allowed only once per late payment, only after the rent is more than 5 days late (or any longer grace period in the lease), and only if the written lease states the grace period and the maximum fee. There is no flat-dollar alternative to the percentage cap. Charging more makes you liable for the excess, trebled for bad faith, plus a civil fine of $100 to $5,000 for each unlawful fee. See the late-fee row for the full rules.

title: Clearance Report or Lead-Free Certificate Before Lease When a Person at Risk Will Occupy
bodyText: The District has no lead-safe certificate that must be attached to a lease as an exhibit, and no lead-safe registry or certificate requirement for every rental. Its closest rule is the clearance report: for a pre-1978 unit that a child under 6 or a pregnant woman will live in or regularly visit, the owner must give the tenant, before the tenant is obligated under the lease, the completed District lead disclosure form and a clearance report issued within the previous 12 months (a report by a certified risk assessor, lead-based paint inspector or dust sampling technician that the tested area passed a clearance examination). If a tenant later notifies the owner in writing that such a person lives in or visits the unit, the owner must provide a current clearance report within 30 days. Instead of the form and clearance report, an owner may provide a risk assessor's or inspector's report certifying the unit lead-free, or three clearance reports issued at least 12 months apart within the previous 7 years if the property has had no housing code violations in the past 5 years and none outstanding. Giving the report is required; attaching it to the lease is not, but the District lead clause ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosures (District Form and Clearance Report)" clause) records which document you gave.

title: District Lead Disclosure Form Before Lease; Clearance Report When a Child Under 6 or Pregnant Woman
bodyText:
Pre-1978 units: before the tenant is obligated under the lease, give the District's lead disclosure form (the Mayor's form, which carries the federal Lead Warning Statement elements), completed with what you reasonably know about lead-based paint, lead-based paint hazards and pending District lead orders in the unit. If a child under 6 or a pregnant woman will live in or regularly visit the unit, you must also give, before the lease binds the tenant, a clearance report issued within the previous 12 months.

If a tenant later tells you in writing that such a person lives there or visits regularly, provide a current clearance report within 30 days. A lead-free certification or three clearance reports at least 12 months apart within 7 years (with no recent code violations) may substitute. All pre-1978 units and common areas must be kept free of lead-based paint hazards.

If you learn of lead-based paint, tell the tenant within 10 days and give the Lead Warning Statement and pamphlet. District lead orders can require repairs and paid temporary relocation with a right to return on the same terms. Penalties reach $25,000 a day. Federal disclosure rules also apply. Use the District lead clause ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosures (District Form and Clearance Report)" clause) to record delivery.

title: District Lead Rights Notice and Lead Plumbing Form at Every Lease and Renewal
bodyText:
Beyond the pre-1978 lead paint disclosure, District law requires these notices for rentals of any age: Lead rights notice: give each tenant the Mayor's form explaining tenants' rights under the District's lead-hazard law whenever the tenant signs or renews a lease and whenever you give a rent-increase notice. Lead plumbing disclosure: before the tenant is obligated to lease or renew, give the Mayor's lead plumbing disclosure form, completed with what you know about water lead test results, lead-bearing plumbing or a lead service line, whether the private and public portions of the service line were replaced (and when), any fines imposed on you under this rule, and whether DC Water lists the property as having a lead service line.

The form warns that homes built before 1986 are presumed to have lead lines or plumbing. If you learn of lead plumbing or a lead service line, tell the tenant within 48 hours and give a completed form. Water test kits: in a multiple dwelling, a tenant may ask in writing for a DC Water lead test kit; you must order it within 15 days (subject to unit-count limits) and share and post results. Use the District lead notices clause to record delivery.

title: Mandatory Lease Arbitration Void for Consumer Tenants
bodyText: The District's arbitration act makes a mandatory binding arbitration provision in a consumer arbitration agreement void and unenforceable, except to the extent federal law provides for its enforceability. A consumer includes an individual who leases real property primarily for personal, family or household purposes, and a consumer arbitration agreement is a standardized contract written by one party that requires disputes arising after signing to go to binding arbitration. A standard residential lease clause requiring tenants to arbitrate future disputes therefore falls within the District's ban; whether the Federal Arbitration Act would nonetheless enforce it in a given case is a federal question. A residential lease also may not waive the tenant's right to a jury trial. Voluntary dispute resolution remains available. After a dispute arises, the parties may agree to arbitrate it, and the Rent Administrator runs a voluntary conciliation and arbitration service for housing providers and tenants: no one can be compelled to take part, and a panel recommendation binds only once the parties enter an agreement under it that the Rent Administrator approves. This library does not offer an arbitration clause for the District. Practical step: leave mandatory arbitration out of District residential leases; if you want an alternative to court, offer voluntary mediation or post-dispute arbitration.

title: What a District Lease Must Say
bodyText: No District statute lists everything a residential lease must contain, but several District rules work only if the lease says something, and others forbid certain terms. Put these in the lease when they apply: the maximum late fee and the grace period (no late fee otherwise); the security deposit's terms and conditions (or put them on the receipt); the maximum number of occupants (or tell the tenant in another writing); any sole-discretion ban on subletting or assignment; and, if you want a tenant notice to vacate longer than 30 days, the statements the law requires about the initial term and your own longer rent-increase notice. For a new tenancy in a rent-stabilized unit, the Rent Administrator's rent-history disclosure form goes with the lease. If a real estate licensee represents only one side, its brokerage-relationship disclosure must appear in the application or the lease, whichever comes first (not for terms under 2 months). Inclusionary Zoning rental units need the program's lease rider, and voucher tenancies need the program's required addendum. Leave out terms the housing regulations forbid: waivers of the tenant protections, owner-negligence exculpation, jury-trial waivers, tenant payment of the owner's court costs or legal fees, and confessions of judgment.

title: Copies of the Lease and Housing Regulations
bodyText: District housing regulations impose two copy duties on every residential owner. First, at signing or within 7 days after it, give the tenant an exact, legible, completed copy of every lease, addendum, application or other agreement the tenant signed. Second, at the start of every tenancy (and to each existing tenant) give the tenant a copy of the landlord-tenant chapter of the housing regulations (14 DCMR chapter 3, sections 300 to 399) and of sections 101 (civil enforcement policy) and 106 (notification of tenants about violations) of 14 DCMR chapter 1. The Office of the Tenant Advocate's Tenant Bill of Rights repeats both duties. These duties apply to month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike, and the lease cannot waive them. No District statute or housing regulation makes a missing copy a defense to enforcing the lease or bars a possession case. The sanction would come from housing-code enforcement or from a court. Practical step: send the signed lease package and the regulation copies electronically or on paper the day the lease is signed, and keep proof of delivery.

title: Documents Due Before and at Signing: Exempt Notice, Rent History, Lead Forms, Housing Code Copy
bodyText:
At or before signing: before a lease is signed for a unit exempt from rent stabilization, give written notice that its rent increases are not regulated by the rent stabilization program; for a rent-stabilized unit, the lease for a new tenancy must include the Rent Administrator's form showing the starting rent and the increases over the past 3 years with their basis.

Pre-1978 units need the District lead disclosure form (and a 12-month clearance report if a child under 6 or pregnant woman will live there or visit regularly). Every unit needs the Mayor's lead rights notice and lead plumbing disclosure form before the lease or renewal binds. If the unit is in a condominium or cooperative, give written notice of that before occupancy.

A real estate licensee must disclose in writing to a party it does not represent its brokerage relationship (not for terms under 2 months). In the lease: set out the deposit terms (or put them on the receipt) and the maximum late fee (and any longer grace period) if you will charge one. At the start of the tenancy: give a copy of the housing regulations' landlord-tenant chapter and its sections on civil enforcement and tenant notification, and an exact signed copy of the lease and application on signing or within 7 days.

title: Lease Length: Deed Formality and Recordation
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation sets a maximum term for a residential lease. Two District rules turn on the term's length instead. First, a lease for a term longer than 1 year is an estate that may be created only by a deed signed and sealed by the lessor in person or through a power of attorney. The District lets an authorized agent sign a lease longer than 1 year only for commercial leases, so a property manager signing a residential lease longer than 1 year should hold a power of attorney from the owner, and the lease should carry the owner's seal. Second, a lease that runs 30 years or more with renewals counts as a deed for the District recordation tax; shorter leases do not, and no District statute or housing regulation requires a residential lease to be recorded. Whatever the term, its end does not end the tenancy: a tenant who keeps paying rent may stay unless the housing provider proves a statutory ground for eviction. Practical step: for a lease longer than 1 year, have the owner (or an attorney-in-fact) sign under seal.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts: Lease Must Authorize It
bodyText:
The District's legal interest rate, where no rate is agreed, is 6% a year on the forbearance of money. A written instrument for the payment of money may set a higher rate, but not more than 24% a year. For tenant balances, the debt-collection law adds a condition: once rent or other money owed under a residential lease is more than 30 days past due, you may collect interest on it only if the lease expressly authorizes that interest (and it is legally chargeable) or a law authorizes it. So any interest must be written into the lease, at or below the legal limit.

The library's optional clause charges interest only on amounts still owed after move-out, starting after the tenant's 30-day window to dispute your notice of unpaid amounts; it does not charge interest on late rent during the tenancy, because that works as a second, repeating late charge beside the single 5% late fee and, for a rent-stabilized unit, counts as rent.

If you use it, a modest rate is safer than one near the 24% ceiling. You may never charge interest on a late fee. After a court judgment, interest runs at the judgment rate (70% of the federal tax underpayment rate, rounded) unless the contract fixes a rate, and the court may lower it for good cause or a debtor's good-faith inability to pay.

title: Deadline to Sue for Unpaid Rent: 3 Years
bodyText: A landlord's suit for unpaid rent or other money owed under a residential lease generally must be brought within 3 years after the claim accrues. The general limitations law gives 3 years for an action on a simple contract and for damage to real or personal property; a lease under seal would otherwise get 12 years, but for consumer debt (rent and charges owed under a household lease) the District's debt-collection law fixes 3 years from accrual for actions commenced on or after September 1, 2021, even for contracts under seal and whatever the legal theory. Once that period has run, a later payment or acknowledgment by the tenant does not revive it. Before it runs, a spoken acknowledgment or promise does not extend the period unless it is in writing and signed by the tenant, though the general law leaves the effect of an actual payment intact. Suing or threatening suit on a time-barred consumer debt is itself a violation of the debt-collection law. A suit to recover possession is not a money claim and is governed by the eviction rules.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to Tenants
bodyText:
District law gives you only narrow room to shift maintenance duties to a tenant. The general rule is the implied warranty: you must keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations and provide and maintain the facilities, utilities and services they require, and lease terms contrary to or waiving the housing-code chapter on leases are void.

The regulations themselves already put some tasks on tenants: keeping the space under the tenant's exclusive control clean and sanitary, supplying garbage receptacles for the tenant's own unit in a multiple dwelling, and carrying the unit's garbage to the building's common storage area unless you provide collection. Common space, vacant areas and anything not under a single tenant's exclusive control remain yours, and the regulations have no provision letting a lease move, for example, common-area garbage removal to a tenant.

The one duty a statute expressly lets you delegate is sidewalk snow and sleet removal, by written agreement; you remain liable for any fine but may seek reimbursement under the agreement. Treat any other tenant task as a limited, specific agreement that does not displace your code duties. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: Minors: Age 18 Majority; Guardian Needed in Court
bodyText: The age of majority in the District is 18. District law has no special statute on leasing to a person under 18 or on naming minors in an eviction case, but the Superior Court rules that apply in landlord and tenant cases cover minors: a minor may defend through a general guardian, committee, conservator or similar fiduciary, and if a minor defendant has no such representative the court must appoint a guardian ad litem or make another protective order. That adds time and cost, and a judgment against an unrepresented minor is open to challenge. An old District statute also lets a minor's guardian, with court approval, surrender a lease held for the minor and take a new one. Whether a lease signed by a minor binds the minor is governed by case law, not by statute. Fair-housing law separately bars discrimination against households because they have children living in them. Practical step: have every tenant who signs the lease be at least 18; list children as occupants, not tenants; and in an eviction case, name only adult tenants and occupants unless a minor is truly a party, in which case raise the need for a guardian with the court.

title: Duty to Mitigate After Early Move-Out
bodyText:
If a tenant moves out before the end of a fixed lease term, or refuses in bad faith to take possession, you may recover only actual damages, and those damages are subject to your duty to mitigate. In practice you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit, and you cannot simply let it sit vacant and bill the tenant for the rest of the term. Keep records of advertising, showings and applications so you can prove mitigation. A month-to-month tenant may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice expiring on the first day of a month, so there is no remaining term to recover.

A lease cannot require more than 30 days' notice of intent to vacate unless it meets District conditions, and a clause demanding longer notice in breach of those rules exposes you to treble damages if used in bad faith. District law has no rule treating a tenant's absence as abandonment that ends the tenancy; get a written surrender or a court judgment before retaking the unit (see the abandoned property row). The District early-termination clause sets a fixed option fee instead.

title: Disclose 3-Year Indoor Mold History at Application; 7-Day Inspection and 30-Day Remediation
bodyText: Yes, for every covered rental unit. When a prospective tenant applies, the Rent Administrator's disclosure form you provide must include information you knew or should have known about indoor mold contamination (mold at or above the District's professional-remediation threshold) in the unit or in common areas during the previous 3 years, unless a District-certified and licensed indoor mold remediation professional remediated it. Keep remediation documentation to support the exception. The same information belongs in the disclosure compilation you keep for tenants. During the tenancy: when a tenant gives written or electronic notice of mold or suspected mold in the unit or a common area, you must inspect within 7 days and remediate within 30 days of inspection (sooner if a court or the Mayor orders). Below the threshold you clean and remove it under District guidelines; if you know or have reason to know there is contamination at or above the threshold, a licensed remediation professional must do the work. A professional mold assessment finding contamination creates a rebuttable presumption of a housing code violation in a tenant's claim, and treble damages are possible for bad-faith failure to remediate within 60 days. These duties cannot be shifted to the tenant by lease.

title: Unpaid Water and Sewer Charges Become a Property Lien
bodyText: Water and sewer service in the District is billed by DC Water, which may collect charges from the owner or the occupant and may shut off service for bills unpaid 30 days, regardless of any change in ownership or occupancy. If an owner fails to pay water and sewer charges for 60 days or more, the District may record a certificate of delinquency that becomes a continuing lien on the property, ahead of every other lien except District taxes, and charges unpaid for more than 180 days can lead to a tax sale (an owner-occupied single-family home cannot be sold this way). The stormwater fee is the owner's obligation and an unpaid fee becomes a lien without further notice. District law has no lease-clause or affidavit procedure that keeps a tenant's unpaid water bill off your property, so your protection is contractual: keep the account in your name and bill the tenant lawfully, or monitor the account. If you fall behind on a rental property billed to you, tenants may take service in their own names without liability for your arrears and deduct what they pay from rent, and a tenant or DC Water may seek a receiver for the rents. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: No General Addendum-Precedence Rule; Voucher and IZ Addenda Required
bodyText:
District law has no general rule on whether a lease or its addenda control when they conflict, and no optional statutory addendum (like a nonstandard-provisions form) that must override the lease. Two program rules do require addenda that win. For a unit rented to a Housing Choice Voucher family, every provision of the HUD-required Tenancy Addendum must be added word for word to your lease, the tenant can enforce it against you, and its terms prevail over any other lease provision.

For a rental Inclusionary Zoning unit, a lease rider with the program's eligibility and certification terms must be attached to the lease and signed by every household member 18 or older, and a signed copy of the lease and rider goes to the District housing agency within 30 days. Separately, some District disclosures must be given before the lease is signed, such as the written notice to a prospective tenant of an exempt unit that its rent increases are not regulated by rent stabilization; those are covered in the disclosure rows, and statutory protections apply whatever an addendum says.

Practical step: attach required program addenda, give the tenant an exact signed copy of everything signed within 7 days, and use the shared precedence clause, which lets legally required addenda control.

title: No Adverse-Proceeding Notice Duty; Attornment Rules Apply
bodyText: District law does not require a landlord to tell tenants about a mortgage default, foreclosure, lawsuit, lien or other claim against the property, and does not require a tenant to forward to the landlord papers about such a claim; if you want tenants to pass along legal papers delivered to the unit, put that in the lease. Foreclosure notices go to the borrower, the record owner and the Mayor, and a foreclosure-sale buyer cannot demand rent or possession until its deed is recorded. Housing-code violation notices are the exception in reverse: after an inspection the District sends the tenant a copy of any notice issued to you, and posts building-wide notices. Old attornment rules still apply. A sale or other transfer of the property is effective without the tenants agreeing to it, and the new owner takes over your rights and duties under the lease; but a tenant who pays rent to you before receiving notice of the transfer is protected. A tenant's attornment to someone else (agreeing to hold under or pay rent to a stranger) is void unless made under a court order, with your consent, or to a mortgagee after forfeiture. Practical step: after a transfer, send each tenant written notice of the new owner and where to pay rent.

title: No Agreed-Notice-Method Rule; Statutory Delivery Methods Control
bodyText: District landlord-tenant law has no general rule letting the parties agree on an extra way (such as text message) to give notices the law requires. Each notice follows its own statute; an agreed method can add to, not replace, a prescribed method. Examples: a nonpayment notice of intent to file must go by certified mail or tracked delivery with return receipt and also by hand delivery or posting on the front door; eviction-related notices to correct or vacate are served personally, on an adult at the unit, or by posting plus first-class mail, in English and Spanish; the 21-day pre-eviction notice must go by phone or electronic message and first-class mail and posting; entry notices may be sent by email or text, but if the tenant does not acknowledge in writing you must also give a paper notice; deposit-withholding notices go personally or by certified mail, while the move-out unpaid-amounts notice may go personally, by email or by certified mail. Under the District's electronic transactions law, an electronic notice satisfies a writing requirement only if both parties agreed to deal electronically and the tenant can save or print it, and it never displaces a specific delivery method another law requires. Practical step: get written consent to electronic notices, and use them only alongside each required method.

title: No Detector Tampering Fee Rule; Cost Recovery Only
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation authorizes, sets or caps a lease fee for removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide detector. Installing detectors is the owner's duty under the District's construction codes, and the law defines owner to exclude the tenant. Two rules shape what a lease may say. First, since August 14, 2026, you may not charge a fee before move-in, during or after the tenancy for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable and compliant with the construction and housing codes; a flat tampering or detector-service fee is therefore risky. Second, the housing regulations forbid a tenant, or anyone there with the tenant's permission, to willfully or wantonly damage, impair or remove equipment of the unit, and the fee law expressly still lets you withhold from the security deposit to replace items the tenant damaged beyond ordinary wear and tear. Practical step: a lease may forbid disabling detectors and require prompt reporting; limit any charge to the actual cost of repairing or replacing a detector the tenant's side removed, disabled or damaged, and do not add a fixed penalty amount. This applies equally to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Algorithm-Specific Rent Rule; General Antitrust Law Applies
bodyText: The District has no statute or housing regulation that specifically bans or regulates setting rents or lease terms with algorithmic pricing or revenue-management software. What does apply is the District's general antitrust law, which makes illegal every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade that takes place at least partly in the District, and bars monopolizing or conspiring to monopolize any part of trade. Whether using a shared pricing tool that pools competitors' data amounts to such a combination is a question for the courts under that general law (and under federal antitrust law), not a rule written for landlords. Practical step: set rents with your own judgment and data; do not adopt rent or occupancy recommendations from a tool that draws on competing landlords' nonpublic information without legal advice. Rent-stabilized units remain subject to the rent stabilization limits however the rent is calculated.

title: No Landlord Entry to Care for Animals
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation gives a landlord a right to enter a rental unit to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal. Caring for a pet is not one of the reasonable purposes for which District law allows entry. Those purposes are tied to the landlord's own duties: keeping the property safe from damage, inspecting, making necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supplying services, showing the unit, and work ordered by a government agency. Each normally needs at least 48 hours' written notice and must fall between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., not on a Sunday or federal holiday, unless the tenant agrees otherwise. The only exception is an emergency for protecting or preserving the premises or the safety of tenants or other persons; an animal in distress may fit only if those facts exist. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: ask the tenant for a written emergency contact and written permission for animal-care entry when the tenant travels, and call animal control or the police for an animal in danger rather than relying on a lease clause.

title: No Application-Fraud Termination Right; Screening Limits Apply
bodyText:
District law gives a landlord no special right to end a tenancy because the tenant lied on the rental application. A lease clause making material misstatements a breach is allowed, but you can act on it only through the ordinary just-cause route for violating a substantial lease obligation: a written notice to correct or vacate giving 30 days, served within 6 months after the violation occurred, and then a court case.

A misstatement discovered more than 6 months after the lease was signed may therefore be hard to use. Many questions cannot lawfully be asked, so a false or missing answer to them can never be a breach: arrests that did not lead to conviction; any criminal history before a conditional offer (except in owner-occupied buildings of 3 or fewer units or where other law requires it); criminal history of household members under 18; eviction cases that did not end in a judgment for you or were filed 3 or more years ago; sealed eviction records; and lease-breach allegations tied to domestic violence, crime victimization, disability or events 3 or more years old.

Practical step: limit the application to lawful questions, keep your screening notices, and use the shared clause, which already excludes information you could not lawfully request or consider.

title: No Periodic Balcony Inspection Law; General Repair Duties Apply
bodyText: The District has no periodic balcony or exterior elevated element inspection law in its statutes and housing regulations: no required engineer's inspection on a fixed cycle, no inspection report to file and no tenant notice of balcony inspections. The general maintenance duties still apply to every rental. Stairways, steps and porches must be firm and safe, with guards or balustrades on open porches more than 24 inches above the ground and handrails on exterior stairs, and the operator of a housing business must keep fire escapes, stairways and other exits in good repair, painted and free of obstruction. A hazardous porch, deck or balcony is a housing-code violation that District inspectors can cite, and in a rent-stabilized unit an unabated serious violation can bear on rent increases.
