Detailed structural standards for balconies, decks and guards are in the District's construction and property maintenance codes (DCMR Title 12). Practical step: have balconies, decks and fire escapes checked as part of routine maintenance and fix loose railings or rot promptly; give 48 hours' written notice before entering a unit to inspect.

title: No Bed Bug Statute; Housing-Code Extermination Rules
bodyText:
District law has no bed bug statute: the Bedbug Control Act of 2022 was never funded and was repealed effective December 6, 2025. Instead, the housing regulations allocate extermination of vermin. In a single-family dwelling the occupant must keep the premises free of vermin. In a two-family or multiple dwelling the occupant handles extermination when only his or her unit is infested, unless the infestation comes from the owner's failure to keep the building rodent-proof or reasonably insect-proof; the owner must exterminate whenever two or more units are infested and must keep common space free of vermin.

Tenants must keep their unit clean and sanitary. You may not charge a fee for extermination that the regulations require you to perform. To enter for inspection or treatment, give at least 48 hours' written notice (or a shorter period the tenant agrees to in writing) and come between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., not on a Sunday or federal holiday, unless the tenant agrees otherwise or there is an emergency.

A lease clause asking tenants to report suspected bed bugs promptly and to follow reasonable preparation instructions is not barred. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Law (2022 Act Repealed Unfunded); Housing Code Extermination Duties
bodyText: The District has no bed bug disclosure or treatment-timeline law for rentals. The Bedbug Control Act of 2022, which would have added bed bug rules and application disclosures, was never funded or put into effect and was repealed in December 2025, so ignore older guidance built on it. Bed bugs fall under the general housing code extermination rules: in a single-family house the occupant must keep the premises free of vermin; in a two-family or multiple dwelling, the occupant handles extermination when only that unit is infested, unless the infestation comes from the owner's failure to keep the building reasonably insect-proof; the owner must exterminate whenever two or more units are infested and must keep common spaces free of vermin. These duties are part of the implied warranty of habitability and cannot be waived in the lease. If pesticides will be applied in a multi-unit property, tell each resident 24 hours to 7 days ahead and post notice in common areas (see the pest-control notice entry). For a tenant cooperation clause, use "Pest Reporting and Treatment" clause.

title: No Benefit-Delay Defense; Subsidy and ERAP Protections Apply
bodyText: District law has no rule requiring a court to continue or reinstate a tenancy because a tenant's Social Security, public-benefit or voucher payment arrived late. Related protections apply instead. You may not charge a late fee for any part of the rent that a rent subsidy provider, rather than the tenant, is responsible for paying, and you may never evict for an unpaid late fee. In a nonpayment case the court may stay the case once while an Emergency Rental Assistance Program application is pending, and you must cancel a scheduled eviction if, at least 48 hours before it, the tenant tells you ERAP has approved enough to redeem the tenancy. A tenant can also redeem a nonpayment judgment by paying the full amount before the eviction. You cannot file for possession at all if less than $600 is owed. Source of income is a protected trait under the District's Human Rights Act, and when screening an applicant who will use an income-based subsidy you may not rely on late or missed rent from a period before the applicant had the subsidy. Practical step: before filing a nonpayment case, confirm whether a subsidy or assistance payment is pending, and do not charge late fees on the subsidy share.

title: No Candidate Access Right; Organizer Canvassing Rules and Voter Packet With Disclosures
bodyText: The District has no statute giving political candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators a right of access to apartment buildings, and none requiring a voter-information area. Related District rules: Tenant organizers: in a multifamily building, an organizer who is not a tenant gets the access other uninvited visitors get unless you have a written, consistently enforced no-canvassing policy (then the organizer must be accompanied by a tenant). Whatever canvassing policy you adopt, put it in writing and enforce it evenly. Political affiliation: the Human Rights Act bars different lease terms, services or facilities based on a person's political affiliation. Voter registration: the Rent Administrator's disclosure form that you give each applicant must include the Board of Elections' voter registration packet; for Housing Finance Agency-assisted projects, the packet goes with the pre-lease notice that rents are not regulated. Use the current official forms rather than building your own.

title: Fire or Casualty: No Statute, Just-Cause Limits
bodyText: The District has no statute dealing specifically with fire or other casualty in private residential leases, so neither side gets an automatic casualty termination right by statute. Several rules decide the result instead. If the unit becomes unsafe or unsanitary through housing-code violations the tenant did not cause, and you do not correct them in the time a violation notice allows (or a reasonable time), the lease becomes void, so the tenant is no longer bound. You cannot end the tenancy because of a casualty: eviction is allowed only on the listed grounds, so to clear a damaged unit you must use, for example, the renovation route (Rent Administrator approval and 120 days' notice) or the 180-day discontinuance or demolition routes. If the District placards the unit as unfit, the tenancy is not terminated until you offer the unit back to the tenant, and while a tenant of a unit covered by the Rental Housing Act is displaced by an administrative order because the premises are unsafe, the tenant owes no rent. If the District pays emergency relocation costs for conditions within your control (not an act of God), it can recover them from you. Practical step: do not include a landlord casualty-termination clause; any rent abatement for an unusable unit should be stated as a tenant benefit.

title: No Certificate-of-Occupancy Disclosure; License Posting and Licensing Prerequisites
bodyText: District law does not require a landlord to give a prospective or current tenant a copy of the certificate of occupancy, or to disclose whether one exists, in the lease. A certificate of occupancy still matters. Every rental needs a basic business license with a residential housing endorsement, and every license category except a one-family rental (a single-family home, townhouse, duplex, individual condominium unit or room) requires a certificate of occupancy at the time of licensing; two-family rentals (an English basement or carriage house) and apartment houses of three or more units need one. You must conspicuously post the business license (or a copy) at the premises, available to any tenant, and the Rent Administrator's application disclosure form must include the building's business license. For rent-stabilized buildings, the Tenant Advocate's public housing database is to show certificate-of-occupancy dates and numbers drawn from your filings. Practical step: confirm the certificate and license before listing the unit, and keep copies with the disclosure documents you maintain for tenants.

title: No General Chemical Warning Requirement for Rentals
bodyText: The District has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: no law requires a residential landlord to post or deliver warnings about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm at a rental property or in the lease. Chemical and environmental information duties that do exist for District rentals are specific: the District lead disclosure form for pre-1978 units and the lead rights notice for all units, the lead plumbing disclosure form before every lease and renewal, the 3-year indoor mold history at application, pesticide notices to residents of multi-unit buildings 24 hours to 7 days before application, and copies of code violation reports with the application disclosure form. Each has its own entry. No general warning sign, lease statement or posting about other chemicals (for example, asbestos, formaldehyde or vehicle exhaust in a garage) is required by District landlord-tenant law.

title: No Tenant Notice of Housing Code Variances; Variance Records Are Public
bodyText: District law does not require a landlord to give tenants a copy of a housing code variance or attach it to the lease. How variances work: an owner, licensee or operator ordered to do something under the housing regulations may ask the District, in writing and within the compliance period stated in the notice (never more than 30 days after service), to be excused in whole or in part because full performance would cause exceptional or undue hardship from excessive structural or mechanical difficulty or impracticability. A variance may be granted only to the extent needed and only when compensating factors adequately protect health, welfare and safety. The District must keep a written record of each variance granted or denied, open to public inspection, so tenants can look it up. An appeal to the Board of Appeals and Review must be filed within 10 days after notice of the variance decision. Related duties: tenants receive copies of District violation notices for their unit, and applicants receive recent or unabated violation reports with the application disclosure form. If you hold a variance that bears on those violations, including a copy in the disclosure compilation is good practice.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice; Weather Eviction Ban
bodyText: District law does not require a tenant to notify you before leaving the unit vacant in cold weather, and it sets no freeze-protection duty on a departing tenant. If you want such a notice, you may ask for it in the lease, but a tenant's failure to give it is a lease matter only. The District's only cold-weather tenancy rule runs the other way: you may not carry out an eviction on any day when the National Weather Service predicts at 8:00 a.m. that the temperature at National Airport will fall below 32 degrees Fahrenheit, while precipitation is falling at the unit, or on a day forecast above 95 degrees Fahrenheit. That ban does not apply where a court has found that the tenant committed an illegal act in the unit, that the tenant's actions or presence cause undue hardship to other tenants or neighbors, or that the tenant has abandoned the premises. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike. Practical step: plan any court-ordered eviction around the forecast, and if you add an absence-notice clause, keep it a reporting request rather than a ground for eviction.

title: Habitability Features: What the District Has and Lacks
bodyText: How the District compares on habitability features found elsewhere. (1) Non-waiver: present. Every lease carries an implied warranty that you will keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations, and any lease term contrary to or waiving that chapter is void and may not be included; bad-faith violations can bring treble damages. There is no separate-writing exception for shifting your duties. (2) Oral notice: the District has no rule on whether a lease may designate oral notice, but a witnessed oral or a written repair request counts toward the retaliation presumption, and mold notices may be written or electronic. (3) Renter's insurance: no rule bars requiring it or bars pushing your repair costs onto it, though a lease cannot exempt you from liability for your own negligence. (4) Operational deadlines: there is no general repair-response deadline; the exception is mold, which you must inspect within 7 days of written or electronic notice and remediate within 30 days of inspection. Otherwise, correction periods come from housing-code violation notices, and heating and hot-water systems need yearly inspections in multi-unit buildings. These points apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: No Contamination Disclosure in Leases; Recorded Cleanup Covenants Run With the Land
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a residential lease to disclose that a property is a brownfield or was environmentally cleaned up, or to incorporate recorded environmental use limitations into the lease. Related District rules: after a cleanup, the Department of Energy and Environment may record instruments with the deed, such as a notice of residual risk, a residual risk restriction on use of the property, an access easement or an environmental covenant. These run with the land and bind later users regardless of privity, so a tenant's use of the property is subject to them. When an environmental covenant is created, the agency may designate who must give a copy to each person in possession of the property, among others; failing to do so does not make the covenant invalid. If you own property under such an instrument, follow any copy-delivery instructions the agency gives and do not permit tenant uses the covenant forbids. Separately, the application disclosure form must disclose known indoor mold contamination in the past 3 years (see the mold entry), and pre-1978 homes carry lead disclosure duties (see the lead entries).

title: No Preset Deposit Deductions; No Cleaning Charges
bodyText: District law does not provide for a lease schedule of preset deposit deductions, and two rules make preset charges risky. First, you may not charge a fee or withhold any deposit money for professional cleaning or for other expenses caused by ordinary wear and tear, so a flat move-out cleaning or carpet-cleaning charge is not allowed. Second, when you withhold, you must refund the balance with an itemized statement of the repairs and other uses of the money and the cost of each, within 30 days after your notice of intent to withhold (which itself is due within 45 days after the tenancy ends). That points to actual, documented costs rather than preset figures. A tenant's promise to return the unit in good repair does not require substantial repairs, replacement of obsolete materials or fixing defects that are not the tenant's fault. Practical step: describe in the lease what the deposit secures, and charge actual costs for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: District law does not give tenants a right to pay a security deposit in installments, and does not require you to offer one. You may agree to an installment plan if you wish. Whatever the schedule, the total of the deposit and any other payment held as security may not exceed the first full month's rent and may be charged only once, so you cannot add installments later to build a larger deposit. Each installment must be placed in the interest-bearing escrow account, interest runs from the date each amount is actually paid, and each payment not made by personal check needs a written receipt. Write the deposit terms, including any installment schedule, in the lease or on the deposit receipt. The cap, escrow and written-terms rules do not apply to federally subsidized units or units leased to federal or District agencies.

title: No Rule on Using the Deposit as Last Month Rent
bodyText: District law has no rule on whether a tenant may use the security deposit as the last month's rent, or whether you may apply it that way. The deposit is money held as security for the tenant's performance, to be returned with interest within 45 days after the tenancy ends or withheld only for expenses properly incurred under the deposit terms. Because nonpayment of the last month's rent is an unpaid amount you may claim after move-out, the practical difference is timing: you can account for unpaid rent in your 45-day notice of intent to withhold and itemized statement. If you collect a separate prepaid last month's rent, remember that any payment held as security counts toward the one-month cap together with the deposit, and keep the two clearly separated in the lease and on receipts. Practical step: say in the lease whether the deposit may be applied to rent, so expectations are clear.

title: No Deposit-Transfer Rule on Sale; Buyer Steps Into the Lease
bodyText: District law has no specific rule on what happens to tenants' security deposits when a rental property is sold, such as a duty to transfer deposits to the buyer, notify tenants, or a rule releasing the seller. General rules fill part of the gap. A buyer or other grantee of the landlord's interest takes over the lease: it has the same rights against the tenant that the seller had, and lease covenants run with the property. The Rental Housing Act's definition of housing provider includes an owner's assignee or anyone entitled to receive the rents, so the buyer becomes bound by the deposit, escrow, interest and return rules. A tenant who pays rent to the seller before receiving notice of the sale is protected. For a rent-stabilized building, the housing provider must notify the Rent Administrator of a change in ownership within 30 days. Practical step: in the sale contract, transfer every deposit with accrued interest into a qualifying District escrow account, and notify tenants in writing of the new owner and where deposits are held.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule; Qualified-Worker Rules
bodyText: District law has no rule on lease clauses that name who may make repairs or require a tenant to use your repairer, so such a clause is a contract term. Some work has its own qualification rules. Mold assessment and remediation must be done by District-certified and licensed professionals when you know or have reason to know of indoor mold contamination, and no one may engage in that business without a license. Workers eliminating lead-based paint hazards under a Mayor's order must follow lead-safe work practice standards and be trained, and a tenant may refuse access to anyone not properly certified to do lead work. For lead work you must give at least 48 hours' written notice describing the work, containment and relocation requirements and expected dates, and entry needs the occupant's permission or a warrant. Annual heating, water-heating and air-conditioning inspections must be done by licensed qualified persons. Since you, not the tenant, carry most repair duties in the District, a designated-repairer clause matters mainly for any tasks the tenant has agreed to do. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Disaster-Displaced Guest Rule
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation lets a tenant house people displaced by a disaster or emergency despite lease guest or occupancy limits, or bars a landlord from enforcing those limits against them. The ordinary District rules apply instead. The housing regulations' minimum floor-area-per-occupant standards still govern how many people may live in a unit, and you must tell the tenant the maximum number of occupants in writing. Occupancy limits stricter than the Human Rights Act's family-status presumption (two persons in an efficiency, two per bedroom plus one) are presumed discriminatory against families with children. A guest who overstays is a lease-compliance matter: eviction is available only after a written 30-day notice to correct and only for a substantial lease obligation. Applies to all District rental units, month-to-month or fixed-term. Practical step: during a declared emergency, consider written temporary permission for displaced guests within the housing-code occupancy limit, rather than enforcing a guest clause strictly.

title: No Disaster Tenancy Rule; General Rules Apply
bodyText: The District has no statute saying what happens to a residential tenancy after a declared natural disaster: nothing ends the tenancy automatically, and no disaster-specific rule suspends rent; but for a unit covered by the Rental Housing Act, if the tenant is displaced by an administrative order because the premises are unsafe, the tenant's obligation to pay rent is suspended and the tenancy continues until the unit is offered back and the tenant waives the right to return (14 DCMR § 4300.19). The general rules apply instead. If the unit becomes unsafe or unsanitary through code violations the tenant did not cause and they are not corrected in time, the lease becomes void. If the District placards the unit, the tenancy continues until you offer the unit back. You cannot evict because of the disaster itself, and evictions may not be carried out in extreme cold, heat or precipitation. During a Mayor's natural-disaster or public emergency, the District's anti-price-gouging law bars charging more than a normal price for goods and services; whether it reaches rent is not settled, so avoid emergency rent increases. When the District relocates tenants, it recovers costs from the owner only for conditions within the owner's control, not acts of God. Practical step: document damage, communicate repair timelines in writing, and do not charge rent for a period the unit cannot be used without legal advice.

title: No Flag or Sign Display Right; Neutral Rules and Organizer Posting Rights
bodyText: The District has no statute giving tenants a right to display a flag, banner or political sign, and none barring a lease rule on window, balcony or door displays. Nor does District law limit a condominium or homeowners association's rules on an occupant's political signs. A lease may therefore set neutral display rules (size, placement, no damage, no blocking exits or windows needed for light and air). Two limits apply. The Human Rights Act bars different lease terms or restrictions based on a protected trait, which in the District includes political affiliation, religion and national origin; a display rule enforced against one party's or one faith's displays but not others' invites a discrimination claim. And in a multifamily building you may not interfere with tenants or tenant organizers posting tenant-organization information on all building bulletin boards, distributing literature in common areas or placing it under doors. Practical step: write display rules in neutral terms, apply them evenly, and leave bulletin boards open to tenant-organization notices. Enforce a breach only through the 30-day notice to correct.

title: Disturbances: Lease Duty and the 30-Day Cure Notice
bodyText:
District landlord-tenant law does not itself impose a duty on tenants not to disturb neighbors, so your lease clause is what creates it; separately, the criminal code makes an unreasonably loud noise between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. that is likely to disturb people in their residences a misdemeanor. A tenant may be evicted only on a listed ground, so a disturbance is enforced as a violation of an obligation of tenancy, which must be a substantial obligation in a valid lease or one the housing regulations impose.

Serve a written Notice to Correct or Vacate giving 30 days to correct; it must describe the facts and cite the lease provision, say what the tenant must do, warn that you may go to court if it is not corrected, and say that a copy goes to the Rent Administrator. You cannot base the notice on a violation more than six months old. If a court finds that the tenant or another occupant committed an illegal act in the unit or building, a 30-day notice to vacate applies instead (a 10-day notice for certain violent crimes, though a regulation still says to wait 30 days before filing); an occupant's act counts only if the tenant knew or should have known that the illegal act was taking place. Victims of intrafamily offenses have a defense. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: District law has no statute on double-letting, that is, renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period, and no statutory rent-abatement remedy for it. A tenant's rights against you in that situation come from the lease and general law. Be careful, because the Rental Housing Act's protections attach to anyone entitled to possession of a rental unit, including subtenants, so a second person you put in possession may become a tenant you can remove only on a statutory ground with the required notice, and the housing regulations' occupancy limits still apply to the unit. Do not confuse double-letting with the District's "double rent" rule, which lets a landlord recover double rent from a tenant who gives notice to quit and then holds over without reasonable excuse. Practical step: do not sign a new lease or hand over keys until the prior tenancy has ended and the unit is vacant. These points apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: No Drug-Free Addendum Statute
bodyText: The District has no statute or housing regulation that authorizes, requires or prescribes a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. You may include a lease term forbidding illegal activity, but it cannot change how a tenancy ends: a lease violation still needs written notice and 30 days to cure, an illegal act supports eviction only after a court determines it occurred (with a 30-day notice, or a 10-day notice for certain violent crimes, though a regulation still says to wait 30 days before filing), and an occupant's act counts against the tenant only if the tenant knew or should have known of it. For drug activity, the District has a separate expedited court action against a rental unit used as a drug haven, which a housing provider, the Mayor and some community groups can bring; the court weighs listed factors, and a tenant who could not reasonably have known, or who reported the activity to police, has a defense. Victims of intrafamily offenses have defenses as well. An addendum that promises automatic termination or eviction without court would misstate District law. Use the optional District illegal-act clause ("Illegal Acts" clause) instead of a separate addendum.

title: No Defective-Drywall Disclosure; Code-Violation Disclosure and Implied Warranty Apply
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to disclose defective (for example, sulfur-emitting imported) drywall to a prospective or current tenant, and no drywall-specific remediation rule for rentals. General District rules still apply. Every lease carries an implied warranty that the owner will keep the premises in compliance with the housing code, and a lease is void if, at its start, the unit has housing code violations that make it unsafe or unsanitary and that the owner knew or should have known about. The application disclosure form must include housing code and property maintenance code violation reports for the building or unit issued within the last 12 months, or older ones not yet abated. If a drywall problem is known to cause a code violation, fix it before renting. Some separate disclosure duties may overlap with drywall damage, notably the 3-year indoor mold disclosure (see the mold entry). There is no District form or notice for drywall itself.

title: No Emergency-Contact Duty; Manager, Agent and Eviction-Notice Rules
bodyText:
District law has no rule requiring a landlord to give tenants a 24-hour emergency phone number or to collect an emergency contact from each tenant. Three related rules apply.

First, the tenant's emergency contact matters at eviction: on the day of a court-ordered eviction you must mail a notice to the tenant's emergency contact, if one was provided, and post it at the unit, naming an agent who can let the tenant back in to retrieve belongings during the 7-day period. Collecting an emergency contact in the application or lease makes that notice possible.

Second, your rental housing license application must name a property manager or resident manager responsible for maintenance and repairs, you must keep that appointment in place and report any change within 5 days, and the license must be posted on the premises and available to tenants.

Third, a non-resident owner must appoint and keep a registered agent in the District for service of legal papers, or face a $300 penalty, with the licensing agency serving as agent if none is appointed.

Practical step: give tenants a maintenance and emergency contact for your manager, collect each tenant's emergency contact, and keep license and agent information current.

title: No Employee-Housing Statute; Just-Cause Rules May Reach On-Site Staff
bodyText: The District has no statute on employee housing: no District statute or housing regulation requires a signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating conditions for an employee who lives on site, ends the employee's right to occupy when the job ends, or requires an offer of a rental agreement afterward. That gap matters because the Rental Housing Act defines tenant broadly to include anyone entitled to the possession, occupancy or benefits of a rental unit owned by another, and its eviction rules apply to every covered unit: a tenant may be evicted only on the listed grounds with the required notice, and the end of a lease or of a job is not one of those grounds. A resident manager or building employee who occupies a unit as part of the job may therefore be treated as a tenant whose occupancy can be ended only through the statutory process; how the Act applies to job-linked occupancy is a question for case law. Practical step: if an employee will live on site, put the housing terms in a separate written lease with its own rent (or stated rent credit) and get legal advice before relying on the end of employment to recover the unit.

title: No Employee-Screening Mandate; Limits if You Screen
bodyText: District law does not require landlords to run background checks on maintenance staff, leasing agents or other employees who have access to units. If you choose to screen, the District's Fair Criminal Record Screening law limits how: an employer with more than 10 employees in the District may not ask about arrests or criminal accusations that are not pending or did not lead to a conviction, may not ask about convictions until after a conditional job offer, and may then withdraw the offer only for a legitimate business reason weighed against the job's duties, the offense's bearing on them, time elapsed, age at the time, frequency and seriousness, and evidence of rehabilitation. A rejected applicant may request the records you used and a notice of the right to complain to the Office of Human Rights. Separate rules govern who may do mold and lead work in units. Practical step: adopt a written policy that runs any criminal check after a conditional offer and documents the business reason for any withdrawal. These points do not depend on whether tenancies are fixed-term or month-to-month.

title: No Landlord Environmental-Event Termination
bodyText: District law gives a landlord no right to end a tenancy because of an environmental event or hazard, and a lease clause creating one would conflict with the District's closed list of eviction grounds. Hazards are handled through repair and relocation instead. If the District orders an owner to fix lead-based paint hazards, the owner must pay reasonable temporary relocation expenses for an at-risk tenant until the unit passes clearance, give at least 14 days' written notice before relocating the tenant (unless the Mayor orders or the parties agree to less), try to keep the household nearby, and let the tenant return on the same terms. Mold must be inspected within 7 days of a tenant's written or electronic notice and remediated within 30 days. If code violations the tenant did not cause make the unit unsafe and are not corrected in time, the lease becomes void, which frees the tenant, not you. To take a unit out of use you must follow the renovation, rehabilitation or discontinuance routes with their notice periods. Practical step: do not include a landlord environmental-termination clause in District leases.

title: EV Charger Removal at Move-Out
bodyText: No District law now in force says what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends. Until then, the parties' written installation agreement and the general rules on alterations and move-out condition govern, so put removal, restoration, any buy-out price and responsibility for damage in that agreement. Watch item: the Comprehensive Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Access, Readiness, and Sustainability Amendment Act of 2024 contains an end-of-tenancy rule, but it applies only after funding, which has not occurred. Once in effect, at the end of the lease the tenant would have to remove a removable charger, sell it to the housing provider at an agreed price, or transfer ownership without sale to the housing provider or another tenant, and a housing provider would bear the cost of removing a shared charger it needs to remove for repairs. Deposit deductions for removal damage follow the ordinary security-deposit rules (no deduction for ordinary wear and tear). Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: address charger removal in the written approval you give the tenant; do not rely on the shared Colorado-based clause, which the District lease does not use.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking Areas
bodyText: No District law now in force governs a tenant's charger in a parking area other tenants can use, or what a landlord may charge for one. Today it is a matter of agreement: you may refuse, or allow it on written terms covering the space, electricity, insurance, damage and removal, subject to the rule that rent-stabilized units may not carry unapproved mandatory fees. Watch item: the 2024 electric vehicle act would, once funded, let a housing provider charge a tenant who installs a charger in an area accessible to other tenants a reasonable fee to reserve that specific space and otherwise charge only the actual cost of electricity; unless a written agreement says otherwise, the provider could require that tenant (and each later tenant with exclusive rights to the space) to pay the electricity, pay for damage from installation, maintenance, repair, removal or replacement, keep the charger in repair, and carry insurance naming the provider as additional insured. A provider could also install shared chargers for all tenants and set terms of use including actual electricity cost. None of this is in effect yet. Practical step: write the reservation fee, electricity reimbursement and damage terms into the approval agreement.

title: No Eviction Penalty or Fee-Shifting Clauses
bodyText: No District statute is framed as a ban on eviction-penalty clauses, but District rules leave little room for one. A residential lease may not require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees, and including or demanding such a clause is prohibited, with treble damages for bad faith. Attorney's fees are not available to either side in an eviction action under the eviction statute. In an eviction case the court itself awards the prevailing party taxable costs (filing fee, notary, postage, up to $10 per defendant for a special process server, and writ and Marshals fees), so a lease charge for filing or serving is not needed and risks double recovery. Late-fee rules close another route: a late fee may be charged only once per late payment, may not exceed 5% of the rent due, and nonpayment of a late fee can never be the basis for an eviction. Fees for notices or other services you must provide are risky under the District fee rules (see the notice-fee row). This applies to every residential tenancy. Practical step: leave out any eviction fee, notice fee, filing charge or penalty triggered by a notice or lawsuit; recover only rent, lawful late fees, proven damages and court-awarded costs.

title: No Lease-Named Agent for Eviction Papers
bodyText: District law does not let a lease name a person to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. The eviction summons must be served as the forcible entry and detainer statute provides: at least 14 days before the initial hearing, by delivery to the tenant, by leaving a copy with someone over 16 residing on or in possession of the premises, or by posting on the premises (then mailing a copy first-class within 3 calendar days and filing a timestamped photo). Pre-filing eviction notices have their own delivery rules. The District's agent rule runs the other way: if you are a non-resident owner of even one District rental unit, you must appoint and keep a registered agent for service of process, a District resident or District-incorporated organization, filed with the licensing agency; otherwise the agency's Director serves as your agent, and you face a $300 penalty. Practical step: if you live outside the District, appoint your registered agent before licensing, and put your agent and a notice address in the lease.

title: No Lease Exemption-Waiver Rule; Exemptions Bar Distraint
bodyText: District law has no statute on a tenant's waiver, in a lease, of the homestead or property exemptions that protect a debtor from collection. It neither supplies waiver wording nor expressly forbids a lease waiver, so whether such a clause could be enforced is a question for the courts, which may refuse to enforce lease terms they find unconscionable. The exemptions themselves are broad: a District householder's household furnishings and goods (up to set dollar limits), a vehicle interest, tools of the trade, health aids, family pictures, benefits such as Social Security and unemployment, three months' provisions, and the debtor's interest in the home are free from distraint, attachment, levy and execution sale; limited exemptions also cover earnings. Those protections reach a landlord's distraint for rent as well as a judgment levy. Separately, a District lease may not contain a confession-of-judgment clause or require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees. Practical step: leave exemption-waiver language out of District leases; collect unpaid rent through a court judgment and the ordinary collection process, which respects the exemptions.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: District law has no expedited or alternative procedure for handling a security deposit, such as a quicker refund in exchange for waiving the itemized statement, a fee for faster processing, or a separate track for tenants who are evicted or abandon the unit. One timeline applies to every tenancy that ends, however it ends: within 45 days after termination, either pay back the deposit and any interest due without demand, or deliver written notice of intent to withhold personally or by certified mail; then within 30 days after that notice, refund the balance with an itemized statement of repairs and their costs. Missing these steps is prima facie evidence the tenant is owed the full deposit, and a bad-faith failure to return a deposit can cost treble damages. A lease term that waives these steps would be void as contrary to the housing regulations. Nothing stops you from refunding sooner.

title: No Extended-Absence Notice Rule
bodyText:
District law does not require a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, and it gives you no special right to enter while the tenant is away. If you want advance notice, put it in the lease; a lease term asking for notice of absences longer than a set number of days, with recovery of actual damages if the tenant willfully fails to give it, is not barred.

The ordinary entry rules still apply during an absence: give at least 48 hours' written notice (or a shorter period the tenant agrees to in writing), enter only for a reasonable purpose such as inspection, repairs or agreed services, and come between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., not on a Sunday or federal holiday, unless the tenant agrees to another time.

You may enter without notice only in an emergency to protect the premises or people. An absence alone does not end the tenancy; treating the unit as abandoned requires care, and the cold-weather eviction ban lifts only where a court has specifically found abandonment. A breach of the notice term can support eviction only if it is a substantial lease obligation, after a 30-day notice to correct. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Rule Requiring Landlords to Allow Home Child Care
bodyText: District law does not require a residential landlord to let a tenant run a child care business in the unit, and it sets no lease conditions (such as liability waivers or insurance) for doing so, so your lease controls. Anyone who operates a child development facility, which includes a home that provides care, supervision and guidance to children on a regular basis, must hold a District license, with narrow exemptions such as care by relatives. A separate rule protects condominium owners, not renters: condominium instruments entered into, amended or recorded after November 11, 2023 may not prohibit a licensed child development facility, and associations may require reasonable insurance (generally capped at $500,000) and retrofit and utility cost-sharing. If you rent out a condominium unit, the association's rules may therefore allow what your lease restricts. If you permit home child care, require proof of the license, adequate liability insurance naming you, and compliance with building and occupancy rules, and put the terms in writing. A ban or condition must be applied without discrimination, including on the basis of familial status or source of income. The same approach applies to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Farmland Lease or Tenant Hunting-Rights Rule
bodyText: This topic does not arise for District rentals. The District has no farmland leasing statute and no rule giving, or withholding, hunting or fishing rights to a tenant of rented land. The Council is authorized to restrict, prohibit and regulate hunting and fishing and the taking of wild animals in the District, so any hunting or fishing question is governed by those public rules rather than by the lease. For residential leases, nothing about hunting or fishing needs to appear in the lease. If a lease covers outdoor space (a yard or waterfront), the general lease terms on permitted use of the premises and any District restrictions on firearms and wildlife apply; the firearms rules are discussed in the firearms row. Practical step: do not add a hunting-rights clause to District leases; if a rental includes unusual outdoor space, describe its permitted uses in plain terms.

title: No Deposit-Alternative Statute; Existing Limits Apply
bodyText: District law has no statute or regulation on deposit-alternative programs (a monthly or one-time fee, surety bond or insurance product instead of a security deposit). Existing rules still limit them. Any money the tenant pays you as security for performing the lease is a security deposit, so a refundable alternative is subject to the one-month cap, escrow, interest and return rules. No fee other than the application fee may be charged before the lease is signed, so an alternative fee cannot be collected up front at application or approval. In a rent-stabilized unit, a fee that tenants are required to pay is a mandatory fee and is barred unless approved, so a program must be truly optional (opt-in). After move-out, any claim for damage or unpaid rent must follow the 45-day written notice with photos or other documentation, and you must keep proof of service for 60 days before sending the amount to a debt collector; debt-collection limits apply. Practical step: offer any alternative only as an optional choice alongside an ordinary deposit, and disclose it in the screening notice.

title: No District Limit on Lease Firearm Rules; Carry-Law Signage for Common Areas
bodyText: District law does not limit a private landlord's lease rules on firearms. No District statute protects a tenant's right to keep a firearm in the unit, and none bars a rule against firearms stored in a locked vehicle in the parking area. (Public housing run by the D.C. Housing Authority has its own rules; they do not reach private landlords.) District carry law does shape how such rules work. A person licensed to carry a concealed pistol is presumed barred from carrying it onto private residential property unless the owner or person in control authorizes it personally in advance; in a tenant's own unit, the tenant is normally the person in control. The statute's definition of a residence leaves out a building's adjacent common areas, which appear to fall under the separate rule for non-residential private property: carrying is presumed allowed there unless the property is posted with conspicuous signage prohibiting it or the owner tells the licensee personally. Anyone keeping a firearm where a minor is likely to reach it must lock it up. Practical step: if you restrict firearms, say so in the lease and post signs in common areas; enforce a breach through the 30-day notice to correct or vacate.

title: No Flood Disclosure; Violation and Mold Disclosures May Capture Water Damage
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to tell a prospective or current tenant whether a rental is in a floodplain, has flooded before, or carries flood insurance, and there is no District flood disclosure form, rider or tenant termination right tied to flood history. The District's floodplain rules regulate building and development, not leases. Related duties still reach flood damage: the application disclosure form must include housing code violation reports for the building or unit from the last 12 months (or older unabated ones), and must disclose indoor mold contamination known or that should have been known in the unit or common areas in the past 3 years, unless a licensed professional remediated it, which often follows water intrusion. A lease of a unit that is unsafe or unsanitary at the start because of code violations the owner knew or should have known about is void. Practical step: although not required, many landlords voluntarily tell applicants about known flooding and recommend renter's insurance, since standard renter's policies typically exclude flood.

title: No Pre-Lease Foreclosure Disclosure; Auction Buyer Needs Recorded Deed Before Acting Against Occupants
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord whose property is in foreclosure, or who has received a foreclosure notice, to tell new or current tenants before signing a lease, and no District foreclosure disclosure form for rentals. What District law does provide: a purchaser at a foreclosure or other auction may not issue a notice to quit, sue for possession or ejectment, or charge rent or use and occupancy against a current occupant until a deed to the purchaser is recorded, and that rule does not alter the rights of tenants whose tenancies survive foreclosure. Because the District's just-cause eviction rule protects a tenant who keeps paying rent regardless of lease expiration and binds whoever is the housing provider, a foreclosure buyer generally takes the building subject to existing tenancies (see the foreclosure tenant-rights entry). The applicant disclosure form also asks about pending conversions and ownership. Practical step: although not required, telling applicants about a pending foreclosure avoids misrepresentation claims and practical disputes over where to pay rent.

title: No Foreign-Ownership or Foreign-Adversary Leasing Restriction
bodyText: The District has no foreign-adversary land law: no District statute or housing regulation bars citizens, governments or companies of particular countries from buying or leasing District real estate, voids a lease to them, or requires a lease to identify a foreign tenant or owner. Two old provisions address aliens. One extends to aliens, for District real estate, the rights to acquire, hold, own and dispose of real estate conferred by an 1897 federal act on the territories; the other exempts legations and residences of foreign-government representatives from an 1887 federal restriction on alien ownership. What those federal acts provide today is federal law, but neither District provision restricts residential leasing. Foreign missions are a separate federal regime: a rental unit operated by a foreign government as a residence for diplomatic personnel is outside the Rental Housing Act, and embassy property is subject to the federal Foreign Missions Act. Leasing to an individual foreign national is otherwise an ordinary tenancy, and the Human Rights Act forbids discrimination based on national origin. Practical step: no foreign-ownership statement is needed in a District lease; screen all applicants on the same criteria.

title: No Rule on Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation addresses whether a landlord may have the tenant reimburse government fees charged to the landlord, such as the annual $30-per-unit rental unit fee, business license or registration fees. The law simply makes the housing provider liable to pay them. Several rules limit a pass-through in practice. Any money you require as a condition of occupancy is rent under the Rental Housing Act, so a reimbursement charge works as part of the rent: in a rent-stabilized unit it would be a mandatory fee for an unapproved service or facility and could push the rent above the lawful amount; for any unit, a new or higher charge is a rent increase that cannot take effect until more than 60 days after written notice. Fees for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable, such as trash, may not be charged at all. If you finance energy work through a property-assessed special energy assessment and raise rents to pay it, you must pass the energy savings through to those tenants. Practical step: build government fees into the base rent rather than billing them separately.

title: Grilling and Fire Safety Rules
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation sets rules for tenants' grills, barbecues or open-flame devices on porches and balconies, or for keeping flammable materials in a rental unit. Those subjects belong to the District's Construction Codes, which by statute control fire and explosion hazards from the storage, handling or use of substances, materials and devices, the use and occupancy of buildings and premises, and mechanical equipment including barbecues.

The Construction Codes are model codes as adopted and amended by the District in Title 12 of the municipal regulations (including the fire code), so the specific distances and fuel rules may be stricter than a lease clause. A lease may add its own reasonable restrictions, such as banning grills on balconies or within a set distance of the building, because no District statute or housing regulation protects a tenant's right to grill.

Violations are lease-compliance matters (written 30-day notice to correct; only a substantial lease obligation supports eviction). Applies to all District rental units.

Practical step: keep the shared fire-safety clause and check the current District fire code for balcony grilling rules in multi-unit buildings.

title: No Guaranty Statute; Draft Guaranty Scope Expressly
bodyText: District law has no statute on lease guaranties: nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to set a maximum amount or end date, or caps a deposit taken from a guarantor. The scope of a guaranty is a matter of contract law. That matters more in the District than elsewhere, because a tenant who keeps paying rent cannot be evicted when the lease term ends; the tenancy simply continues, usually month to month, and rent can change under the District's notice rules. A guaranty that speaks only of "the term of this Lease" may be read not to cover that continued tenancy. Two screening rules also touch guarantors: if you approve an applicant only on condition of a co-signer that your written criteria or advertisement did not call for, that is an adverse action requiring a written notice of the specific grounds and the applicant's dispute rights; and before the lease is signed you may charge a prospective tenant no fee except an application fee. Practical step: have the guarantor sign a separate guaranty that says expressly whether it covers renewals, any continued tenancy after the term, and rent increases, and spell out any cap or end date you intend.

title: No Statutory Guest Day Limit; Voucher Households Have a 30/90-Day Program Limit
bodyText:
District law sets no maximum number of days a guest may stay in a private rental and does not stop a lease from setting one, such as 14 consecutive days. A day limit is a lease term like any other: put it in the lease, apply it evenly to every household, and allow reasonable exceptions a disabled tenant needs (for example, a caregiver). Two program rules run alongside your lease. For a Housing Choice Voucher household, the Housing Authority limits a guest to 30 consecutive days or 90 cumulative days in any 12 months (with exceptions it may approve), and that rule binds the family whatever your lease says.

Public housing has its own shorter limits, which do not apply to private landlords. A guest who overstays becomes a lease-compliance issue, not a trespasser you can remove yourself: you must give written notice and 30 days to correct before seeking possession, and only a court can order an eviction. See the general guest-policy entry for the rest of the District rules.

title: No Guest-Policy Statute; Fair Housing, Damage, Voucher and Cure-Notice Limits
bodyText:
No District statute sets or limits a private landlord's guest policy, so a lease may include reasonable guest rules. Several District rules shape them. Apply guest rules the same way to every household: the Human Rights Act bars different lease terms based on traits such as familial status, family responsibilities, marital status or disability, and a disabled tenant may need a reasonable accommodation (for example, a regular caregiver). The tenant answers for guest damage: damage caused by a guest's negligence or abuse is not ordinary wear and tear, and a tenant may not let anyone on the premises willfully damage the unit.

A long-staying guest who pays rent or claims a right to the unit may become a subtenant, which brings in the lease's occupancy and sublet terms. Tenants in the Housing Choice Voucher program must also follow the Housing Authority's own guest-stay limits, which apply apart from your lease. Enforcement: a guest-rule breach supports eviction only after a written notice and 30 days to correct; the end of the lease term does not end the tenancy. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No General Guest Access Right; Tenant Organizer and Cable Access Rules
bodyText: The District has no general statute guaranteeing tenants' guests, delivery people or service suppliers access to a multi-unit building, and none bars a fee for guests. Three narrower rules apply. Tenant organizers: in a multifamily building, an organizer who is not a tenant gets the same access as other uninvited outside parties unless you have a written, consistently enforced no-canvassing policy; even then, an organizer accompanied by a tenant gets the access invited visitors get. You may not interfere with meetings in units, community rooms or lobbies, or with literature and bulletin-board postings, and you may not attend or record meetings without permission. Penalties include civil fines of up to $10,000 (inflation-adjusted). Cable television: you may not interfere with installation of cable facilities (you may set reasonable conditions and make the operator or tenant bear the cost) and may not charge tenants for allowing access or charge cable subscribers different rent. Supportive housing: clients of a permanent housing program may receive visitors under their lease. Practical step: keep any canvassing policy in writing and enforce it evenly.

title: No Required Fitness Statement; Deliver Chapter 3 Instead
bodyText: District law does not require the lease itself to say that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation, because the warranty applies automatically: every lease or rental agreement is deemed to include an implied warranty that the owner will maintain the premises in compliance with the housing regulations. What you must hand over instead is the text: at the commencement of every tenancy, and to each existing tenant, you must provide a copy of the housing-code chapter on leases and tenant rights (14 DCMR chapter 3) together with the sections on civil enforcement (§ 101) and notification of tenants about violations (§ 106). At application you must also give the Rent Administrator's disclosure form, which includes recent housing-code violation reports and the Office of the Tenant Advocate's Tenant Bill of Rights. Do not add lease language that limits or waives the warranty; such terms are void and may not be included. Practical step: attach the required chapter 3 copy to every new lease as an exhibit and keep proof of delivery. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: No Holdover-Rate Statute; Double Rent Only After Tenant Notice
bodyText: The District has no statute that caps or sets a lease-stated holdover rate (such as a percentage of daily rent), and none that authorizes one. In practice a holdover rate has little room to work: a tenant who stays after the term while paying rent is not holding over, and you cannot end the tenancy by notice or at the end of the term, so a clause charging a higher rate for staying past the term cannot lawfully be triggered by the term's end. The only statutory holdover rate is double the lease rent, owed when the tenant has given written notice of intention to quit and then stays without reasonable excuse; it runs for the time of the wrongful holding over and can be claimed with possession up to judgment. A lease figure above that is not backed by any District statute and could be challenged as an unenforceable penalty or as unconscionable. In a rent-stabilized unit, any higher charge for continued occupancy would also have to fit the rent-increase limits. Practical step: do not set a separate holdover rate in a District lease; rely on the double-rent rule for a tenant who gives notice and stays.

title: No Home-Business Statute; Lease and Zoning Control
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation makes a home-based business a protected use of a rental unit or limits a landlord's ability to restrict one. Your lease may prohibit or condition business use. Whether a home occupation is allowed at all is a zoning question under the District's zoning regulations (Title 11 of the DCMR); a home occupation permit may be required under those rules. If you allow business use, put the limits in writing: no customer traffic, signage, employees, inventory or equipment that disturbs neighbors, overloads utilities or violates occupancy rules; proof of any required permit or license; and adequate insurance. A breach of a substantial lease term on business use can be enforced only through the 30-day notice to correct or vacate. Licensed child care in the home is covered separately. The same approach applies to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No House-Rules Statute; Prohibited Terms, Retaliation and Cure Notice Limit Rules
bodyText:
No District statute sets conditions for enforcing private house rules or limits a landlord's changes to rules during a tenancy (public housing has its own rules). Whether a rule adopted after signing binds the tenant is a contract question, so the safest course is rules attached to the lease at signing, and written tenant agreement for later rules that add duties.

Limits that do apply to every covered unit: no rule or lease term may waive the housing code's tenant protections, exempt you from liability for your own negligence, waive jury trial, make the tenant pay your court costs or legal fees, or confess judgment; such terms are void, and including them in bad faith can bring treble damages.

Courts may also strike other unconscionable terms. You may not charge fees for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable. A new rule that increases a tenant's obligations or cuts services can be retaliatory, and is presumed so within six months after a tenant's repair request, complaint or organizing. In a rent-stabilized unit, a substantial cut in services or facilities can lead to a rent reduction.

A rule breach supports eviction only after written notice and 30 days to correct; the end of a lease term does not end the tenancy.

title: Immigration Status: No Specific District Rule; National-Origin and Debt-Collection Limits
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation specifically bars a private landlord from asking about an applicant's immigration status, and none makes it unlawful to rent to a person who is not lawfully present. Several District rules still protect immigrant tenants. The Human Rights Act forbids discrimination in any rental transaction based on actual or perceived national origin, and also on place of residence and source of income, so a citizenship or immigration screen that operates as a national-origin screen is risky; federal fair housing law adds its own limits. The District's debt-collection law covers landlords collecting rent or other amounts more than 30 days past due from a residential lease, because it treats the original creditor as a debt collector, and it forbids collecting by disclosing or threatening to disclose a tenant's citizenship status to anyone. Public housing and voucher programs run by the Housing Authority follow federal eligible-status rules. Practical step: verify identity and income with documents any applicant can supply, do not ask about immigration status, and never mention status when collecting money.

title: No Health or Care-Facility Lease Termination Right
bodyText: The District has no statute letting a tenant end a fixed-term lease early because of age, illness, disability or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and none releasing the estate when a tenant dies. A tenant in that position under a fixed term stays liable under the lease, but your damages are limited by your duty to mitigate: if the tenant leaves before the term ends, you must take reasonable steps, such as trying to re-rent, to reduce your loss. A month-to-month tenant can always leave on a 30-day written notice. Two other rules may apply. A tenant who is a victim of an intrafamily offense can be released from the lease on written notice with a protective order or qualified third-party documentation. And District human rights law bars disability discrimination in the terms of a rental and requires reasonable accommodations in rules, policies and practices; a request to end a lease early because of a disability should be considered on that basis rather than refused automatically. Practical step: if you want to offer an early-release option for health or care-facility moves, put it in the lease or agree to it in writing; it must not require more than 30 days' notice to vacate unless the lease meets the District's rent-increase-notice condition.

title: No Lease Initials Requirement
bodyText: No District statute, housing regulation or court rule requires a tenant to initial particular lease clauses, or makes a clause enforceable only if it is initialed or separately signed. What District law does require is that certain terms appear in the written lease in the first place: the maximum late fee and grace period, a sole-discretion sublet ban, the statements needed for a tenant notice to vacate longer than 30 days, and the deposit terms (in the lease or on the receipt). Initials do not cure a term the law forbids, such as a jury-trial waiver or a clause making the tenant pay the owner's legal fees, and do not stand in for a separate later writing where the law asks for one. Applies to all District rental units, month-to-month or fixed-term. Practical step: initials on key clauses are optional good practice that helps prove the tenant saw them; they are not a District requirement.

title: No Specific Penalty for Missing Inspection Notice
bodyText: District law does not attach a specific penalty to skipping the move-out inspection notice. The inspection itself is optional: you may inspect within 3 days (excluding weekends and holidays) before or after the tenancy ends, and if you do, you must give the tenant written notice of the date and time at least 10 days ahead. The consequences come from the return rules instead. If you do not either refund the deposit with any interest due or send a written notice of intent to withhold within 45 days, and then refund the balance with an itemized statement within 30 days of that notice, the tenant is presumed entitled to the full deposit and interest, and a bad-faith failure to return it can cost treble damages. Since August 14, 2026, any post-move-out claim must also come with photographs or other documentation, which an un-noticed inspection makes harder to defend. Housing regulation violations generally can also draw fines.

title: Co-Tenant Liability Rests on the Lease
bodyText:
District law has no statute on co-tenant liability, so a lease clause making all tenants jointly and severally liable for rent and other obligations is lawful and is what creates that liability. One statutory override applies: a tenant who is a victim of an intrafamily offense, or the parent or guardian of a minor victim, is released from the lease on written notice plus a copy of a qualifying court order or documentation signed by a qualified third party (such as a police officer, health professional or domestic violence counselor), requested within 90 days of the incident.

The release takes effect 14 days after you receive both, or earlier if a new tenancy begins, and the tenant owes only rent prorated to the earlier of re-renting or 14 days after the request, notwithstanding any lease penalty; amounts owed before the release are unaffected. When screening, if you approve an applicant only on condition of a co-signer the advertised terms did not require, that is an adverse action that needs a written notice with the reasons and dispute rights. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Key-Control Policy Mandate
bodyText: The District has no rule requiring a written key-control policy, a master-key log or background checks of employees with key access, whatever the size of the complex. What District law does require: give each tenant an adequate lock and key for every entrance door at move-in and keep the locks in repair; in multi-unit buildings, keep exterior doors locking so outsiders cannot enter without a key; change the locks within 5 business days when an intrafamily-offense victim asks in writing and keep keys away from an excluded offender; and enter a unit only for a reasonable purpose, at a reasonable time and after 48 hours' written notice except in an emergency, so staff holding keys must follow those entry rules. If you employ more than 10 people in the District and want to screen staff who will hold keys, the employer fair-criminal-screening law limits when and how you may ask about criminal records (see the senior-housing staff row). Practical step: adopt an internal key log and access policy as good practice.

title: No Landlord Liability Insurance Mandate; Lease May Not Release Owner Negligence
bodyText: The District does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to show proof of insurance to obtain a rental license or registration, or to disclose its insurance to tenants. The licensing rules require a basic business license, a named property or resident manager, and a billing account for inspection fees, but not insurance. Insurance can still be required in narrower settings: some District housing programs (for example, certain affordable-housing transactions) ask owners for proof of insurance as a program condition, and condominium associations carry master policies under their instruments. Lease limits that relate to insurance: a lease may not exempt the owner from, or limit, liability for injuries or property damage caused by the owner's negligence, so a clause telling tenants that the landlord's insurance does not cover them must not be framed as a release of the landlord's own negligence. A lease may require renter's insurance; the District has no statute on that either way. Practical step: carry adequate liability coverage as a business matter and keep lease insurance language within the negligence rule.

title: No Self-Cure-as-Rent Statute; Recover Damage Costs as Damages
bodyText: District law has no statute letting a private landlord cure a tenant's breach (for example, by repairing tenant-caused damage or removing trash) and then bill the cost to the tenant as additional rent. You may still recover the reasonable cost of damage the tenant, a family member or a guest caused through negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse, but as damages, not as rent, and not for ordinary wear and tear. Keep several limits in mind. You may enter the unit to make repairs only for a reasonable purpose, at a reasonable time (9 a.m. to 5 p.m., not Sundays or federal holidays, unless the tenant agrees otherwise) and after at least 48 hours' written notice, except in an emergency. You may not charge any fee for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable. A substantial lease or housing-code violation can lead to eviction only after a written notice giving the tenant 30 days to correct it. Labeling a repair bill as rent invites disputes over rent-based remedies and late fees. Practical step: send a written notice to correct, keep photos and invoices, and recover tenant-caused repair costs by agreement, from the deposit at move-out with the required itemized notice, or by a court judgment.

title: Yard Work: No Separate-Writing Rule; Control Decides
bodyText:
District law has no rule requiring a separate signed writing before a tenant takes on yard work, and no statute assigns lawn care or irrigation to either side. The housing regulations decide by control: the tenant must observe the sanitation rules in the parts of the premises under the tenant's exclusive control, while you remain responsible for vacant areas, common space and anything not under a single tenant's exclusive control. Yards must be kept free of litter and refuse, and untended growth over 10 inches or growth that harbors rodents is prohibited; enforcement notices go to the owner. So a lease term making the tenant of a single-family home or a unit with a private yard responsible for mowing and leaf raking is lawful, but shared yards in a multi-unit building stay your job.

Sidewalk snow removal is the owner's duty within the first 8 hours of daylight after snow stops; you may delegate it to a tenant by written agreement, but you stay liable for any fine and may seek reimbursement under that agreement.

Practical step: list yard tasks specifically in the lease. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Lease Amendment by Notice; Entire-Agreement Clauses
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation lets a housing provider change an existing lease by written notice to comply with a new law, and none regulates entire-agreement clauses. A change to the lease terms therefore needs the tenant's agreement; get it in a writing both sides sign. A new District law that applies to the tenancy governs it whether or not the lease is amended.

An entire-agreement clause also cannot shut out what District law puts into every lease: each lease of a dwelling includes an implied warranty that the owner will keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations, and a lease term that waives or contradicts the landlord-tenant chapter of those regulations (or its enforcement and tenant-notice sections) is void.

Because the end of the lease term does not end a District tenancy and a residential tenancy can be ended by notice only from the tenant, a landlord cannot force new terms on a month-to-month tenant by ending the tenancy. Rent increases follow their own notice rules (see the rent-increase rows).

Practical step: attach every addendum and required disclosure to the lease, and use a signed amendment for any change.

title: No Blank-Space Rule; Completed Copy Required
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires every blank in a written lease to be filled in or treats an unfilled blank as a breach by the landlord. Three District rules still make a complete lease matter. First, within 7 days after the tenant signs (or at signing) you must give the tenant an exact, legible, completed copy of every agreement or application the tenant signed. Second, some charges depend on what the lease actually says: you may charge a late fee only if the written lease states the maximum late fee, and the terms and conditions of a security deposit must be stated in the lease or on the deposit receipt. A blank left where those terms belong can cost you the fee. Third, a court may refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable or contrary to public policy, and a term that waives the tenant protections in the housing regulations is void whether or not it is filled in. Applies to all District rental units, month-to-month or fixed-term. Practical step: complete or strike every blank before signing, and hand over the completed signed copy.

title: No Lease Font-Size or First-Page Placement Rules; Formatting Rules Reach Notices Only
bodyText: District law sets no font-size, boldface or first-page placement rule for any disclosure in a residential lease, and no special occupancy disclosure for single-family home rentals. A District lease may present its required terms (such as the maximum late fee, the deposit terms or the exempt-unit statement) in ordinary type and in any reasonable location. Formatting rules in District law reach notices and filings, not lease text: for example, rent-adjustment notices for rent-stabilized units must show the elderly and disability increase limit in bold 12-point type, receivership notices and certain debt collection notices have type-size rules, a real estate brokerage relationship disclosure combined with other information must be conspicuous, and filings with the Rent Administrator use 12-point type. Housing Authority program forms have their own rules. Practical step: make required lease terms easy to find (clear headings, a disclosures section) even though no type rule applies; that helps show the tenant was informed.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule; Reciprocal Notice Rules Apply
bodyText: District law has no rule requiring the same terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenants, and no cap on the rent difference between lease types. The structure of District law narrows the gap anyway. When a fixed term ends, the tenant does not have to leave: no tenant may be evicted, notwithstanding the lease's expiration, while the tenant keeps paying the rent, so most tenancies continue month to month on the same terms. Only the tenant can end a residential tenancy by a 30-day notice. A lease may not require more than 30 days' notice from the tenant unless it also requires you to give rent-increase notices at least 30 days longer than that, and any longer notice tied to the initial term must expire with that term. In a rent-stabilized unit, a valid written lease that fixes the rent for its term blocks any rent adjustment during that term. Practical step: you may price lease options differently, but keep the notice terms reciprocal as required.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: No District statute, housing regulation or court rule sets a minimum type size for a printed residential lease or makes small print inadmissible or unenforceable. The only District print rule reaching every lease is that the copy you give the tenant after signing must be exact, legible and complete. District type-size rules for certain notices and program documents (such as debt-collection, condominium-foreclosure and receivership notices) do not reach lease text. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: print the lease in a readable size anyway, since a court may refuse to enforce a term it finds unconscionable, and hand the tenant a legible signed copy within 7 days.

title: No Liquidated-Damages Statute; Actual Mitigated Damages Apply
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation authorizes, caps or bans a liquidated-damages clause in a residential lease, so whether an agreed damages figure is enforceable or an unenforceable penalty is left to the courts, which may also refuse to enforce lease terms they find unconscionable. Several District rules shape what such a clause can do. When a tenant leaves before the term ends, your damages are your actual damages and are subject to your duty to mitigate, for example by trying to re-rent. A security deposit cannot be kept as a flat agreed sum: you may withhold only for expenses properly incurred under the deposit terms, with written notice within 45 days and an itemized statement of each repair or other use and its cost within 30 days after that, and never for ordinary wear and tear or professional cleaning. Any deposit or other payment held as security for the tenant's obligations counts toward the one-month cap. Practical step: rather than a liquidated-damages clause, offer an optional early-termination right with a stated fee that the tenant may choose to use (see the District early-termination clause, "Early Termination" clause), and otherwise recover actual, mitigated damages with documentation.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent; Court Eviction Only
bodyText: The District has no opt-in lockout procedure: no statute lets a landlord change the locks, remove doors or shut off utilities to press a tenant who is behind on rent, whatever the lease says. A tenant may be removed only on a just-cause ground after the required written notice, by filing in the Superior Court, and only when a court has ordered it; the eviction itself is carried out by the U.S. Marshals, and you change the locks in their presence at your expense. Before a nonpayment case you must give the notice of intent to file (and you cannot file at all if less than $600 is owed); after judgment, the tenant can still redeem by paying the court-set amount before the eviction is completed. Cutting off services or access in response to a tenant asserting rights is presumed retaliatory in many situations, and substantially reducing or eliminating related services can bring liability for the excess rent, trebled for bad faith. Practical step: never lock out a tenant or interrupt utilities over unpaid rent; send the required notice and use the court process. See the self-help eviction row for the full rules.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge or Tenant Notice; Energy Loan Assessments Fall on Owners
bodyText: The District has no meter-based energy conservation charge that a landlord must disclose to new tenants, and no rule offering a rent deduction for such a charge.
