The nearest District program is property-assessed financing: an owner who signs an Energy Efficiency Loan Agreement has a special assessment levied on the lot and collected with the property, but the statute places that obligation on the property owner and contains no tenant disclosure rule; if you raise rents to pay the assessment, you must pass the energy savings through to the tenants charged. If you want tenants to share energy-related costs, District utility and fee rules control: you may not charge fees for services you must provide (including third-party billing administration fees), starting January 1, 2027 you may not separately charge for common-area or vacant-unit utilities, and in rent-stabilized units you may not impose unapproved mandatory fees. Building energy benchmarking and data release are covered by the energy data entry ("Energy Data Consent" clause).

title: No Drug-Lab Disclosure or Remediation Law; Nuisance Abatement and Habitability Apply
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental was used to make methamphetamine or other drugs, no owner duty to report a suspected drug lab, no contamination testing or remediation standard for former drug labs, and no ban on renting a former lab site. Related District rules: real property used to facilitate drug violations, or used for the sale or manufacture of controlled substances with an adverse impact on the community, is a drug-related nuisance that the District and community groups can sue to abate; courts can order measures such as better locks, lighting, security and escrow of rental income. Separately, a housing provider may bring a possession action against a rental unit used as a drug haven, outside the normal just-cause procedure. Housing Authority and voucher rules bar households with a conviction for making methamphetamine in federally assisted housing, but those are program rules. General duties still apply: a lease of a unit that is unsafe or unsanitary at the start because of conditions the owner knew or should have known about is void, and the implied warranty of habitability requires code-compliant premises. Remediate before reletting.

title: No Military Air Zone or Installation Disclosure
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a military air installation, in an airport or military noise zone, or in an accident potential zone, and no related tenant termination right. Nothing in District landlord-tenant law ties a disclosure to distance from a named military installation or to a military impact district. Separate federal rules may apply on or near federal property, and District zoning and height rules (not part of landlord-tenant law) govern what can be built. For leases, the general duty is honesty: do not misstate a unit's surroundings, including aircraft noise, when asked. Ordinary District disclosures still apply at application (the Rent Administrator's disclosure form, code violation reports, mold history, the Tenant Bill of Rights) and, for pre-1978 units, the lead disclosure form. This entry applies the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies; there is nothing to add to the lease.

title: No Separate Notice Rule; Deposits Must Be Refundable
bodyText: District law has no rule requiring a separate, stand-alone written notice for a nonrefundable deposit or fee. That is because a security deposit, and any similar payment held as security or paid as a condition of the tenancy beyond the rent, must be returned under the District's deposit rules; it cannot be made nonrefundable. Refundability is disclosed through the ordinary documents instead: the written screening notice given or posted before you request any information or fee must say whether each fee or deposit is refundable and under what conditions, and the Rent Administrator's disclosure form given at application lists any nonrefundable application fee and the deposit amount, interest rate and return method. See the nonrefundable-deposit row for which nonrefundable fees are allowed at all.

title: No Notice-Fee Rule; Fee Limits Make Notice Charges Risky
bodyText: District law has no rule that specifically authorizes or caps a fee for preparing or serving a notice (a notice of intent to file, notice to correct or vacate, or similar), and the notices themselves are duties the law puts on you. Several District rules make such a fee hard to justify. A lease may not require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees; only a court may award them. In an eviction case the prevailing party is awarded taxable costs as a matter of course, including the filing fee, notary fee, postage and no more than $10 per defendant for a special process server, plus Marshals and writ fees. For late rent, the only authorized charge is a single late fee of up to 5% of the rent due, stated in the written lease; an extra charge for the notice you send about late rent risks being treated as a second late fee. In a rent-stabilized unit, you may not impose any mandatory fee for a service that has not been approved through the rent stabilization program, on pain of treble damages. Practical step: do not charge tenants for notices; recover service costs only as court-awarded costs.

title: No Rule on Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires a warning on a landlord-supplied move-out notice form that adds terms not in the lease, or says what happens to added terms the tenant signs. Related District rules: a month-to-month tenant may end the tenancy by a 30-day written notice that expires on the first day of a month, and a lease term demanding a longer tenant notice is void unless the statutory conditions are met. Once given, a notice to quit cannot be withdrawn without the other party's consent, and a tenant who gives notice and then refuses without reasonable excuse to leave owes double rent for the holdover. The landlord's own notices to correct or vacate have fixed contents (the facts, the cure needed, the 30-day period, filing with the Rent Administrator, the domestic-violence statement) and must be in English and Spanish. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: accept any clear written notice from the tenant; if you supply a form, keep it to the move-out date and forwarding address and put any new agreement (such as a move-out inspection date or deposit terms) in a separate document the tenant may decline.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition-Permit or Shared-Meter Disclosures; 180-Day Demolition Notice
bodyText: District law has none of these three pre-signing disclosures: no notice to tenants of former military ordnance sites nearby, no notice to prospective tenants that a demolition permit has been applied for or issued, and no notice that a gas or electric meter serves areas outside the tenant's unit. Related District rules: The application disclosure form must say whether the building is registered as, or converting to, a condominium, cooperative or a non-housing use. A demolition does not end a tenancy by itself: to recover a unit for demolition and replacement, a housing provider must file the demolition permit with the Rent Administrator, meet the relocation-assistance requirements and give a 180-day notice to vacate that tells the tenant of the right to relocation assistance. On metering, starting January 1, 2027, you may not separately bill tenants (other than through rent) for utilities used by common spaces or vacant units, although a ratio utility billing system may still allocate master-metered charges; if a tenant's own meter serves any common area, fix it or absorb that usage. Practical step: if a demolition or major redevelopment is planned, tell applicants before they sign.

title: No Parking Rules Notice Requirement
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires a landlord to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, prescribes a heading for them, limits the vehicle information a landlord may ask for, or ties a parking permit to the lease term. Other District rules fill part of the gap. Rules attached to the lease become lease terms, and a lease term cannot be changed during the tenancy without the tenant's agreement, so a mid-term change to parking rules that takes away something the lease gives needs the tenant's consent; in a rent-stabilized unit, substantially reducing a parking facility can also lead to a rent reduction. A tenant can be evicted for breaking a parking rule only after a written 30-day notice to correct, and only for a substantial lease obligation. District public housing and Rental Assistance Demonstration properties have their own towing rules. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: attach the parking rules to the lease, give the tenant a copy with the signed lease, and get written agreement to later changes that reduce parking rights.

title: Parking Terms in District Leases
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation sets general rules for residential parking in a lease. Where tenants may park and under what rules is a matter of agreement, subject to these District limits. Liability disclaimers: the lease may say the landlord does not provide security for the parking area, but it may not exempt the owner from, or limit the owner's liability for, injury or property damage caused by the negligence of the owner or the owner's agents or employees in operating or maintaining the premises or any facility on the property.

A clause saying the landlord is not liable for any damage to or theft of a vehicle reaches that negligence and should not be used. Fees: parking provided with the unit is a related facility; in a rent-stabilized unit a mandatory parking charge needs Rent Administrator approval, and before the lease is signed only an application fee may be collected.

Vehicles parked on private property without the owner's consent may be ticketed and removed by the District (see the towing row). Applies to all District rental units.

Practical step: use the District parking clauses (designated areas and rules, no security promise, no negligence disclaimer).

title: No Payment-Method Rule; Receipts and Fee Limits Apply
bodyText:
District law does not tell a private landlord which rent payment methods it must accept, does not bar requiring electronic payment, and has no specific ban on a fee for paying by a particular method (card, online portal or cash). You may set the accepted methods in the lease. Three District rules still shape the choice.

First, you must give a written receipt for every payment of rent, deposit or other money unless the tenant pays by personal check, so cash, money-order and electronic payments each need a receipt showing the amount, date and purpose.

Second, before the lease is signed you may charge only an application fee, and at no time may you charge a fee for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable, including administrative fees for third-party billing.

Third, in a rent-stabilized unit you may not impose any mandatory fee for a service or facility that has not been approved through the rent stabilization program; a processing fee the tenant cannot avoid because it attaches to the only accepted method risks that ban. Units in District Housing Authority programs follow their own program rules on payment form.

title: No No-Notice Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: District law has no exception allowing entry without notice for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes or pest treatment, even if the lease says so conspicuously. Entry to supply necessary or agreed services and maintenance is a reasonable purpose, but outside an emergency it still requires written notice at least 48 hours ahead, or a shorter period the tenant agrees to in writing, and a reasonable time (9 a.m. to 5 p.m., not Sundays or federal holidays, unless the tenant agrees otherwise). Email or text notice counts only if the tenant acknowledges it in writing. A practical way to run scheduled services is to give one written schedule at least 48 hours before the first visit that lists each date and time window, and to get the tenant's separate written agreement to any shorter notice or other hours. Pest treatment that is your duty (common areas, or infestations in two or more units) cannot be billed to the tenant as a fee. Use the District entry clause ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause).

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires a landlord to give a tenant a fact sheet about pets and eviction, or any other pet-specific notice, with the lease or at any other time. Related District rules still matter when a tenant has an animal. Animals and other belongings left in a unit after a court-ordered eviction are covered by the District's eviction property rules (21-day pre-eviction notice warning that property left behind is deemed abandoned 7 days after the eviction; access for the tenant to remove it during those 7 days), and a landlord may not remove a tenant's property outside that process. In District public housing, the Housing Authority's pet rules require written notice of a refused pet registration with appeal rights, which binds the Authority, not private landlords. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: no fact sheet is required, but if a tenant facing eviction has a pet, mention it in your communications and give the tenant every chance to arrange care for the animal before the eviction date.

title: Pet Liability Insurance Requirements
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation bars or regulates a private landlord's lease term requiring a tenant with a pet to carry liability insurance covering the pet, or naming the landlord as an interested party. Limits still apply. A tenant with a disability who has a service animal may not be charged extra for the animal, so do not require pet insurance (or any added cost) for a service or other assistance animal.

If you buy coverage and bill the tenant for it rather than having the tenant buy a policy, the charge counts as rent and, in a rent-stabilized unit, a mandatory charge for an unapproved service exposes you to treble damages. In District public housing the Housing Authority does not require pet owners to carry liability insurance; that rule binds the Authority, not private landlords. Applies to all District rental units.

Practical step: the shared pet-insurance clause, which exempts assistance animals, may be used as written; let the tenant choose the insurer and keep proof of coverage on file.

title: No Consumer-Statement or Lease Preapproval Law
bodyText: The District has no plain-language consumer-contract law of the kind that requires a readability test, a separate statement listing every consumer restriction or waiver in the lease, or optional Attorney General preapproval of a lease form, and no dollar-value exclusion that would sort leases into or out of such a law. What the District does have is a short list of lease terms that are forbidden outright, so there are no lawful waivers to list in a consumer statement: the housing regulations void any lease term that waives their landlord-tenant chapter and forbid owner-negligence exculpation, jury-trial waivers, clauses making the tenant pay your court costs or legal fees, and confessions of judgment. The Consumer Protection Procedures Act separately treats ambiguity about material facts and unconscionable lease terms as unlawful trade practices. Practical step: no consumer statement or agency preapproval is needed for a District lease; instead keep prohibited terms out of the form, write it clearly, and give the tenant a legible signed copy (see the plain-language and prohibited-lease-terms rows).

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law; Consumer-Protection Limits Apply
bodyText: The District has no plain-language statute for residential leases or consumer contracts: no District statute or housing regulation requires a lease to be written in plain or everyday language, pass a readability test, or be divided into captioned sections. The nearest rules work differently. The Consumer Protection Procedures Act covers leasing and treats ambiguity or innuendo about a material fact, failure to give a copy of a lease the consumer signs, and unconscionable lease terms as unlawful trade practices; in judging unconscionability it looks at, among other things, whether the merchant took advantage of a consumer's reading ability or difficulty understanding the language of the agreement. The housing regulations require you to give the tenant an exact, legible, completed copy of anything signed, and let courts refuse to enforce unconscionable lease terms. The District's Automatic Renewal Protections Act requires renewal terms to be shown clearly and conspicuously, but whether it reaches a residential lease is not settled by its text. Eviction notices must be given in the tenant's primary language when you know it is a covered language other than English or Spanish. Practical step: write District leases in plain English with headings anyway, and keep material terms such as rent, fees and renewal easy to find.

title: No Tenant Right to Window Units; Owner-Provided Air Conditioning Must Be Maintained
bodyText: District law gives tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and a lease may restrict or condition window units (for example, on safe installation, approved brackets or no units on fire escapes). Nothing requires the lease to disclose such a restriction in any particular way, but put it in the lease or rules so the tenant knows before signing. If you provide air conditioning, through individual units or a central system, you must keep it in safe, good working order so it cools the inside at least 15 degrees Fahrenheit below the outside temperature, have it inspected every year between September 1 and May 1 by a District-licensed refrigeration and air conditioning mechanic, file the inspection findings, and correct defects by June 1. Air conditioning is a related service: in a rent-stabilized unit, a substantial cut in services can lead the Rent Administrator to reduce the rent. Separately, you may not carry out an eviction on a day forecast above 95 degrees Fahrenheit, with narrow court-ordered exceptions.

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In Solar; Association Solar Protection Runs to Owners
bodyText: The District gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, and no statute voids a lease term restricting solar equipment. A landlord may refuse, permit or condition such devices in the lease (for example, on safe mounting, no wiring changes, insurance and removal at move-out). The District's solar protection runs to owners, not tenants: a homeowners, condominium or cooperative association may not prohibit an owner or member from installing or using a solar energy collection device on the owner's own property or unit, or on a roof covering only that unit. The association may still ban devices on other common elements and adopt reasonable, non-aesthetic guidelines to prevent nuisance, and may make the owner responsible for maintenance and damage. So if you rent out a condominium or cooperative unit, you as owner hold that right; your tenant does not, unless your lease grants it. Practical step: if you allow tenant solar devices, say so in the lease and set conditions, and check any association guidelines first.

title: No Possession Bond; Confessed Judgments Barred
bodyText: The District has no statutory end-of-term possession bond: no law lets a landlord require a tenant to post a bond or sign a confessed judgment promising to surrender possession when the lease ends, and such a device would conflict with District law in two ways. First, a District residential lease may not authorize anyone other than the tenant to confess judgment against the tenant, and a bad-faith violation can bring treble damages. Second, the end of the term does not entitle you to possession; a tenant who keeps paying rent may stay, and you can recover possession only on a statutory ground after the required notice and a court judgment. Any money you require as security for the tenant's obligations, whatever it is called, counts as a security deposit, which is capped at one month's rent, charged once, held in an interest-bearing District escrow account, and returned under the deposit rules. Practical step: do not ask for a possession bond, surrender bond or confession of judgment in a District lease; rely on the security deposit and, if needed, the court process.

title: No Delivery-Delay Statute; Lease Clause and Housing-Code Rules Govern
bodyText:
District law has no statute on a landlord's failure to deliver possession on the start date, so the lease controls, with common-law remedies behind it. A clause that suspends rent until you deliver possession and lets the tenant cancel and get back everything paid if you cannot deliver within a set time is consistent with District law.

Two District rules matter for delays caused by the unit's condition. A lease of a unit that is unsafe or unsanitary at the start of the tenancy because of housing-code violations you knew or should have known about is void, so do not hand over a unit with known violations to meet the start date. And if a tenant is later displaced by a government order because the premises are unsafe, the tenant's duty to pay rent is suspended but the tenancy does not end until the unit is offered back and the tenant waives that right; the District can also recover emergency relocation costs from an owner whose failures caused the closure.

Practical step: give a realistic start date, keep the start-date delay clause, refund promptly if the tenant cancels, and fix code violations before move-in rather than delivering a defective unit.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule; Lead Plumbing Form and Water Test Kits Apply Instead
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to test a private drinking-water well or give well test results to tenants. District rentals are generally served by the public water system, and District law addresses drinking-water lead risk instead of private wells. For water, the duties that do apply are: give every tenant, before the lease or a renewal binds the tenant, the Mayor's lead plumbing disclosure form (water lead tests, lead-bearing plumbing and lead service lines), notify the tenant within 48 hours if you learn of lead plumbing or a lead service line, and, in a multiple dwelling, order a DC Water lead test kit within 15 days of a tenant's written request (subject to limits on how many units must be tested) and share and post the results. The housing code also requires a water heating facility able to deliver hot water at 120 degrees Fahrenheit or more. If a property in the District does use a well, District groundwater and well-construction rules may apply; they are outside this entry and set no tenant disclosure.

title: No Written-Repair-Promise Rule
bodyText: District law has no rule like some other jurisdictions' that a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit must be put in writing with a completion date before the lease is signed. Whether an oral promise binds you is left to general contract law and the courts. Two District rules make writing it down the sensible course anyway. First, you must give the tenant an exact, completed copy of anything the tenant signs, at signing or within 7 days, so a promised repair written into the lease or an addendum becomes part of the paper record. Second, the housing code's repair duties apply regardless of any promise: every lease carries an implied warranty that the unit meets the housing regulations, and the lease cannot waive it. If you agree to make extra repairs or improvements, you may enter to do them only on 48 hours' written notice (or a shorter period the tenant agrees to in writing), at a reasonable time. Practical step: list any agreed move-in work, with a target date, in the lease or a signed addendum.

title: No Property-Tax Portion Statement; Renters Claim a Credit on a Deemed 20 Percent of Rent
bodyText: The District does not require a landlord to give tenants an annual or rent-change statement of the portion of rent attributable to property taxes. The related District rule works without the landlord: eligible renters may claim an income tax credit (often called Schedule H) based on rent paid for their principal residence, and the statute deems a fixed percentage of rent (currently 20 percent) to be rent constituting property taxes. Rent paid for that purpose excludes deposits, advance rent for another period, charges for medical services or food, and rent for property exempt from District real property tax; utilities count only if included in the rent paid to the landlord. Tenants rely on their own rent records. Practical step: give written receipts for all rent (required whenever rent is paid other than by personal check) and respond to reasonable tenant requests for a rent history, which also helps them claim the credit. For a property exempt from District real property tax, tell tenants that rent there does not qualify.

title: No Lease-Voiding Rule for Unlawful Use; Illegal-Act Ground Applies
bodyText: District law has no statute that automatically voids or annuls a residential lease, or lets the landlord declare it void, because the tenant uses the premises for an unlawful purpose. Unlawful use matters in other ways. Under the eviction statute, once a court has finally determined that the tenant (or another occupant, if the tenant knew or should have known that the illegal act was taking place) performed an illegal act in the unit or building, you may serve a 30-day notice to vacate (a 10-day notice for certain violent crimes in cases filed after 2025, though a regulation still says to wait 30 days before filing), file it with the Rent Administrator, and sue for possession; intrafamily-offense victims have defenses. A separate fast possession case is available for a unit used as a drug haven. The owner also faces exposure: anyone who owns, uses or rents out a place used for prostitution or for using, keeping or selling illegal drugs is guilty of a nuisance, and an abatement order can require the contents to be sold and the building closed for a year unless the owner posts a bond and abates; civil drug-, firearm- and prostitution-nuisance suits can escrow rents or close the property. Practical step: a lease use clause can require lawful residential use, but enforce it only through the statutory illegal-act or drug-haven routes.

title: No Radon Disclosure or Testing Duty; Radon Contractors Must Be Qualified
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to test for radon, disclose radon test results or radon risk to tenants, or give a radon pamphlet, and no floor-level or lease-length limit on any such duty. The only District radon statute regulates the radon business: a person or company may not perform radon screening, testing or mitigation in the District for a fee unless the person doing the work is listed as proficient by the federal Environmental Protection Agency or holds a certificate of proficiency from an organization the Mayor has approved. If you test or mitigate, use a qualified provider. District law also does not include a radon-resistant new construction mandate in the landlord-tenant or housing code materials searched; building code requirements are outside this entry. Because there is no District disclosure duty, no radon clause is needed in a District lease; if you have radon results, sharing them voluntarily is good practice and avoids misrepresentation claims.

title: No Religious-Display Statute; Human Rights Act Bars Rules Targeting Religion
bodyText: The District has no statute specifically protecting a tenant's right to put a religious or cultural item, such as a mezuzah, on a door frame or entry, and none specifically barring a lease rule on door or hallway displays. The Human Rights Act does apply: it is unlawful to include a lease clause, condition or restriction, or to set different terms or restrict facilities or services, wholly or partly because of a tenant's religion, national origin or other protected trait. A display rule that is written or enforced so that it singles out religious or cultural items, or is applied to one faith's items and not others, risks a discrimination claim. Practical step: if you limit what tenants may attach to doors, frames or hallways, write a neutral rule (size, placement, fire-door and code safety, no damage), apply it the same way to every item and every tenant, and consider allowing small door-frame items. Enforce a breach only through the 30-day notice to correct. The same applies to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Rent-Concession Rule; Frame Concessions Carefully
bodyText:
District law has no specific rule on rent concessions such as a free month, move-in credit or discounted first months. You may offer them, but write them precisely. For a rent-stabilized unit, be careful how a concession is framed: the Rental Housing Act defines the rent charged as the entire amount the tenant must actually pay, and the lawful rent is the base for later increases, so a concession written as a lower monthly rent may lower that base, while a one-time credit against a stated rent is less likely to.

Record the full rent and the concession separately in the lease and in your rent records, and make sure the rent shown on the disclosure form and any rent-history form matches. For any unit, the concession is part of the price you offer, so advertising must not mislead about the rent the tenant will actually pay over the term. Exempt units have no rent-increase limit, but every increase still needs the 60-day written notice.

title: No Rule on Rent Installments
bodyText:
District law has no rule on splitting monthly rent into installments or on whether scheduled installments count as partial payments. You and the tenant may agree on any payment schedule in the lease. If you do, apply the late-fee rules to each installment as a separate rent due date: no late fee until that installment is more than 5 days late (or any longer grace period stated in the lease), no more than 5% of the rent then due, and only one fee per late payment.

Give a written receipt for each installment not paid by personal check. For a nonpayment eviction, the total unpaid rent must be at least $600 before you may send the 10-day notice or file. Units in District Housing Authority programs may have their own repayment-agreement rules.

title: Repair Duty Follows Owner and Rent Collector
bodyText: Some jurisdictions say expressly that whoever collects the rent keeps the repair duty, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. District law has no such express rule, but its definitions reach the same people. The housing regulations bind every "owner", which includes anyone with legal title and anyone with charge, care or control of the building as owner, agent, fiduciary or court officer, and anyone representing the actual owner must comply as if they were the owner. The Rental Housing Act's duties fall on the "housing provider", defined to include the landlord, owner, lessor, sublessor, assignee, their agent and anyone receiving or entitled to receive the rent. Between landlord and tenant, a lease clause that waives the housing-code warranty is void, and a clause excusing you from liability for your own negligence in maintaining the property may not be used. How duties are split among owners, managers and lenders by private contract is not addressed by District statute. Practical step: make sure whoever manages and collects rent is set up to meet the repair duties.

title: No Renter's Insurance Statute
bodyText:
No District statute or housing regulation forbids a lease from requiring renter's insurance, lets the tenant pick the carrier by statute, sets rules for landlord-placed coverage, or requires a written statement that the landlord does not insure the tenant's belongings. Other District rules still limit how an insurance requirement works.

If you, rather than an insurer, charge the tenant for coverage (for example a master-policy or force-placed charge), that money is demanded as a condition of occupancy and counts as rent under the Rental Housing Act; in a rent-stabilized unit a mandatory charge for a service not approved by the Rent Administrator exposes you to treble damages, and before the lease is signed you may collect nothing but an application fee.

An insurance clause also cannot excuse you from liability for your own negligence or that of your agents, and the tenant's coverage does not shift your repair duties. Applies to all District rental units, month-to-month or fixed-term.

Practical step: require the tenant to buy a policy from an insurer of the tenant's choice and show proof, and do not bill the tenant for insurance yourself.

title: No Termination for Costly Repairs; Implied Warranty Applies
bodyText: The District gives a landlord no right to end a tenancy, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value. Every residential lease carries an implied warranty that the owner will keep the premises in compliance with the housing code, and you must make the repairs that requires whatever the cost. If code violations not caused by the tenant or the tenant's guests make the unit unsafe or unsanitary and are not corrected in the time allowed, the lease is void, which can undercut your claim for rent. If the building truly needs major work, the only routes to recover possession are the eviction statute's own grounds, each with long notices and conditions: renovations that cannot be done with the tenant in place (Rent Administrator approval, a 120-day notice, relocation assistance and a right to return); approved substantial rehabilitation (120 days, right to re-rent); demolition with a permit (180 days); or permanently withdrawing the unit from housing use (180 days, no re-rental or rehabilitation for a year). Refusing repairs after a tenant complains is also presumed retaliatory. Practical step: budget for code repairs and, for large projects, plan around the statutory renovation or rehabilitation procedures.

title: No Residential Submetering Disclosure; Owner Reselling to Occupants Is Not an Electric Company
bodyText: The District has no submetering disclosure rule for residential leases. Its submetering statute and the Public Service Commission rules under it cover only nonresidential (commercial) rental units. A building owner, lessee or manager who runs the building's internal wiring and supplies electricity only to the building's occupants is excluded from the definition of an electric company, so reselling electricity to residential tenants does not by itself make you a regulated utility. Rules that do limit utility charges to residential tenants: since August 14, 2026, you may not charge fees for services you must provide, expressly including administrative fees for third-party utility billing. Starting January 1, 2027, you may not separately charge tenants (other than through monthly rent) for utilities used by common spaces or vacant units; a ratio utility billing system (by square footage, occupancy or bedrooms) remains allowed within those limits. In a rent-stabilized unit, you may not impose a mandatory fee for any service or facility that the Rent Administrator has not approved. Practical step: if tenants pay any utility other than directly to the utility, spell out the method, the allocation formula and the billing period in the lease.

title: Residential-Use Clauses Are Enforced Through the Cure Notice
bodyText:
District law has no statute limiting a rental unit to residential use or setting a special remedy when a tenant uses it for another purpose, so a residential-use-only clause is a lease term and lawful. Because a tenant may be evicted only on the grounds the Rental Housing Act lists, a non-residential use is enforced in one of two ways. If it breaches a substantial lease obligation, serve a written 30-day Notice to Correct or Vacate that describes the conduct, cites the lease provision and says what the tenant must do; you may file for possession only if the tenant does not correct it, and the notice cannot rest on a violation more than six months old.

If a court has finally determined that the tenant or another occupant committed an illegal act in the unit or building (an occupant's act counts only if the tenant knew or should have known of it), a 30-day notice to vacate applies instead (10 days in a case filed after December 31, 2025 for a dangerous crime or crime of violence not committed in self-defense or defense of another, and only after you consider in good faith all reasonable ways to keep non-offending occupants housed; the regulation, 14 DCMR § 4302.2(a), still bars filing until 30 days after the notice, so the cautious course is to wait 30 days).

Expiration of the lease is not a ground in itself. Home occupations are also controlled by zoning rules. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Cap on Returned-Payment Fees; Put the Fee in the Lease
bodyText:
District law sets no cap on a returned-check or failed-payment fee for private residential landlords, and no rule on postdated checks or on requiring certified funds after a bounced payment. A reasonable returned-payment fee written into the lease is the safer course: once a balance is more than 30 days past due, you may collect an added fee only if the lease expressly authorizes it. For a rent-stabilized unit, check that the fee is tied to the failed payment and not presented as a charge for a service or facility, because mandatory fees for unapproved services or facilities are barred there.

Separately, the District's dishonored-check law lets a merchant who sends a written demand in the prescribed form, by first-class and certified mail, recover the check amount plus twice the amount or $100 (whichever is greater), costs and attorney fees if unpaid within 30 days; the extra damages require a conspicuous posted notice. Whether a landlord collecting rent is a merchant under that law is not settled in the text. Housing Authority units follow program rules (for example a $15 returned-check fee in converted public housing).

title: No Seasonal-Tenancy Rule; Seasonal Leases Get Full Protection
bodyText: The District has no special rules for seasonal or summer residential tenancies. If you rent a house, apartment or room for residential occupancy, even for a season, it is a rental unit under the Rental Housing Act, and the tenant gets the same protections as any other tenant: the end of the season or term does not end the tenancy, and a tenant who keeps paying rent can be removed only on a just-cause ground after the required notice and a court case. Two kinds of stays fall outside those rules. Guests in a hotel or inn, or in a building used primarily for transient occupancy where the operator pays the transient-lodging sales tax, are not in a housing accommodation under the Act. And a transient guest of a licensed short-term rental (lodging booked through a booking service, with the host present, or a vacation rental of the host's own residence) is not a tenant. Licensing also matters: a one-family rental license is not issued for a property rented for less than 90 days, and short-term rentals need their own license endorsement. Practical step: if you intend only transient lodging, comply with the short-term rental or hotel rules; if you sign a residential lease, expect the tenant to have the right to stay.

title: No Deposit-Standards Posting Rule; Deposit Disclosures Required
bodyText: District law has no rule requiring a landlord who uses differing standards to set deposit amounts to post or hand out those standards. What it does require: the deposit may not exceed the first full month's rent and may be charged only once (this cap and the escrow rules do not apply to units with federally subsidized rents or units leased by federal or District agencies). Before you request any screening information or fees, you must tell applicants in writing, or by a posting they are reasonably likely to find, the amount and purpose of every fee or deposit, when it will be charged, and whether and on what conditions it is refundable. At application, the Rent Administrator's disclosure form must give the initial deposit amount, its interest rate and how it is returned. The lease or the deposit receipt must clearly set out the deposit's terms and conditions, and each year you must post in the lobby and rental office where deposits are held and the interest rates. These apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike. Practical step: adopt one written deposit policy and make sure your screening notice and disclosure form match it.

title: No Senior-Housing Staff Work Card
bodyText: The District has no work-card or mandatory background-check rule for staff of senior (55-plus or 62-plus) apartment buildings or other ordinary rental housing. The District's mandatory criminal background checks for unlicensed staff apply to licensed health-care and community-residence facilities, such as nursing homes and assisted-living-type facilities, whose staff come into direct contact with patients; those facilities are outside the Rental Housing Act anyway. If you hire maintenance or leasing staff and employ more than 10 people in the District, the District's fair criminal record screening law for employers applies instead: you may not ask about arrests or non-conviction accusations at all, may ask about convictions only after a conditional job offer, and may withdraw the offer only for a legitimate business reason weighed against listed factors. Practical step: if you want to screen building staff, do it after a conditional offer and document the business reason.

title: No Service Animal Misrepresentation Law
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation penalizes a person for falsely claiming that an animal is a service animal or other assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else. What District law gives a landlord instead is a documentation process. For a service animal you may require a physician's or other licensed healthcare professional's verification that the person has a qualifying physical or mental disability and a showing of the link between the disability and the animal's function, while allowing at least 30 days and asking nothing about the nature or severity of the disability. An animal that serves only as a companion or crime deterrent is not a service animal under that law, though it may still be a reasonable accommodation under the Human Rights Act. The tenant remains liable for any damage the animal does. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: rely on the documentation process rather than accusations of fraud; if a request appears false, get legal advice before refusing it, because wrongly denying a service animal is itself an offense.

title: No District Servicemember Statute; Federal SCRA and Form 114 Apply
bodyText: The District has no servicemember lease-termination or eviction-protection statute of its own and no extension of federal protections to National Guard members on District orders; servicemember tenants rely on the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which applies in the District as it does everywhere. District court rules build that Act into eviction cases. If a tenant has not appeared, no default judgment for possession or money can be entered until you file a Civil Action Form 114 complying with the federal Act, and the clerk must dismiss the case without prejudice if, within 90 days after a default, you neither file that form nor ask to present proof when required. The same form is required for defaults in small-claims and general civil cases. The District's own just-cause eviction rules, notices and other protections apply to servicemember tenants as to everyone else, and the library's early-termination clause preserves any federal termination right. Practical step: when a tenant may be in military service, check status before seeking a default, file Form 114 with every default request, and honor a valid federal lease-termination notice from a servicemember tenant.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty; Fair Criminal Record Screening Limits Apply
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to tell tenants whether a registered sex offender lives in the building or nearby, and no required lease statement about the sex offender registry. Registry information is released by the Metropolitan Police Department, which is authorized to notify the community and the public at large, so tenants can look it up themselves. Screening limits matter more than disclosure. Unless you own and live in a building with 3 or fewer rental units (or another law requires or allows the inquiry), District fair criminal record screening rules apply: you may not ask about criminal history until after a conditional offer; afterward you may consider only pending accusations or convictions within the past 7 years for listed serious offenses (which include sexual abuse offenses), and you may withdraw the offer only after weighing the required factors and giving written notice. Registration status itself is not a listed basis. Federally assisted and Housing Authority housing follow separate federal and program rules on lifetime registrants; those do not govern private landlords outside those programs.

title: No Sex-Offender Residency Rule; Screening Law Applies
bodyText: The District's statutes and housing regulations contain no sex-offender residency restriction: no distance rule keeping registrants away from schools, child-care centers or parks, no ban on two registrants living together, no landlord fine or lease-statement safe harbor, and no duty to check the registry before renting. The registry is kept by the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency and published by the Metropolitan Police Department. What does apply is the District's fair criminal record screening law (for housing providers other than owner-occupants of buildings with 3 or fewer rental units). You may not ask about criminal convictions or pending charges until after a conditional offer. After that, you may consider only a conviction or pending charge within the past 7 years for listed offenses, which include first- and second-degree sexual abuse, child sexual abuse and sexual abuse of a minor, and you may withdraw the offer only after weighing the statutory factors and giving written notice. You may not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction. Federal rules bar admission of lifetime registrants to public housing and voucher programs, which the Housing Authority applies. Practical step: apply the screening law's steps uniformly; do not add lease clauses about registrant status.

title: No Shoreline or Water-Access Disclosure
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to disclose shoreline, waterfront or public water-access rights, easements or restrictions to tenants, and no coastal or shoreland disclosure rule for rentals. District waterfront statutes deal with development financing, special assessment districts and land transfers along the Anacostia River and Southwest Waterfront, not with leases. If a rental property is subject to a recorded easement or restriction (waterfront or otherwise), the tenant's use is subject to it as a matter of property law, and a lease may describe it; District law does not require that. Ordinary District disclosures still apply at application and signing (see the application and lease-signing disclosure entries). This applies the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection for Federal Workers
bodyText: The District has no law that delays rent, waives late fees or pauses evictions for federal employees or contractors affected by a federal government shutdown, even though many District tenants work for the federal government. The general rules apply: a late fee is allowed only after the rent is more than 5 days late (or any longer grace period stated in the lease), may not exceed 5% of the rent due, and can never be a ground for eviction; you may not send the 10-day nonpayment notice or file for possession unless at least $600 in rent is unpaid. Nothing prevents you from agreeing in writing to a deferral or payment plan for an affected tenant; if you do, give receipts and keep the terms in writing. Practical step: watch for emergency legislation during any future shutdown.

title: No Owner-Occupancy Limit on Renting Single-Family Homes in Statute or Housing Regulations
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation limits renting a home in a single-family zone to owners who live on the lot, or caps the number of rental homes in a residential zone. Zoning is set by the District's zoning regulations (DCMR Title 11), so check them for any use or occupancy condition on your property. What the law does require for every long-term rental of a single-family home, townhouse, duplex, condominium unit or room: a one-family rental business license, and registration of the unit with the Rental Accommodations Division unless the small-owner exemption is claimed. The licensing regulation also says that, under the zoning regulations, a one-family rental license will not be issued for a home rented for less than 90 days, so shorter stays fall under the separate short-term rental rules. An English basement or carriage house rented while the main house is occupied needs a two-family rental license and a certificate of occupancy (see the accessory-dwelling-unit row). These rules apply to month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike. Practical step: license and register before the first lease, and check zoning if you plan to divide a single-family house into more units.

title: No Small-Landlord Repair Remedy Exemption
bodyText: The District has no tenant rent-escrow statute for repairs, and no notice that lets a small landlord opt out of tenants' repair remedies. The housing-code warranty, the rule voiding a lease when serious code violations go uncorrected, retaliation protection and the tenant-receivership remedy apply however few units you own, and a lease clause waiving the housing-code chapter is void. Rent is paid into the court registry only under a protective order in an eviction case, and that is a court process, not a landlord exemption. The District's small-owner carve-outs are elsewhere and do not touch repair duties: a building of 4 or fewer units owned by not more than four natural persons who hold no other District rental interest may be exempt from rent stabilization if a claim of exemption is filed, and you must then tell the prospective tenant in writing before the lease is signed that rent increases are not regulated; and an owner-occupant renting 3 or fewer units is outside the criminal-record screening rules. Practical step: plan to meet every repair duty regardless of building size.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute; General Rules Apply
bodyText: The District has no statute or housing regulation specifically governing smart locks, keypad or app-based entry, key fobs or other electronic access systems in rental housing. The general rules still apply to them. At move-in you must give the tenant an adequate lock and key for every entrance door, lockable from inside and outside, so an app-only lock should come with a working key or equivalent the tenant controls; exterior doors of multi-unit buildings must let people leave without a key. Entry logs and remote unlocking do not change the entry rule: outside an emergency you may enter only for a reasonable purpose, at a reasonable time and after 48 hours' written notice. You may not charge fees for lock-related services you must provide. If your system collects biometric data, such as fingerprints or face scans, used to authenticate tenants, a data breach exposing it, combined with names, triggers the District's breach-notification duties. Practical step: describe the access system in the lease, give a non-app alternative, and do not use access logs to track tenants.

title: No Smoke-Drift Statute; Elevator and Staffed-Hallway Smoking Bans; Waivers of Negligence Void
bodyText: The District has no statute on secondhand smoke drift between apartments, no required smoking-policy disclosure for private rentals, and no rule making a tenant accept smoke drift. Relevant District rules: Smoking (including vaping and cannabis) is banned in any elevator except in a single-family home, and in every enclosed place of employment, defined to include hallways that employees normally frequent but to exclude a private residence. Enclosed common hallways of an apartment building where building staff normally work therefore appear to fall within the ban; the units themselves do not. An owner may ban smoking throughout a building or any part it controls, may ban or regulate marijuana use on its property, and may post signs barring smoking on the public sidewalk up to 25 feet from the building. A lease clause that waives or limits your liability for injury or property damage caused by your own negligence is void, so a smoke-drift waiver cannot shield you from your own failures (for example, ventilation you must maintain). Practical step: if you want a smoke-free building, say so in the lease and enforce it through the 30-day notice to correct.

title: Smoke-Free Leases Are Allowed; No Smoking Statute for Rentals
bodyText:
District law neither requires nor limits a smoking policy in private rental housing, so you may make a unit or building smoke-free by lease. A 2019 law that would have regulated tobacco smoking in rental housing was never funded and has been repealed. The District's indoor smoking bans cover workplaces and public places but exclude private residences; smoking is, however, prohibited in any elevator except in a single-family dwelling. Adult marijuana use is lawful in the District, but the statute expressly lets anyone who owns or controls real property prohibit or regulate marijuana possession, use, display or growing on it, so a ban that includes cannabis, vaping and home growing is permissible.

To enforce a ban by eviction, it must be a substantial obligation in a valid lease and you must give the 30-day notice to correct or vacate; a rule announced mid-tenancy that the tenant never agreed to is not a lease obligation. Charge only actual, documented repair costs for smoke damage; do not charge for professional cleaning or ordinary wear and tear. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Fire Sprinkler Disclosure for Rentals
bodyText: The District has no law requiring a landlord to tell tenants or applicants whether a building or unit has an automatic fire sprinkler system, or to post a sprinkler notice in high-rise or other residential buildings. District sprinkler law is about construction and policy, not leases: a District fire protection study commission was charged with studying low-cost residential sprinklers and which buildings should be required to have them, and the Department of Buildings must, by July 1, 2027, write rules allowing single-stairway multifamily buildings, considering fire-resistive construction and automatic sprinklers throughout such buildings. Whether a particular building must have sprinklers is a building and fire code question (those codes are in a separate title of District regulations). Buildings must still meet the housing and property maintenance codes. Some landlords voluntarily note sprinkler coverage in listings or the lease because it affects renter's insurance; District law does not require it.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit or Disclosure Rule in Statute or Housing Regulations
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires a landlord to retrofit an existing rental building with fire sprinklers or to disclose whether a unit has them. Sprinkler requirements for new construction, additions and changes of use come from the District's Construction Codes (the adopted International Building, Residential and Fire Codes in DCMR Title 12), so check them for your building. Two statutes touch sprinklers. A 2026 law directs the Department of Buildings to adopt code rules by July 1, 2027 allowing single-stairway multifamily buildings up to six stories, and to consider requiring automatic sprinklers throughout such buildings. An older law created a Fire Protection Study Commission to study which residential buildings should be required to install sprinklers; it imposes no duty on owners. Where sprinklers or other fire protection systems exist, keep them in working order, since the operator of a housing business must keep required fire alarm systems operable and exits clear. Practical step: confirm with a fire protection contractor what the current Title 12 codes require for your building type and keep inspection records.

title: No Fast Squatter Removal; Unlawful Entry Crime and Court Possession Case
bodyText: The District has no fast-track squatter removal procedure outside the courts: no statute lets an owner have police or a sheriff remove an occupant on an affidavit, and no ex parte removal process exists. What exists is the general unlawful-entry crime and the ordinary possession case. Entering or attempting to enter a private dwelling or other property against the will of the lawful occupant or person in charge, or refusing to leave on their demand when without lawful authority to remain, is a misdemeanor; being found in property that is vacant and boarded up or otherwise secured, or posted no trespassing, is prima facie evidence of entry against the owner's will. For anyone claiming a right to be there, use the Superior Court possession action, which covers any person who holds possession without right; a guest or occupant who has been paying you, or whom a tenant let in, may be a tenant under the Rental Housing Act, which treats as a tenant anyone entitled to possession or occupancy of a rental unit, and then the just-cause rules apply. Practical step: secure and post vacant units, call police for a clear break-in, and otherwise file in court rather than removing occupants yourself.

title: No Radiator-Cover Rule; General Heating Duties Apply
bodyText: The District has no rule in its statutes or housing regulations requiring landlords to install steam radiator covers on request, to give a radiator-cover lease rider, or to address burn hazards from heating pipes or radiators. Heating duties that do apply: every heating facility must be safely installed and maintained in good working condition, the heating system must be able to keep habitable rooms at 70 degrees F, and where the tenant does not control the heat you must keep the unit at least 68 degrees F from 6:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. and 65 degrees F overnight. Equipment and safety standards for heating systems also come from the District's Construction Codes (DCMR Title 12). These rules apply equally to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies. Practical step: in buildings with exposed steam radiators or risers, consider providing covers or guards voluntarily, particularly for households with young children, and respond promptly to tenant requests about hot surfaces; no lease rider is required.

title: No Duty to Supply Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: Neither the District's rental statutes nor its Title 14 housing regulations require you to supply a stove or refrigerator. They do require a kitchen sink with hot and cold water in every dwelling unit except a bachelor apartment. If you do furnish any facility for cooking, food storage or refrigeration, you must keep it in safe, good working condition, and you are responsible for the fire-safe installation and maintenance of heating and cooking appliances you furnish; a tenant who brings its own appliance is responsible for meeting fire rules for it. Once you furnish an appliance it becomes part of what you must maintain, and in a rent-stabilized unit it is a related facility included in the rent, so removing it can support a rent-reduction petition. In the Housing Choice Voucher program, the program's rules do not allow a separate charge agreement for a range or refrigerator. Practical step: list furnished appliances in the lease (for example with the appliance list) and repair them like any other required facility.

title: No Residential Submetering Disclosure Rule
bodyText: The District has no statute or housing regulation that prescribes a lease disclosure, type size or separate signed page for submetered or ratio-billed residential utilities. The District's submetering law, which requires lease authorization, billing on the utility's cycle, capped late charges and record access, applies only to commercial (nonresidential) rental units. For residential units, the rules that do apply are substantive: you may allocate master-metered charges through a ratio utility billing system based on square footage, occupancy or bedrooms; from January 1, 2027 you may not separately bill tenants for common-space or vacant-unit utilities; you may never charge tenants administrative fees for third-party billing; and in a rent-stabilized unit a mandatory utility charge is a mandatory fee that needs rent-stabilization approval. Housing Authority program units follow their own checkmeter and excess-utility rules. Practical step: describe in the lease which utilities are billed back, the allocation method or submeter, and who reads and bills them, even though no form is prescribed; check Public Service Commission rules before reselling metered service.

title: Voucher Inspections Are Not a Reason to Refuse
bodyText: No District law lets you turn down a voucher holder because the program will inspect the unit. Refusing to rent because a tenant will pay with a Housing Choice Voucher or other income-based subsidy is source-of-income discrimination under the Human Rights Act, and the Act also makes it unlawful to act for a reason you would not have given but for the applicant's source of income. Objecting to the program's inspection or paperwork is therefore likely to be treated as refusing because of the subsidy itself. Exemptions are only the general ones for small owner-occupied buildings and certain single-family homes rented without a broker or discriminatory advertising. How inspections work: before approving a voucher tenancy and signing the payment contract, the Housing Authority confirms the unit is eligible and has passed its housing quality inspection and that the lease contains the required terms, including who pays utilities and the program's tenancy addendum. Units are then reinspected on the program's schedule, and the Authority keeps the right to inspect at any time. Practical step: when a voucher applicant qualifies on your written criteria, schedule the inspection promptly and fix any deficiencies; do not cite the inspection as a reason to decline.

title: No Proration Formula; Voucher Abatement Shields Tenant
bodyText: District statutes and housing regulations do not set a formula for reducing rent in proportion to an uninhabitable part of a unit, either for the tenant's share or for a subsidy-paid share. Three narrower rules apply. First, under the Housing Authority's voucher rules, if the Authority recaptures its housing assistance payments because the unit failed inspection and you did not make repairs, the family is not responsible to you for any part of the Authority's recaptured portion; if the contract is later cancelled and the tenant stays, the tenant may become liable for that portion. Second, you may never charge a late fee on any part of the rent a subsidy provider, rather than the tenant, is responsible for paying. Third, in a rent-stabilized unit, if related services or facilities lapse and are not promptly restored, you must reduce the rent by their monthly value. Housing-code violations can also void a lease. Practical step: do not bill a voucher tenant for an abated or recaptured subsidy share.

title: No Tax-Escalation Rule; Pass-Throughs Are Rent Increases
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation addresses a residential lease clause that passes real estate tax or insurance increases to the tenant. Other rules control the outcome. Any amount you require as a condition of occupancy is rent under the Rental Housing Act, so a tax or insurance pass-through is a rent increase. In a rent-stabilized unit it cannot be used: no rent adjustment is allowed during a written lease that sets the rent for its term, any increase must fit the annual cap and 12-month spacing, and a separate mandatory charge would need approval. For an exempt unit, a pass-through is possible only if written into the lease, and each resulting increase should be noticed in writing more than 60 days before it takes effect. If you take a District energy special assessment and raise rents to pay it, you must pass the energy savings through to those tenants. Practical step: for most District residential leases, build expected tax and insurance costs into the base rent.

title: No District Tenant-Bankruptcy Rule; Federal Law Governs
bodyText: District law has no landlord-tenant rule on a tenant's bankruptcy: nothing in the District's housing statutes, housing regulations or court rules makes bankruptcy a ground for ending a tenancy, sets a procedure when a tenant files, or limits a lease clause that treats bankruptcy as a default. A tenant's bankruptcy is governed by federal bankruptcy law, including its automatic stay on collection and eviction activity and its rules on keeping or rejecting a lease; those federal rules apply in the District and generally override lease clauses. District rules still shape what you can do. Bankruptcy itself is not one of the District's eviction grounds, so you can seek possession only for nonpayment or another listed ground, after the required notice, and only as federal bankruptcy law permits. The District's debt-collection law, which reaches landlords collecting their own past-due rent, bars seeking a written reaffirmation of a debt from a consumer who has been declared bankrupt without clearly disclosing its nature and consequences and that the consumer is not legally obligated to sign. Practical step: when a tenant files for bankruptcy, pause collection and eviction steps and get advice on federal bankruptcy law before acting.

title: No Tenant Camera Statute; Voyeurism and Audio-Recording Laws Set Limits
bodyText: The District has no statute giving tenants a right to install security cameras or video doorbells, and none barring a lease rule on them. A lease may permit, condition or restrict tenant-installed devices (for example, no drilling into doors or exterior walls without consent, no cameras aimed into other units or at shared laundry or restrooms, removal and repair at move-out). District criminal law sets the outer limits for both tenants and landlords: it is a crime to install a camera or other device to secretly observe a person using a bathroom, undressing or engaged in sexual activity, or to record such a person without express and informed consent where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy. Security monitoring in one's own home, and in a building with prominently displayed signs saying the premises or parts are under surveillance, are exempt. Recording conversations (audio) is lawful only for a party to the conversation or with one party's prior consent, so a doorbell that records audio of other people's private conversations can be unlawful. Practical step: address cameras in the lease's alterations or rules section, and post surveillance signs if you run cameras in common areas.

title: No Tenant-Death Statute; Just Cause and Estate Rules Apply
bodyText:
District law has no statute on what happens to a private residential lease when a tenant dies: it does not end the lease automatically, give the estate an early-termination right, set a procedure for the tenant's belongings, or require you to offer a contact-person designation. Those questions are left to the lease, probate law and case law.

Three District rules still matter. First, the just-cause eviction rules apply: if other household members remain in the unit, you can recover possession only on a statutory ground with the required notice and a court case, and the Rental Housing Act treats as a tenant any person entitled to possession or occupancy of the unit.

Second, do not remove a deceased tenant's belongings on your own; deal with the personal representative or heirs, since the post-eviction 7-day rules apply only after a court eviction.

Third, District Housing Authority and voucher program units have their own rules on a sole tenant's death. Practical step: ask each tenant to name an emergency contact in the application or lease (the District's eviction-day notice must be mailed to an emergency contact if one was provided), and when a tenant dies, work with the estate on surrender, the deposit and the belongings, documenting each step.

title: No Statutory Duty to Forward Legal Notices; Attornment Rules
bodyText:
District law does not require a tenant to forward to you a summons or notice of a proceeding against the property, so if you want that, put it in the lease; a clause asking the tenant to tell you promptly and hand over any written notice is lawful. Two old District statutes on attornment still apply.

First, a sale or other grant of your interest in the property is effective without the tenant's attornment, and the buyer or assignee steps into your rights under the lease; but a tenant is not prejudiced by paying rent to you, or treated as in breach for nonpayment, before the new owner gives the tenant notice of the transfer. So when you sell, make sure the buyer notifies tenants in writing where to pay.

Second, a fraudulent attornment by a tenant to someone else is void and does not change your possession, unless it was made under a court judgment or order, with your consent, or to a mortgagee after the mortgage is forfeited. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike.

title: No Rule on Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: District law has no statute on whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's own renter's insurance, or file a claim against it, and no statute on requiring renter's insurance at all; those questions are left to the lease and insurance law. Related limits do apply. A lease may not exempt you, or limit your liability, for injury or property damage caused by your own negligence or that of your agents or employees in operating or maintaining the premises, and it may not require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees. You also may not charge a tenant a fee for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable, so do not use a tenant's policy as a funding source for repairs that are your responsibility. If you sell a damage-waiver or similar product, any mandatory charge is a fee: it cannot be collected before the lease is signed, must be disclosed before screening, and in a rent-stabilized unit a mandatory fee needs approval. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Tenant Portals: No Statute, Several Limits
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation addresses tenant portals or forbids requiring rent payment or signatures through one. Several District rules limit a portal-only policy. Electronic dealings: the electronic transactions law requires no one to use electronic records or signatures and applies only between parties who agreed to deal electronically; a tenant who agreed may refuse further electronic dealings, and a lease cannot waive that right. So a lease clause requiring that every signature and notice go through a portal is not enforceable against a tenant who opts out, and statutory notices keep their own delivery methods. Payments: you must give a written receipt for every payment other than a personal check, stating amount, date, purpose and any non-rent balance; a portal can satisfy this. After a nonpayment judgment, the court's redemption notice says the landlord must accept the full redemption amount until the eviction is complete, and once the Marshals arrive payment is by cash, cashier's check or money order. Fees: District law bars fees for services the landlord must provide (and names administrative fees for third-party billing), and rent-stabilized units may not carry unapproved mandatory fees, so avoid portal convenience charges. Practical step: offer a portal as one option alongside a paper method.

title: Tenant Repair Agreements: No Statute, Code Duties Stay With You
bodyText:
District law has no statute authorizing, or setting formalities for, an agreement that a tenant will perform repairs or maintenance, and no separate-writing or consideration rule. What it does say limits such agreements. Every lease carries an implied warranty that you will keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations, you must provide and maintain the facilities, utilities and services they require, and any lease provision contrary to or waiving the housing-code chapter on leases is void and may not be included. So a tenant may agree to specific minor tasks, such as changing air filters or light bulbs or yard care for a private yard, but not to take over your code duties, and you remain responsible if the work is not done to code. A tenant's promise to keep the unit in good repair does not require substantial repairs or fixing defects that are not the tenant's fault.

Sidewalk snow removal is the one duty a statute expressly lets you delegate by written agreement, and you stay liable for any fine. In a rent-stabilized unit, ending a service you used to provide can be challenged as a reduction in related services. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Lease Statement; What the District Requires Instead
bodyText: The District has no truth-in-renting law of the kind some places use: no District statute or housing regulation requires the lease to carry a notice that District law sets the parties' rights, a warning that some clauses may be unenforceable, or an agency truth-in-renting statement delivered with the lease. The District reaches the same goal in other ways. At application you must give the Office of the Tenant Advocate's Tenant Bill of Rights with the Rent Administrator's disclosure form (see the tenant-rights-statement row). At the start of the tenancy you must give a copy of the landlord-tenant chapter of the housing regulations and two enforcement sections (see the lease-copy row). The Rent Administrator publishes a public booklet on tenant and housing-provider rights in English and Spanish, but you are not required to hand it out. And the housing regulations themselves void and forbid certain lease terms, such as waivers of the tenant protections in that chapter, owner-negligence exculpation, jury-trial waivers, fee shifting and confessions of judgment (see the prohibited-lease-terms row). Practical step: no extra statement is needed in the lease; deliver the required documents and keep proof.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires parking to be priced or leased separately from the rental unit, or forbids bundling it. Whether you bundle or unbundle, District rent and fee rules still apply. Parking provided with the unit is a related facility under the Rental Housing Act, and money demanded as a condition of using a related facility is rent. In a rent-stabilized unit, parking included in the registered rent cannot be taken away or separately charged without going through the Rent Administrator, and a mandatory parking charge that has not been approved exposes you to treble damages; an optional parking lease a tenant may decline is a different matter. Before the lease is signed only an application fee may be collected, so do not take a parking fee in advance. Zoning and land-use rules on parking, which may address unbundling for new buildings, are in District regulations. Applies to all District rental units; the stabilization points apply only to rent-stabilized units. Practical step: if you offer parking separately, make it optional, put it in a separate written agreement, and list it on the registration where required.

title: No Utility Allowance Rule; Fee Limits Apply
bodyText: District law has no rule addressing a private landlord's utility allowance, that is, a lease term where you pay a utility up to a monthly cap and bill the tenant for the overage. The District's utility-allowance rules in the housing regulations govern only the Housing Authority's subsidy programs. Three rules make an overage charge risky. First, you may not charge any fee for services required to keep the unit habitable, including fees related to utilities and administrative fees for third-party billing; a utility you supply under your own account is arguably such a service. Second, in a rent-stabilized unit, any mandatory charge for a utility counts as a mandatory fee and is barred unless approved through the rent stabilization program, with treble damages. Third, from January 1, 2027 you may not bill tenants separately for common-area or vacant-unit utilities. The law does expressly allow a ratio utility billing system to allocate master-metered charges among tenants by square footage, occupancy or bedrooms, subject to those limits. Practical step: either include the utility in the rent or have the tenant hold the account.

title: No Separate Utility-Deposit Rule; Deposit Rules Apply
bodyText: District law has no separate return rule for a utility deposit held by a landlord. Money you require as security for the tenant's lease obligations, including a deposit labelled for utilities, falls under the general security-deposit rules: together with any other deposit it may not exceed the first full month's rent and may be charged only once, it belongs in an insured, interest-bearing escrow account at a District financial institution, and it must be returned within 45 days after the tenancy ends, or withheld only after written notice and then itemized within 30 days. You may not charge any fee other than an application fee before the lease is signed, and you may not charge fees for utility-related services you are required to provide. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies. Deposits a utility company itself requires are governed by Public Service Commission rules outside the housing regulations, and a utility deposit or refund owed by a utility is presumed abandoned one year after it becomes payable. Practical step: do not take a separate utility deposit; fold any security for utilities into the single capped deposit and itemize any utility charges you withhold.

title: No Required Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires a utility disclosure attachment to a residential lease: no prescribed form explaining apportioned or submetered billing, no fee table, no required statement of dispute rights. The District's submetering law, which does require lease authorization, applies only to commercial rental units.
