What does apply to residential units is substantive: you may allocate master-metered utilities by a ratio formula (square footage, occupancy or bedrooms); from January 1, 2027 you may not separately bill tenants for common-space or vacant-unit utilities; you may not charge administrative fees for third-party utility billing; and in a rent-stabilized unit a mandatory utility charge needs rent-stabilization approval. Voucher and public-housing leases follow the Housing Authority's own requirements (for example, the voucher lease must say who pays which utilities). Practical step: although no attachment is required, spell out in the lease which utilities the tenant pays, how any shared bill is allocated and billed, and when; see the utility-apportionment and submetering rows for detail.

title: No Residential Submetering Regime; Utility Supply Duties
bodyText: District law has no special regime for landlord-submetered electricity in residential rentals: the District's submetering statute covers only nonresidential (commercial) rental units. Other rules still govern interruptions. Any utility that is your responsibility or under your control must be furnished in the quantities needed for normal occupancy, and where tenants do not control the heating or hot-water equipment you must supply heat and continuous hot water. Shutting off a utility to pressure a tenant is not a lawful way to recover possession, since eviction requires the statutory notice and a court process, and reducing services after a tenant complains or asserts rights is presumed retaliatory. If you allocate master-metered water, sewer, electric, oil or gas charges, a ratio utility billing system is allowed, but you may not charge administrative fees for third-party billing, and from January 1, 2027 you may not bill common-space or vacant-unit utilities separately from rent. If a utility company threatens shutoff for your unpaid master-metered account, tenants may take service in their own names and deduct payments from rent. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Statute on Proof of Utility Payment
bodyText:
District law does not address whether a tenant must show you proof of paying utilities, so a lease term requiring reasonable evidence on request is lawful. It matters because water and sewer charges can be collected from the occupant and DC Water may shut off service for bills unpaid 30 days regardless of any change in occupancy, and unpaid charges on an account the owner fails to pay can become a lien on your property.

Keep the request reasonable and tied to utilities the lease makes the tenant's responsibility. Do not attach a charge to it: administrative fees for third-party utility billing are barred, and in a rent-stabilized unit any mandatory fee for an unapproved service is barred. A tenant's failure to provide evidence is a lease breach you can enforce only through the 30-day notice to correct or vacate, and only if it is a substantial obligation. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Statutory Duty to Keep Utilities On
bodyText:
District law does not impose a statutory duty on tenants to keep utility service on, so a lease term saying the tenant will not let water, gas, electricity, sewer or trash service to the unit be interrupted is lawful where the tenant holds those accounts. Its limits come from your own duties: any utility that is your responsibility or under your control must be furnished in the quantities normal occupancy needs, and where the tenant does not control the heating or hot-water equipment you must supply heat and continuous hot water, so the clause cannot shift those services to the tenant.

DC Water may collect from the owner or occupant and may shut off service for bills unpaid 30 days regardless of a change in occupancy, so a tenant's lapse can affect the next occupant and your property. If service lapses because you did not pay a master-metered account, tenants may take service in their own names and deduct what they pay from rent. A breach is enforced only through the 30-day notice to correct or vacate. See also the utilities-responsibility row. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Landlord Utility Cutoff for Non-Transfer
bodyText: District law has no procedure letting a landlord cut off utilities still in the landlord's name when a tenant fails to transfer them into the tenant's name within a set number of days, and a lease clause giving you that power would cut against several rules. Any utility that is your responsibility or under your control must be furnished in the quantities needed for normal occupancy, a lease cannot waive the housing-code chapter, reducing services is listed retaliation, and an electric or gas company may not cut service to an apartment house of 3 or more apartments at the owner's request without a Public Service Commission finding. You may require in the lease that the tenant open accounts in the tenant's own name for utilities the tenant is to pay, and you can enforce that like any other lease obligation, through notice to correct the violation and, if necessary, the courts. In the meantime, you cannot charge a fee for utilities you must provide. Practical step: set the transfer deadline in the lease, keep service on, and bill any utility cost the lease puts on the tenant only as the lease allows.

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans; VASH Vouchers
bodyText: The District's statutes and housing regulations contain no landlord incentive for renting to veterans: no tax credit, rent guarantee, deposit fund, risk-mitigation pool or fee waiver tied to leasing to a veteran, and no veteran-specific lease terms or rights. Programs that may still matter to a District landlord: the Housing Authority administers Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing (VASH) vouchers, which pay part of the rent for eligible veterans and follow the general voucher program rules (inspection, payment contract and the program's lease addendum); and the Department of Housing and Community Development Unified Fund may be used to support the housing needs of veterans. A veteran-owner's own homestead tax deduction does not apply to rented property. Because a VASH voucher is a housing subsidy, refusing a veteran because of the voucher is source-of-income discrimination. Practical step: if you want to house veterans, list the unit with the Housing Authority's VASH program and screen voucher applicants on the same criteria as others.

title: No Waiver-by-Acceptance Statute; Use Without-Prejudice Stipulations
bodyText: District statutes do not say whether accepting rent after a tenant's breach, or after serving a notice, waives the breach or the notice, and they prescribe no reservation-of-rights wording; the question is left to case law. A few rules point the way. In a possession case that does not claim unpaid rent, the court may enter a protective order over the tenant's objection only if the tenant declines to stipulate that your acceptance of rent from then on is without prejudice to your case, so the usual practice is to obtain that stipulation or a protective order rather than refusing rent. For Inclusionary Zoning units, the regulations expressly say that accepting rent for up to 6 months after a notice to vacate for a lease violation does not waive the violation or void the notice; District Housing Authority rules say the same for its units. In a nonpayment case, accepting the full redemption amount before the eviction ends the case by law. Because a District tenant who keeps paying rent may stay after the term, accepting rent does not by itself create a new tenancy the way it can elsewhere. Practical step: when you accept rent while pursuing a violation notice, say in writing that acceptance is without prejudice, and raise the stipulation at the first court hearing.

title: No Waterbed Statute; Deposit Cap and Cure Notice Still Apply
bodyText: The District has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in private rentals. It neither guarantees a tenant the right to have one nor limits a landlord's lease rule on them, and it sets no insurance, deposit or installation requirements. A lease may ban waterbeds, require written consent, or condition them on things such as liability insurance, a structurally suitable floor and professional installation. Two general District rules still apply. Any extra charge must fit the District's deposit and fee rules: the security deposit (all security payments together) is capped at one month's rent and may be charged only once (federally subsidized and government-agency units are outside that rule), so a separate waterbed deposit on top of a full deposit is not allowed, and you may not charge fees for services you must provide anyway. And a lease rule breach supports eviction only after written notice and 30 days to correct. (Housing Authority-administered housing has its own written-approval rule; it does not apply to private landlords.)

title: No Window-Guard Rule; Window Maintenance Duties Apply
bodyText: The District has no window-guard law in its statutes and housing regulations: no duty to install window guards or stops where children live, no annual window-guard notice or lease rider, and no prescribed bold lease text about window falls. The window rules that do apply to every rental are maintenance rules: each window must have panes without open cracks or holes, sashes in good condition that fit their frames, and (except fixed windows) hardware that lets the window be opened easily and held open or closed; windows and frames must keep out rain and substantially keep out wind. The owner must also provide screens for openings to the outside from March 15 through November 15. Window-opening control and emergency-escape standards for new work come from the District's Construction Codes in DCMR Title 12. Because escape openings must remain usable, any guard or stop you install voluntarily should be a type that can be released from inside in an emergency. Practical step: if a household includes young children, offer window stops or releasable guards on upper-floor windows and keep a record of the offer; no lease rider is required.

title: Notice of Intent to File for Nonpayment: Required Text and Service
bodyText:
Before filing a nonpayment eviction for any District rental unit, you must serve a written notice of intent to file, and only if at least $600 of rent is unpaid; for less, you may notify the tenant of the debt but cannot seek eviction. The notice must use the statute's prescribed wording or substantively similar language (see the notes for the exact text), filled in with the total rent owed and with a ledger attached showing rent charges and payments for the period of delinquency.

The housing regulations also require it to say that, once a case is filed, the tenant may stay if the tenancy is redeemable and all unpaid rent is paid before the court orders eviction. Serve it both by certified mail or a tracked delivery service with return receipt requested and by hand delivery to the unit or posting on its front door; serve it in English and Spanish, and also in the tenant's primary language if you know or should know it is a covered language.

Late fees cannot be the basis of the case. Timing: the statute now says 10 days before filing, but the prescribed text and the regulation still say 30, so wait 30 days. A lease cannot replace or waive this notice.

title: Deposits Are Always Refundable; Disclose Any Nonrefundable Fee
bodyText: In the District there is no such thing as a nonrefundable security deposit. Any money a tenant pays as a deposit or other payment held as security for performing the lease is a security deposit, and within 45 days after the tenancy ends you must return it, and any similar payment made as a condition of the tenancy beyond the stated rent, with interest due, unless you give written notice of intent to withhold for expenses properly incurred. Nonrefundable fees are tightly limited too: before signing only the application fee is allowed; no fee may be charged for services needed to keep the unit habitable, for professional cleaning or for ordinary wear and tear; and in a rent-stabilized unit a mandatory fee needs approval. Where a nonrefundable charge is lawful, disclose it: the screening notice must say whether each fee or deposit is refundable, the application disclosure form must show any nonrefundable application fee, and a housing regulation still requires notice of any pending rent ceiling adjustment request before you accept a nonrefundable application fee or deposit, although the statute it implemented has been repealed; giving the notice is the cautious course.

title: Registered Agent for Non-Resident Owners
bodyText: A person or entity that owns even one District rental unit and is not a District resident must appoint, and keep in place, a registered agent for service of process. The agent must be a District resident or an organization incorporated in the District, and the appointment and any later change are filed with the licensing agency on its prescribed form. If no agent is appointed, or the agent stops serving with no successor, the District official becomes the agent; the penalty for violating the rule is $300. For a rent-stabilized unit, a nonresident housing provider who has not appointed and kept this agent may not raise the rent above base rent. No District statute or housing regulation requires the lease itself to name the agent, bars a nonresident individual owner from suing until the agent is filed, or requires tenants to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. An out-of-state company is different: a foreign corporation or limited liability company must register with the Mayor, naming a registered agent, before doing business in the District, and while it is doing business unregistered it may not maintain an action, an eviction included; its leases stay valid, and if it has no registered agent who can be found, the Mayor may be served for it. Whether renting out property is doing business for this rule is a case-law question; the statute's list of activities that are not doing business does not mention it (D.C. Code §§ 29-105.02, 29-105.03, 29-105.05 and 29-104.12(d)). Renting under a trade name carries a similar bar: no suit until the trade name is registered (D.C. Code § 47-2855.03(d)). And whoever you are, having an interest in District real property lets a District court hear a claim arising from it (D.C. Code § 13-423(a)(5)). Practical step: file the agent appointment with the rental license, keep it current, and give tenants the agent's name and address along with the owner and manager contacts.

title: Which District Tenant Protections Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: The District has one broad anti-waiver rule and several targeted ones. Broad rule: any provision of any lease or agreement contrary to, or waiving, the landlord-tenant chapter of the housing regulations (14 DCMR chapter 3, which carries the implied warranty of habitability, the deposit rules, receipts, copies, retaliation and the prohibited-terms list) or its civil-enforcement and tenant-notice sections is void, and including or demanding one is prohibited, with treble damages for bad faith. Because the implied warranty requires compliance with the whole housing code, code duties cannot be shifted away either. The Rental Housing Act itself has no general anti-waiver section. Instead particular rules carry their own protection: a tenant notice-to-vacate period over 30 days is void unless the lease makes the statutory statements; a sublet ban is only effective as the statute allows; the domestic-violence lease release applies notwithstanding any lease penalty; a tenant may not waive the right to receive an offer of sale before the building is sold; and an intrafamily-offense victim's right to call police cannot be waived. Some rights may be waived only by a separate voluntary writing, such as certain elderly or disabled tenants' rent-increase protections. Practical step: assume a District tenant protection cannot be contracted away unless the statute itself provides a waiver procedure.

title: How Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText:
District law sets delivery methods notice by notice, and a lease cannot swap them out. Notices to quit go in English and Spanish to the tenant personally, or to a person of proper age at the unit, or by conspicuous posting plus first-class mail within 3 days; nonpayment notices go by certified mail or tracked delivery and also by hand or door posting; the 21-day pre-eviction notice goes by phone or electronic message, first-class mail and posting (see the agreed-notice-method row for the full list).

Anyone may deliver these notices: no District statute, housing regulation or court rule limits service of a notice to quit to a sheriff, marshal or process server. Electronic delivery: the District's electronic transactions law applies only between parties who agreed to deal electronically, and a party who agreed may refuse further electronic dealings; that right cannot be waived, so a lease cannot lock a tenant into e-mail notices.

An electronic notice meets a writing requirement only if the tenant can save or print it, and never replaces a method another law specifies. Entry notices may be e-mailed or texted, but without the tenant's written acknowledgement a paper notice must follow. Rent Administrator filings and notices may be served electronically only on written consent.

Practical step: offer e-mail as an extra, never the only, method.

title: Notice-to-Quit Waiver Statute Displaced for Covered Units
bodyText: An old District statute lets the parties to a lease agree in writing to a longer or shorter notice to quit, or to waive notice entirely. For residential units covered by the Rental Housing Act (essentially every rental unit), later and more specific rules leave little for that statute to do. You cannot shorten or waive the notices you must give to recover possession: no tenant may be evicted for any reason without the written notice the eviction statute requires for the ground used, with its minimum waiting period, and you cannot end a residential tenancy by a notice to quit at all. On the tenant's side, a lease may not require more than 30 days' notice of the tenant's intent to vacate unless it also requires you to give written notice of any rent increase at least 30 days longer than that period; a longer notice requirement tied to the end of the initial term is void unless the lease says it expires with that term and that the tenant may then leave on 30 days' notice while month to month. Including a void provision in bad faith can bring treble damages. Practical step: use 30 days as the tenant's notice to vacate, and never include a waiver of eviction notices.

title: Lease Notices Clause and District Notice Rules
bodyText:
A general lease notices clause works in the District only as a backstop. District law prescribes how the most important landlord notices are delivered (see the notice-delivery-methods row), and those rules control over any address or method the lease names. Language matters too: every notice to correct or vacate, nonpayment notice of intent to file, and other eviction-grounds notice must be written in both English and Spanish, and also in the tenant's primary language if you know or reasonably should know it is one of the languages the District designates for limited-English-proficient residents.

Notices for reasons other than nonpayment must also be filed with the Rent Administrator. For ordinary communications (repair scheduling, rule reminders, the tenant's own notices to you), the lease may set addresses and allow e-mail, subject to the tenant's right to stop dealing electronically. Applies to all District rental units, month-to-month or fixed-term.

Practical step: list a District mailing address and an e-mail address for the landlord in the lease, keep the tenant's current contacts on file, and use the statutory method and languages for every eviction-related notice.

title: District Choices That Need Lease Text
bodyText: Several District rules give you a choice only if the written lease (or another writing) makes it; a silent lease takes the default against you. (1) Late fees: none may be charged unless the written lease states the maximum fee and the grace period. (2) Subletting: a sole-discretion ban on subletting or assignment is allowed only if it is in the lease; otherwise you may require only that a subtenant meet your reasonable rental criteria ("No Subletting or Assignment" clause). (3) Sidewalk snow: the owner must clear the sidewalk unless a written agreement delegates the job; you then may seek reimbursement of a fine from the tenant ("Clearing the Public Sidewalk" clause). (4) Occupancy: tell the tenant the maximum number of occupants in the lease or another writing ("Permitted Occupants and Maximum Occupancy" clause). (5) Entry: 48 hours' written notice applies unless the tenant agrees in writing to a shorter period; the optional clause ("Shorter Entry Notice for Requested Repairs" clause) asks for that agreement entry by entry, for repairs the tenant requested. (6) Tenant move-out notice: more than 30 days binds the tenant only if the lease contains the statutory statements and your matching longer rent-increase notice. Some choices are not available at all: the lease cannot let you end the tenancy at the end of the term without a statutory ground, and an agreement shortening or waiving notices to quit yields to the Rental Housing Act's eviction notices.

title: Facilities the Housing Code Requires
bodyText: Beyond the general duty to keep a rental in repair, the District's housing regulations require the owner of every residential building to provide and maintain the facilities, utilities and services the regulations list, properly installed and in safe, good working condition. These include: adequate heating, lighting and ventilation; a kitchen sink for each dwelling unit (except a bachelor apartment) and a toilet, washbasin and bath or shower with hot and cold water; at least two electric outlets in each habitable room; lighting in shared halls and stairways; screens on all openings to the outside from March 15 through November 15; an adequate lock and key for every entrance door when the tenant moves in; and, in multiple dwellings, covered metal trash receptacles. Anything you choose to furnish for cooking, food storage or refrigeration, and any air conditioning you provide as a service, must also be kept working. These duties are read into every lease as an implied warranty and a lease cannot waive them. They apply to every rented habitation, whatever the lease term. Building, fire and property-maintenance codes in other parts of the District's regulations add further requirements.

title: Ownership and Agent Information at Application; Registered Agent for Non-Resident Owners
bodyText: Before signing: at application, the Rent Administrator's disclosure form you give a prospective tenant must include the building's business license and registration or claim of exemption, and the ownership information from your registration filing, which lists each owner's name, street address (no P.O. box), email and phone, a non-resident owner's registered agent and any managing agent. Post your business license (or a copy) where tenants can see it; the license names a property or resident manager responsible for repairs. Non-resident owners of even one rental unit must appoint and keep a registered agent for service of process who is a District resident or District-incorporated organization, and report changes within 7 business days ($300 penalty; otherwise the Mayor becomes the agent). Consequences: in a rent-stabilized unit, rent cannot be increased unless the housing is registered, licensed and, for a non-resident owner, has a registered agent; willful failure to give the disclosures also bars increases. A possession complaint cannot be filed without a valid registration or claim of exemption and a current rental housing license (courts may waive the license in extenuating circumstances; not for subtenant cases), and a writ requires license documentation. Missing disclosures alone do not bar eviction.

title: Owner Move-In Is a Statutory Ground Only; No Lease Reservation
bodyText: In the District you do not need, and cannot usefully write, a lease clause reserving a right to end the tenancy so the owner can move in. The owner-occupancy ground comes from the eviction statute itself, applies whether or not the lease mentions it, and cannot be widened by the lease. It is available only to a natural person who holds a freehold interest in the unit (or a cooperative shareholder with a right of possession) and who in good faith wants the unit for that person's own immediate use as a dwelling; family members count only if they will live there with that person. You must serve a 90-day notice to vacate stating the factual basis, file it with the Rent Administrator with a sworn affidavit of good-faith intent, and not demand or receive rent for the unit from anyone for 12 months after recovering it. If you then re-rent it or do not move in, you owe the former tenant relocation costs and up to 12 months of rent-based damages. A lease clause allowing an owner or relative move-in on shorter notice, for a family member living alone, or by a company is not lawful. Practical step: leave owner move-in out of the lease and, if the need arises, follow the statutory ground exactly.

title: Vehicle Rules and Towing Tenant Vehicles
bodyText:
A District lease may set vehicle rules for the property (which vehicles may park, registration information, no repairs or washing outside designated areas), and the District lease uses its own version of the vehicle-rules clause ("Parking & Vehicle Requirements" clause). Two District points shape it. Charges: parking provided with the unit is a related facility, so in a rent-stabilized unit you may not impose an unapproved mandatory charge for tags, decals or access cards; the District clause issues them free and charges only actual cost for a replacement the tenant requests.

Towing a tenant's own car: the District's removal process for private property reaches vehicles parked without the owner's consent and abandoned or dangerous vehicles, as those terms are defined. A vehicle counts as abandoned on private property only after more than 30 days and only if it is apparently inoperable, harbors pests, or lacks valid tags; expired tags alone do not count until they are at least a year out of date.

Removing another person's vehicle is unlawful unless done by the owner, someone the owner authorized in writing, District employees, or a tow operator with valid District authorization.

Practical step: enforce vehicle rules first through the lease (notice to correct), and tow only through an authorized tow operator under District towing rules.

title: Occupancy Limits and the Required Maximum-Occupant Notice
bodyText:
The District sets occupancy by floor area, not persons per bedroom. A dwelling unit needs at least 130 square feet of habitable floor area for the first occupant, 90 more for each additional occupant up to seven, and 75 more for each occupant beyond seven; a sleeping room needs 70 square feet for one person and 50 square feet per person when shared, and no one may sleep in a room with a furnace, water heater, gas meter or unvented open-flame heater.

You must tell each tenant in writing, in the lease or otherwise, the maximum number of occupants the regulations allow for the unit, and neither you nor the tenant may permit occupancy above it. Separately, under the Human Rights Act an occupancy limit stricter than two persons in an efficiency, or twice the number of bedrooms plus one in a larger unit, is presumed to be familial-status discrimination when applied against a household with children. So list the occupants, give the maximum in the lease, and do not use an occupant list to bar a tenant's new child or a family within those numbers. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Multi-Unit Owners Must Give Residents 24-Hour to 7-Day Pesticide Notice
bodyText: Yes, for multi-unit properties. At least 24 hours, and not more than 7 days, before pesticides are applied on a multi-unit property, the owner must give each resident and tenant of the property that will be treated the pesticide information the operator must supply: the operator's name and District license number, the applicator, phone numbers including the poison control hotline, any re-entry period on the label, the pest, the pesticide or active ingredient, and the District's required caution statement (including whether reduced-risk pesticides are being used). Deliver it to each resident's door or mailbox, or by email or fax, and also post it conspicuously in common spaces near where the pesticide will be applied. The pest control operator must give you that information at least 48 hours before the application, so schedule accordingly. For lawn and exterior landscape treatment, the applicator posts signs visible from the main access points for 48 hours; the owner removes them afterward. No general pest control disclosure is required in the lease itself. Extermination responsibilities follow the housing code (see the bed bug entry).

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees
bodyText:
District law has no pet-fee statute in force, so ordinary deposit, rent and fee rules decide pet charges. Pet deposit: any money a tenant pays as security is a security deposit, so a pet deposit counts toward the single cap of one first full month's rent for all security, is charged only once, goes into the interest-bearing escrow account, and is returned under the 45-day rules.

A "nonrefundable pet deposit" does not exist; a one-time pet charge paid as a condition of the tenancy is at risk of being treated as a returnable deposit. Pet rent: a monthly pet charge is part of the rent, because rent includes everything demanded as a condition of occupancy. In a rent-stabilized unit, adding it raises the rent charged and must fit the program's limits; a mandatory charge for an unapproved service or facility exposes you to treble damages.

Timing: nothing but an application fee may be collected before the lease is signed. Assistance animals: no deposit, fee or pet rent. Not yet in effect: the Pets in Housing Amendment Act of 2024 would cap a separate pet deposit at 15% of monthly rent and pet rent at 1% of the first month's rent, and later bar breed, size and weight limits, but it applies only after funding, which has not occurred.

title: Pet Rules in District Leases
bodyText:
A private District landlord may allow, limit or forbid pets by lease, with these exceptions.
- (1) Assisted senior and disability housing: the owner or operator of a building of 4 or more rental units that receives District housing assistance and is designated for elderly tenants (60 or older) or tenants with disabilities may not prohibit those tenants from keeping common household pets or discriminate against them for having one; it may require removal of a pet found to be a threat or nuisance to other occupants' health or safety (fine up to $300 per violation).
- (2) Assistance animals are not pets (see the assistance-animal row).
- (3) Enforcement: you may not enter to remove a pet except in a genuine emergency, and you may not seize a tenant's animal or other property yourself; a pet-clause breach needs a written 30-day notice to correct or vacate, and only a substantial lease obligation supports eviction.
- (4) Not yet in effect: the Pets in Housing Amendment Act of 2024 would let landlords adopt reasonable pet policies, cap pet deposits and pet rent, and bar breed, size and weight restrictions for leases beginning after October 1, 2026, but it applies only after funding, which has not occurred.

Practical step: use the District pet clause and recheck the 2024 Act's funding.

title: No Cooperation Mandate; Lease May Not Bar or Penalize Police Calls by Violence Victims
bodyText: The District has no statute requiring tenants to cooperate with police or authorizing a crime-free lease addendum, and no general ban on such lease terms. One rule limits them: the Human Rights Act makes it unlawful, where a person living or intending to live in the unit is a victim of an intrafamily offense (domestic, dating or family violence), to bar or limit that person's right to call the police or emergency help, or to penalize anyone for making such a call. That right cannot be waived in a lease. So do not use lease terms that count police or 911 calls against a tenant, charge for them, or treat them as a breach. If a tenant or occupant commits a crime at the property, eviction requires a court determination of the illegal act and a 30-day notice to vacate (10 days, in cases filed after December 31, 2025, for a dangerous crime or crime of violence not committed in self-defense or defense of another, and only after you consider in good faith all reasonable ways to keep non-offending occupants housed; the regulation, 14 DCMR § 4302.2(a), still bars filing until 30 days after the notice, so the cautious course is to wait 30 days); an occupant's act counts against the tenant only if the tenant knew or should have known of it. A lease clause on tenant cooperation is therefore of limited practical use; describe prohibited conduct instead (see "Illegal Acts" clause). Two reporting duties do bind you and your staff as they bind anyone. Any person who knows or has reasonable cause to believe that a child is a victim of sexual abuse must report it to the police immediately (a 911 call or a report to the Child and Family Services Agency counts), and a willful failure carries a $300 civil fine (D.C. Code §§ 22-3020.52(a) and 22-3020.54(a)). And anyone who learns of a violent, sudden and unexpected, or suspicious death, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must promptly notify the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, and the body may not be disturbed without the medical examiner's permission; a willful failure to notify is a misdemeanor with a fine of $100 to $1,000 (D.C. Code §§ 5-1405(b) and 5-1406). Reporting the abuse of a vulnerable adult is voluntary unless you are in a listed profession (D.C. Code § 7-1903(a)).

title: Apartment and Condominium Pools: Semi-Public Pool Rules
bodyText: A pool operated for residents of an apartment, condominium or cooperative building is a Class C semi-public swimming pool, regulated by the Department of Health under DCMR Title 25-C. A District statute eases several of those rules for residential buildings. No lifeguard is needed for a pool open only to residents and their guests, unless the pool has a diving board, is deeper than 5 feet and was built after June 30, 2018, or expects a bather population that is half or more children under 15. Showers, toilets, eye-wash stations and dressing rooms are not needed if use is limited to residents and guests and the farthest unit is under 300 feet away by walkway. An apartment, condominium or cooperative building also need not provide a pool operator, a fence around a rooftop pool, a safety line or a facility license, among other listed items. The District's statutes and housing regulations have no pool-barrier or fencing rule for single-family rentals and no pool-safety notice that must be given at lease signing. Practical step: if a rental includes a pool, check the current Title 25-C rules and the Construction Codes for barrier requirements, post your pool rules, and address pool use and supervision of children in the lease or house rules.

title: Unit-Count Thresholds in District Law
bodyText: Most District landlord-tenant duties apply to every rental unit, whatever the landlord's size, including a room or basement unit in an owner-occupied home. A few rules turn on unit counts; read each one's limbs together. Rent stabilization exemption for small owners: all conditions must be met at once: 4 or fewer rental units (counted across buildings), owned by not more than 4 natural persons, none of whom has any other District rental interest, and a claim of exemption filed with the Rent Administrator. An LLC or corporation owner does not qualify (a decedent's estate or testamentary trust may keep an existing exemption). Criminal-record screening rules do not apply to a housing provider who owns and lives in a building with 3 or fewer rental units. Buildings with 3 or more units: an apartment-house license with a certificate of occupancy, a per-unit proactive-inspection fee, and a duty to order a water lead test kit within 15 days of a tenant's written request. Annual rental unit fee: paid by housing providers of rent-stabilized units and by small-owner-exempt providers. Practical step: record unit counts and ownership with the registration, and recheck the small-owner exemption whenever ownership or other District rental holdings change (a change must be reported within 30 days).

title: Evicted Tenant Property: 21-Day Notice, 7-Day Storage, Access
bodyText: District law tightly controls an evicted tenant's belongings. At least 21 days before a scheduled eviction you must send the tenant a final notice by phone or electronic message, first-class mail to the unit and conspicuous posting, giving the eviction date, warning that property left behind will be treated as abandoned 7 days after the eviction (not counting Sundays and federal holidays), listing the Marshals, Office of the Tenant Advocate and court phone numbers, and explaining the tenant's access rights. On eviction day you must mail a notice to the tenant's emergency contact, if one was given, and post it, naming an agent who can let the tenant in. The belongings stay in the unit for 7 days; you must store them with reasonable care and give the tenant at least 16 hours of access between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. over no more than 2 days (including a Saturday on request), with no rent or storage fee. After that, the property is abandoned and you must dispose of it, never by leaving it outdoors except while moving it to a licensed disposal site or lawful receptacle. Lawful disposal carries immunity; a missed notice can stay the eviction. These rules do not apply to District Housing Authority evictions.

title: Acts the Housing Regulations Prohibit Tenants From Doing
bodyText:
The District's housing regulations bind tenants directly, whether or not the lease repeats them. A tenant may not willfully or wantonly destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the structure, the unit, or its facilities, equipment or appurtenances, and may not let anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission do so. A tenant must keep the occupied part of the premises clean and sanitary, dispose of garbage properly, keep plumbing fixtures clean, and properly use electrical, gas, plumbing and heating fixtures and appliances.

No tenant may occupy or permit occupancy in violation of the housing regulations, for example above the occupancy limit, and no one may tamper with a posted violation notice. A tenant who has alleged a housing code violation may not unreasonably prevent your access to assess and fix it and must give access within 48 hours of your written request. A tenant who causes a violation faces the same penalties as an owner. To evict for a breach, the obligation must be substantial and you must give a 30-day notice to correct or vacate. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Prohibited Lease Terms: The District List and Beyond
bodyText: The housing regulations' prohibited-terms section is the core District list. A residential lease may not: waive or contradict the landlord-tenant chapter of the regulations or their civil-enforcement and tenant-notice sections; exempt you from, or limit, liability for your own negligence; waive the tenant's right to a jury trial; require the tenant to pay your court costs or legal fees; or authorize anyone to confess judgment against the tenant. Including such a term, or demanding that a tenant sign one, is itself prohibited, and bad faith brings treble damages. That list is not complete. Courts may strike other terms as unconscionable or against public policy, and separate laws void or forbid more: a tenant notice-to-vacate period over 30 days without the statutory statements; a sole-discretion sublet ban not written in the lease; late fees over 5% or not stated in the lease; deposits over one month's rent; mandatory binding arbitration in a consumer arbitration agreement; waivers of the right to receive a purchase offer before sale; discriminatory clauses; penalties on domestic-violence lease releases; and fees for services you must provide (see the repair-fee row). Timing rules matter too: a lease for a unit unsafe at the start is void, and the tenant must get a signed copy within 7 days. Practical step: review every District lease form against these lists.

title: Screening Questions the District Bans
bodyText: The District's Human Rights Act has no general rule for housing that bans asking about, or keeping records of, protected traits (its education part has one; its housing part does not). The housing part instead bans discriminatory acts and any notice, statement or advertisement indicating a preference based on a protected trait, so questions that reveal race, religion, national origin, familial status and the like are risky evidence even though not separately banned. Several District rules do ban specific questions in rental screening. You may not ask about a sealed eviction record or require its disclosure. You may not ask about an arrest that did not lead to a conviction, and before a conditional offer you may not ask about pending charges or convictions (owner-occupied buildings with 3 or fewer rental units are excluded from that chapter). You may not ask about eviction cases that did not end in a judgment for you or were filed 3 or more years ago, or about lease-breach allegations tied to domestic violence, crime victimization or disability. In verifying disability for a service animal you may ask only for a professional's verification and the disability-related need, not the nature or severity of the disability, and must allow 30 days. Practical step: keep the application to income, rental history and the permitted criminal-history steps.

title: Quiet Enjoyment Protected by Statute
bodyText: District statutes do not write a general covenant of quiet possession into residential leases, but the Rental Housing Act treats the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment as part of every covered tenancy. If you enter a unit without a reasonable purpose, a reasonable time and 48 hours' written notice (outside an emergency), or keep making unreasonable demands for entry, a court may order you to stop and award the tenant damages for breach of that right. Separately, you may not retaliate against a tenant who uses a legal right: harassing the tenant, violating the tenant's privacy, cutting services, refusing to honor the lease or refusing to renew are all listed forms of retaliation, and a court presumes retaliation if you act within 6 months after a repair request, a code complaint, tenant-organizing or a lawsuit. Forcibly entering premises, or holding them by force against someone in peaceable possession, is a crime. These rules cover month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike. Practical step: route all entries and disputes through written notice and the courts, never self-help.

title: Private-Collection Buildings Must Tell Occupants Yearly What to Recycle
bodyText: Yes, for many apartment buildings. District law requires all solid waste to be separated at the point of discard into recyclables and trash (and compostables once the Mayor's program reaches them). If the District does not collect trash from your property (a private collection property), you as owner must provide adequate waste collection, including: containers that make source separation accessible, with enough capacity (at least the equivalent of 32 gallons of storage per occupied unit per week), signed or color-coded by category, and equal in volume for recycling and trash; communicating to everyone who discards waste at the property, at least once a year, which materials must be separated there; annual source-separation training for any janitorial staff; and designating an agent responsible for compliance. Larger properties must also file a source separation plan with the Mayor that describes how the owner educates tenants and residents. Practical step: give tenants a recycling sheet at move-in and again each year (a lease rules attachment works for the first), and post signs at the containers. Buildings served by District collection follow the District's own program rules.

title: Redemption Before Eviction and ERAP Cancellation Rules
bodyText: A District tenant with a judgment for possession based on unpaid rent can redeem the tenancy by paying the full redemption amount before the eviction is completed; the judgment is then permanently stayed. The court sets the amount (or you file the court's notice of the payment required to avoid eviction within 7 days), it grows with new rent and costs, it cannot include late fees, and the right ends when the Marshals execute the writ. See the forfeiture-redemption row for the full procedure. Emergency rental assistance adds rules. The court may stay a nonpayment case once if the tenant shows a pending Emergency Rental Assistance Program application. If, at least 48 hours before a scheduled eviction, the tenant tells you an ERAP application has been approved that would pay the full amount needed to redeem, you must cancel the eviction, and any rescheduled date must be at least 3 weeks later. If you fail for more than 45 days to give an ERAP provider the payment information it requested, the court may deem the rent that ERAP would have paid waived, unless delay was caused by a third party, you had good cause, or ERAP has since paid. Practical step: answer ERAP payment-information requests promptly and accept full redemption payments, including those funded by assistance programs.

title: Substandard Units: Void Leases and Rent-Increase Bars
bodyText: District law has no single rule worded as a ban on demanding rent for a substandard unit, but several rules have that effect. A lease is void if the unit is unsafe or unsanitary from housing code violations at the start of the tenancy that you knew or should have known about, and becomes void later if such violations, not caused by the tenant or guests, are not corrected in the time allowed by a notice or, without a notice, within a reasonable time after you knew or should have known. After a court finds a breach of the warranty of habitability or a void lease, you need a certificate of compliance before re-letting the unit. You may not file to recover possession without a valid rental registration or claim of exemption and a current rental housing license. In a rent-stabilized unit, rent may not be increased unless the unit and common areas substantially comply with the housing code, and the Rent Administrator may roll rents back for prolonged violations. For any covered unit, willfully failing to give the required disclosure form blocks rent increases.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases: 60-Day Notice; Barred in Stabilized Leases
bodyText: No District rule bars a lease clause that schedules rent changes during the term, but two rules shape it. First, every rent increase for any covered unit takes effect only on the first regular rent day more than 60 calendar days after written notice of the increase is given to the tenant, so a scheduled step-up or index adjustment should come with a written notice at least that far ahead; a 30-day mid-term increase clause does not work in the District. If the lease requires the tenant to give more than 30 days' notice to leave, your rent-increase notices must be at least 30 days longer than that period. Second, in a rent-stabilized unit, no rent adjustment under the Act may be made during a valid written lease that sets the rent for its term, and any increase must respect the 12-month spacing and the annual cap, so mid-term escalation is effectively unavailable. Retaliation: an unlawful rent increase within 6 months after a tenant's repair request, complaint or other protected act is presumed retaliatory.

title: Rent Increases Need More Than 60 Days Written Notice
bodyText: For any unit covered by the Rental Housing Act, rent-stabilized or exempt, a rent increase takes effect only on the first regular rent day that falls more than 60 calendar days after you give the tenant written notice. This applies to month-to-month tenants and to tenants staying on after a fixed term ends; because a lease's expiration does not end the tenancy in the District, there is no separate nonrenewal route around the notice. If your lease requires the tenant to give more than 30 days' notice to move out, your rent-increase notice must be at least 30 days longer than that. In a rent-stabilized unit you must also use the Rent Administrator's Notice to Tenant of Rent Adjustment form, which shows the prior rent, the dollar and percentage increase, the new rent and its due date, and the protections for elderly tenants and tenants with a disability; certify that the unit substantially complies with the housing code; and file a copy with the Rent Administrator within 30 days after the increase takes effect. No increase is allowed during a written lease that fixes the rent for its term.

title: Protective Orders (Rent Into Court) and Tenant Counterclaims
bodyText: In a District possession case for unpaid rent, either party may ask the court for a protective order requiring the tenant to pay the monthly rent into the court registry while the case is pending. The court first informs the tenant of common defenses that can reduce the amount (such as current housing-code violations or a dispute about the rent), enters a preliminary order at the ledger or lease rent, and then holds a hearing on those defenses. Payments are prospective only, unless a continuance makes the order relate back to the first request. If the tenant misses payments, you may move for sanctions; in a nonpayment case the court can enter a judgment for possession only after you prove liability and damages, and that judgment remains redeemable. Without a nonpayment claim, possession cannot be a sanction. Paying into court is not a precondition to raising defenses. In a nonpayment case, or where rent arrears are claimed, the tenant may assert recoupment or set-off or a counterclaim based on rent paid or expenditures credited against rent, or for equitable relief about the premises; other counterclaims, including personal injury, must be filed elsewhere. Either party may demand a jury; a tenant doing so files a verified answer. Practical step: bring your rent ledger and repair records to the first hearing.

title: Rent Payment Terms Come From the Lease
bodyText:
District law does not set a default due date, place of payment or weekend rule for rent; those terms come from the lease. What the law does control: you must give a written receipt for every payment not made by personal check, stating the amount, date and purpose and any amount still owed for late charges or other charges beyond rent; a late fee is allowed only after more than 5 days (or the lease's longer grace period) and only if the lease states the grace period and maximum fee; a lease term cannot waive the tenant's housing-code rights, including the implied warranty of habitability, so a no-deduction clause should be limited to what the law allows, since District law recognizes lawful rent withholding after notice of housing-code violations.

A tenant who keeps paying the rent may not be evicted even after the lease term ends. These rules apply alike to month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies in every covered unit.

title: Written Receipts Required for Non-Check Payments
bodyText:
In every lease or rental of a dwelling in the District, you must give the tenant a written receipt for all money paid to you as rent, security deposit or anything else, unless the tenant pays by personal check. That covers cash, money orders, cashier's checks and electronic payments. Each receipt must show the exact amount received, the date received and the purpose of the payment, and must also show any amount still owed for late charges, court costs or other charges beyond rent.

If the tenant pays by personal check and still owes such charges, you must give a receipt stating the nature and amount of those charges. The duty applies on its own, without any request or notice from the tenant, for month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike. District law does not make a missing receipt a stated defense to eviction, but receipts and ledgers are evidence in court.

Practical step: issue receipts automatically from your payment system.

title: Rent Payment Reporting Offer (If the Mayor Establishes the Program)
bodyText: District law lets the Mayor set up a rent payment reporting program. It began as emergency legislation and was made permanent by the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Act of 2026 (effective October 2, 2026). Only if the program is established, housing providers must offer each tenant the option to have rent payments reported to credit reporting agencies. Participation is the tenant's choice. The offer must be a written notice that says reporting is optional, names each credit reporting agency, explains which payments are reported and when a payment counts as timely, late or missed, explains how to opt out at any time (and that the tenant cannot rejoin for 6 months after withdrawing), and has a signature block the tenant signs and dates to accept. You must stop reporting within 30 days of a tenant's request, and must stop while a tenant who gave written notice is withholding rent over habitability conditions. Landlords receiving District financial assistance may be required to participate. Practical step: watch for the Mayor's program launch and the Department of Housing and Community Development's notice template; until the program exists, no offer is required.

title: Residential Rent Is Not Subject to Sales Tax
bodyText: Ordinary residential rent is not subject to the District's sales tax. The sales tax reaches the charge for rooms, lodgings or accommodations only when they are furnished to transients by a hotel, inn or other place that regularly furnishes rooms to transients, and a transient is someone who occupies, or has the right to occupy, the space for 90 days or less in one continuous stay. So a lease or occupancy of more than 90 days is outside the tax, while short stays of 90 days or less in a place regularly renting to transients are taxable and the operator must collect the tax. The two regimes connect: a unit counts as transient occupancy for Rental Housing Act purposes only if the landlord is subject to and pays that sales tax, so a unit rented to residents for longer stays stays inside the Act's tenant protections. Self-storage space rented for household goods is a separately taxable service. Practical step: do not add a sales or occupancy tax line to a residential lease.

title: Rent Stabilization: Coverage and Increase Limits
bodyText: The District has rent stabilization, set by the Council for the whole District (there is no separate city or county layer). It applies to rental units unless exempt, for example federally or District-subsidized or tax-credit units, buildings permitted after 1975, and units of a small owner (natural persons owning 4 or fewer units in the District) who has filed a claim of exemption. Give an exempt unit's applicant written notice, before the lease is signed, that rent increases are not regulated by the program. In a rent-stabilized unit, rent may rise by no more than the annual inflation adjustment plus 2% (never more than 10% in total), with at least 12 months between increases, no increase during a written lease that fixes the rent for its term; and no increase unless the unit substantially complies with the housing code and the building is registered and licensed. Elderly tenants and tenants with a disability are limited to the least of the annual adjustment, the Social Security cost-of-living rise, or 5%. On vacancy, rent may rise 10% (20% after a tenancy over 10 years). Every increase in any unit needs written notice more than 60 days before it takes effect. The program is set to end December 31, 2030 unless extended.

title: Rental Licensing Inspections and Tenant Consent
bodyText: Every District rental needs a basic business license with a housing endorsement, and as a condition of that license you must let District inspectors inspect the premises. The District runs both complaint-based and proactive rental inspections, and buildings with 3 or more units pay a proactive-inspection fee of $35 per unit (capped at $2,000) at each license issuance and renewal. District inspectors may enter a housing accommodation at reasonable hours, but if the tenant does not give permission to inspect the part of the premises under the tenant's exclusive control, the inspector may enter that part only with an administrative search warrant or in an exigent danger. No District rule lets a lease give that permission in advance for the tenant, so do not rely on a lease clause to admit an inspector; the tenant decides at the time. A tenant's refusal does not cost you your license, and anyone who hinders an authorized inspection commits a misdemeanor. Your own entries to do government-ordered work follow the 48-hour written-notice entry rule.

title: No Lease Fees for Required Repairs, Warranty Deductibles or Cleaning
bodyText: District law bars lease terms that charge tenants for repairs or maintenance you are required to provide. Since August 14, 2026, you may not charge a prospective tenant, a tenant, or a former tenant any fee before move-in, during the tenancy or after move-out for services needed to keep the unit consistent with the implied warranty of habitability and the construction and housing codes, including fees related to utilities, trash, locks and administrative fees for third-party billing. The housing regulations say the same and add that you may not charge a fee, or withhold from the deposit, for professional cleaning or for damage from ordinary wear and tear. So a lease may not pass home-warranty deductibles, service-call fees or repair co-pays to the tenant for code-required repairs. What remains allowed: you may withhold from the security deposit to replace items the tenant damaged beyond ordinary wear and tear, and recover actual costs of damage the tenant's side caused. In a rent-stabilized unit, any mandatory fee for a service or facility not approved through the rent stabilization program is barred, with treble damages. Practical step: remove repair, maintenance, warranty-deductible and lock-change fees from District leases; limit charges to proven tenant-caused damage.

title: Repair Notice: Knowledge, Not Paperwork
bodyText:
District law does not make a written repair request a precondition to your repair duty, and a lease cannot make it one. Your housing-code duties run from what you know or reasonably should know: a lease becomes void if the unit becomes unsafe or unsanitary through code violations the tenant did not cause and you fail to correct them within the time a violation notice allows or, without a notice, within a reasonable time after you knew or should have known of them.

A lease term saying you are notified only in writing is contrary to that rule and void, because the housing-code chapter cannot be waived. For retaliation, a repair request counts if it was written or made orally in front of a witness, and any action you take against the tenant within 6 months is presumed retaliatory. Mold is different: once a tenant gives written or electronic notice of mold, you must inspect within 7 days and remediate within 30 days of the inspection.

Practical step: ask tenants to report problems in writing or through a portal, but act on any report you receive, written or not.

title: Which Fees Must Be Disclosed or Written in the Lease
bodyText: District law has no single rule that every fee must be listed in the lease, but several rules together push you to list them. Before screening, you must give or post a written list of every fee and deposit, mandatory or optional, with its amount, purpose, timing and refundability. A late fee is lawful only if the written lease states the grace period and the maximum fee, and security-deposit terms must appear in the lease or on the deposit receipt. Once a tenant's balance is more than 30 days past due, you may collect interest or any added fee or charge only if the lease expressly authorizes it (or a law does). In a rent-stabilized unit, a mandatory fee is allowed only for a service or facility approved by the Rent Administrator. No fee may be charged before lease signing other than an application fee, and none at any time for services needed to keep the unit habitable. There is no statutory notice period for adding a new fee mid-lease; any new required charge works as a rent increase needing more than 60 days' written notice.

title: Retaliation Ban With 6-Month Presumption
bodyText: District law bars retaliation against a tenant for exercising any right under the Rental Housing Act, its rules, or any other law. Retaliation includes an unlawful attempt to recover possession, an unlawful rent increase, cutting services, adding obligations, harassment, violating the tenant's privacy, refusing to honor or renew a lease, ending a tenancy without cause, or any other threat or coercion. A court must presume retaliation, and rule for the tenant unless you prove otherwise by clear and convincing evidence, if within the 6 months before your action the tenant: made a witnessed oral or a written repair request needed for housing-code compliance; complained to District officials about code violations (in writing or orally before a witness); lawfully withheld rent after reasonable notice of a violation; was involved in lawful tenant-organization activity; tried to secure or enforce lease rights; or sued you. The housing regulations separately bar eviction, rent increases or service cuts in retaliation for good-faith complaints about housing deficiencies, tenant organizing or asserting housing-code rights, and the Human Rights Act bars retaliation for exercising fair-housing rights. Remedies include cease-and-desist orders and fines. Practical step: document a legitimate, independent reason for any adverse action, especially within 6 months after a complaint.

title: Give the Tenant Advocate's Tenant Bill of Rights at Application; Housing Code Copy at Move-In
bodyText: Yes. The District's equivalent is the Tenant Bill of Rights published by the Office of the Tenant Advocate. You must give it to every applicant for a covered rental unit at the time of application, as part of the Rent Administrator's disclosure package, and give a tenant a free copy of the disclosure documents (which include it) within 10 business days of a written request, once a year. The requirement for a new version starts 90 days after the agency notices it in the D.C. Register. The Tenant Advocate published a revised Bill of Rights (form dated September 25, 2026); because the start date of the revision could not be confirmed, give the version the agency currently publishes. Separately, at the start of every tenancy (and to existing tenants) give a copy of the housing regulations' landlord-tenant chapter and its civil-enforcement and tenant-notification sections. No District statute requires the guide again at renewal or a signed acknowledgment, but keeping the tenant's signed receipt (the revised form includes a receipt line) is good evidence of delivery.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: Selling a tenanted District property: before an owner sells a housing accommodation, the tenants generally must get an opportunity to purchase under the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (see the TOPA rows). The sale does not end the lease: the buyer takes the seller's rights against the tenant and the tenant keeps its rights under the lease covenants. A tenant who pays rent to the seller before receiving notice of the sale is protected, so the buyer should send written notice of the transfer and where to pay. Filings: within 30 days after a change of ownership the housing provider must file a new rental registration (or claim of exemption), and within 30 days after a change of managing agent or contact information an amendment; a copy of an amended form goes to tenants within 15 days of its return, and a late filing counts as a failure to register. The rental license holder must also tell the licensing agency of a change in the property or resident manager. A buyer may recover a unit for personal use only through the statutory 90-day notice route after TOPA. Showings to buyers need 48 hours' written notice. No District statute, housing regulation or court rule transfers the security deposit on sale (see the deposit-on-sale row).

title: Deposit Cap: One Month Rent, Charged Once
bodyText:
A security deposit, together with any other payment you require as security for the tenant's performance, may not exceed the first full month's rent charged that tenant, and may be charged only once. There is no separate allowance for pets, furniture, alterations or higher-risk tenants, so a pet deposit counts inside the same one-month limit. Because the deposit may be charged only once, you may not demand an additional deposit later to keep pace with a rent increase.

Holding deposits credited to the security deposit count toward the cap. The cap applies to month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike. It does not apply to units leased by federal or District agencies or units whose rents are federally subsidized, which follow program rules. A rare older rule also bars demanding a deposit from a tenant who has occupied the unit since July 17, 1985 without one.

title: Deposit Escrow, Posting and Written Terms
bodyText:
You must put every security deposit (and any other payment held as security) into an interest-bearing escrow account, held in trust solely for deposits, at an insured financial institution in the District of Columbia. One account may serve all your buildings. Write the terms and conditions of the deposit in the lease or on the deposit receipt. At the end of each calendar year, post in the building lobby and rental office where tenants' deposits are held and the prevailing interest rate for each 6-month period; when a tenancy ends, list for the tenant the rate for each 6-month period of the tenancy.

You may not assign the account or use it as security for a loan, except where no interest is owed to the tenant. The escrow, cap, posting and written-terms rules do not apply to units leased by federal or District agencies or units with federally subsidized rents; the return and interest rules still do. The landlord chooses the institution, but not a non-escrow or out-of-District account, and no bond substitute is provided.

title: Deposit Interest: Statement Savings Rate, Paid After 12 Months
bodyText:
Interest on a security deposit (and on a decorating fee or similar deposit or fee) belongs to the tenant. It starts on the date the tenant actually pays the money and accrues at no less than the statement savings rate at the District financial institution holding your escrow account, reset on each January 1 and July 1 for the following 6-month period or part of it. Interest is payable to the tenant when a tenancy of 12 months or more ends, together with the deposit, unless it is applied to amounts properly withheld under the deposit rules.

If you invest the deposit at a rate above the statement savings rate, you may keep up to 30% of the excess interest for administrative costs or other purposes. Failing to pay interest owed makes you liable for the interest, or treble that amount for bad faith, and a willful failure can bring a civil fine of up to $5,000 per violation. At the end of the tenancy, give the tenant a list of the interest rate for each 6-month period.

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Security Deposit
bodyText:
If you miss the District's deposit deadlines, the tenant's case gets much easier. Within 45 days after the tenancy ends you must either return the deposit with any interest due, or deliver a written notice (in person or by certified mail) that you intend to withhold; then, within 30 days of that notice, refund the balance with an itemized statement of each repair or other use and its cost.

Not doing so is prima facie evidence that the tenant is entitled to the full deposit plus interest, though a good-faith but unsuccessful attempt to serve does not count as a failure. A landlord who fails to return a deposit rightfully owed is liable for the amount withheld, or three times that amount for a bad-faith refusal (frivolous or unfounded and driven by a deceptive or unreasonably self-serving purpose, not simple negligence or an honest mistake).

Unpaid interest follows the same single-or-treble rule, and a willful failure to pay interest can bring a civil fine of up to $5,000. Tenants of any covered unit, rent-stabilized or exempt, can petition the Rent Administrator, and attorney's fees may be awarded to the prevailing party. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies. Calendar both deadlines at every move-out and keep proof of delivery.

title: Returning the Security Deposit
bodyText:
District law sets a two-step return process. Within 45 days after the tenancy ends, either return the full deposit plus any interest due without waiting for the tenant to ask, or deliver written notice of your intent to withhold, in person or by certified mail to the tenant's last known address. If you send that notice, you must within 30 days refund the balance (with unused interest) and an itemized statement of each repair or other use and its cost.

Separately, when the tenancy ends you must ask for a forwarding mailing or email address and, within the same 45 days, send written notice (in person, by email or by certified mail) of any unpaid amounts you claim, with photos or other documentation and a statement of the tenant's right to dispute; the tenant has 30 days to dispute and you must answer within 10 days.

The clock runs from the end of the tenancy, not the lease date: in the District, a fixed term expiring does not by itself end the tenancy, and a month-to-month tenancy ends on a proper tenant notice or lawful eviction. Interest is owed on tenancies of 12 months or more. A refund the tenant never claims can become reportable unclaimed property after three years.

title: How a Security Deposit May Be Used
bodyText:
In the District a deposit may be applied only to expenses properly incurred under the deposit terms set out in the lease or deposit receipt, so write those terms down. Lawful uses include unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant, an immediate family member or a guest, the cost of removing belongings left at move-out, and lawfully imposed late fees that you invoiced with 30 days to pay and that went unpaid.

You may not withhold for ordinary wear and tear (deterioration from intended use, including breakage or malfunction from age), for professional cleaning, or for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable. A tenant's promise to leave the unit in good repair does not oblige the tenant to fix defects that are not the tenant's fault.

District law makes no provision for flat, pre-set cleaning or repair charges: the itemized statement must show each actual repair or use and its cost, and the unpaid-amounts notice must include photos or other documentation. Hold deposits in an insured, interest-bearing escrow account at a District financial institution and do not pledge them as loan security. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Locks, Detectors and Security Duties
bodyText: When a tenant first takes possession, you must provide an adequate lock and key for every door that is or can be used to enter or leave the unit, each lockable from inside and outside, and keep the locks in repair. In a multi-unit building, each exterior door must lock so that people can leave without a key but cannot enter without a key unless a tenant or building employee opens it. You must also install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in every occupied dwelling unit as the District's construction codes require, and the operator of a licensed housing business must keep required fire alarm systems working. District law found in the housing statutes and regulations sets no rule requiring you to re-key between tenants or to install peepholes, deadbolts or window locks as such, though inoperative door or window locks are listed as a serious threat that can support a tenant receivership. You may not charge tenants a fee for lock-related services you must provide. A tenant who is a victim of an intrafamily offense can require a lock change within 5 business days (see the domestic-violence lock-change row). Practical step: re-key at turnover as good practice; use the keys clause ("Keys and Locks" clause).

title: Court-Only Eviction: No Lockouts, Removals or Shutoffs
bodyText: In the District a landlord may remove a residential tenant only through the court. The statutes leave no room for self-help: no tenant may be evicted for any reason without the written notice the eviction statute requires, the prescribed nonpayment notice tells tenants that only a court can order their eviction, a writ of restitution is executed by the U.S. Marshals, and you change the locks only at that time and in the Marshals' presence. Even after an eviction you may not remove the tenant's belongings except under the 7-day storage and access rules. So do not change locks, remove doors or belongings, or shut off utilities or other services to force a tenant out, whether for unpaid rent or any other reason. Related remedies include: liability for the excess rent (trebled for bad faith) and civil fines where services previously provided are substantially reduced or eliminated; a presumption of retaliation for actions within 6 months after protected tenant activity; injunctions and damages for unlawful entry or repeated unreasonable demands for entry; and reimbursement to the District of emergency relocation costs when an owner's utility shutoff leads to a closure. District statutes do not set a separate fixed-dollar penalty for an illegal lockout; the general prohibition on self-help comes from case law.

title: Penalty for Denying a Service Animal
bodyText: The District makes denying housing because of a service animal a criminal offense. Under the District's law on the rights of persons with disabilities, any person, or that person's agent, who interferes with the housing-access rights it protects faces up to 90 days in jail, a fine of up to $300, or both; a $250 civil fine may be imposed instead through the civil-infractions process. The housing-access right covers every rental housing accommodation in the District and includes the right to keep a service animal without an extra charge. Two cautions. The penalty section still describes the protected person as a blind person or a person with another physical disability, while the access section now covers physical or mental disabilities, so its reach to mental disabilities is unclear on the text. And the separate Human Rights Act treats refusing a reasonable accommodation, such as an exception to a no-pets rule for an assistance animal, as unlawful discrimination with its own remedies. Applies to all District rental units, including small and owner-occupied rentals for the service-animal law. Practical step: never refuse or condition a rental because of a service animal; route requests to someone trained on the documentation limits.

title: Services and Utilities You Must Provide
bodyText:
In the District, the housing regulations decide many services for you. You must provide and maintain the facilities, utilities and services the regulations require, and any utility (water, electricity, gas or other fuel, sewer, refuse) that is your responsibility or under your control must be furnished in the quantities needed for normal occupancy.

Where the tenant does not control the heat or hot water, you must keep the unit at least 68 degrees F from 6:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. and 65 degrees F overnight, and supply continuous hot water. Spell out in the lease which services and utilities you provide and which the tenant arranges. You may not charge any fee for services you are required to provide to keep the unit habitable, including fees related to utilities, trash and locks or administrative fees for third-party billing; from January 1, 2027 you may not bill tenants separately for common-area or vacant-unit utilities.

In a rent-stabilized unit, the services and facilities included in the rent are part of the rent: cutting them can lead to a rent reduction, and you may not impose a mandatory fee for any service or facility not approved by the Rent Administrator. Reducing services in response to a tenant complaint is presumed retaliation.

title: Severability and Void Leases
bodyText:
District rules on improper lease terms mostly strike the offending term, not the whole lease, so a severability clause fits District law: a lease provision that waives or contradicts the landlord-tenant chapter of the housing regulations is void on its own, and a tenant notice-to-vacate term longer than the law allows is void without affecting the rest. One District rule voids the entire lease and no severability clause can save it: a lease of a home that is unsafe or unsanitary at the start of the tenancy because of housing-code violations the owner knew or should have known about is void, and a lease also becomes void if such violations arise later, were not caused by the tenant or the tenant's guests, and are not corrected in the time allowed by a violation notice (or within a reasonable time after the owner knew or should have known).

Courts may also refuse to enforce terms they find unconscionable or contrary to public policy. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: keep the severability clause, keep the unit code-compliant at move-in, and fix violations promptly.

title: Shortening Notice for Showings
bodyText: Showing the unit to prospective tenants, buyers or lenders is a reasonable purpose for entry in the District, and the normal rule applies: written notice at least 48 hours before entry, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. other than Sundays and federal holidays. The tenant may agree in writing to a shorter notice period, and may agree to other hours (the law does not say that agreement on hours must be written, but get it in writing). District law does not require the agreement to be in a separate document, and does not create a special end-of-lease showing window. Because the statute speaks of a period agreed to by the tenant, the safest practice is a short, specific written agreement signed when showings begin (for example, 24 hours' notice by text for showings during the last 30 days), rather than relying on a blanket clause in the original lease.
