Electronic notices still require the tenant's written acknowledgement or a paper notice. Repeated unreasonable showing demands can lead to an injunction and damages.

title: Owner Clears Abutting Sidewalk Within 8 Daylight Hours; Delegation to Tenant Only in Writing
bodyText:
Public sidewalk: the owner of a residential property that fronts or abuts a paved sidewalk must, within the first 8 hours of daylight after snow or sleet stops, clear a path the full width of the sidewalk up to 36 inches wide. If clearing would damage the sidewalk, the owner must make it safe with sand or similar material within the same time. The owner may delegate the clearing duty (not, on the statute's wording, the sanding duty) to a tenant only by written agreement.

The owner stays liable for any fine (no more than $25 for a residential property, and no ticket until 24 hours after the snow stops), but may seek reimbursement from a tenant who took over the duty in writing. Owners 65 or older or with a disability are exempt from the fine. On the property: the owner is responsible for common areas and spaces not under a tenant's exclusive control; walkways must be kept clean and safe. A tenant may take on snow clearing for areas the tenant alone uses, if the lease says so.

Use the optional sidewalk clause ("Clearing the Public Sidewalk" clause) for single-family or similar rentals where the tenant will clear the public sidewalk.

title: Source of Income and Housing Vouchers
bodyText: Source of income is a protected trait under the District's Human Rights Act, and Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) assistance paid to an owner directly or through the tenant expressly counts. So you may not refuse a voucher holder, advertise "no vouchers", or set different terms because of how rent will be paid. For an applicant paying with an income-based housing subsidy you also may not rely on past late or unpaid rent or credit problems from a period without the subsidy, or on income level, credit score or lack of one (unless federal law requires it); charging such an applicant fees or deposits others do not pay, or higher rent, is presumed discriminatory. You may not require a holding deposit from a prospective tenant using a government-funded housing voucher. Exemptions are the general Human Rights Act exemptions: an owner-occupied building with no more than two independent units (or four where the tenant would share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner), and a single-family home rented by an owner of no more than 3 homes without a broker or discriminatory advertising. The holding-deposit rule has no exemption. District law has no lease-statement duty for vouchers. Practical step: screen voucher applicants on the same written criteria and use the program's required lease addendum.

title: Statute of Frauds and Written Leases
bodyText: Two District writing rules apply to leases. First, the District statute of frauds: no action may be brought on a contract for any interest in or concerning real estate, or on an agreement that cannot be performed within one year, unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged (or someone that party authorized). How that applies to short oral tenancies is a question for the courts. Second, a validity rule rather than a recording rule: a lease for a term longer than 1 year can be created only by a deed signed and sealed by the lessor in person or by power of attorney (see the lease-term-limitation row). Recordation tax reaches only leases of 30 years or more, and no District statute, housing regulation or court rule requires a residential lease to be recorded. A tenant under an oral or unwritten arrangement still has the Rental Housing Act's protections, but some landlord rights depend on a written lease, such as charging any late fee. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: put every lease in writing, signed by all parties; for terms over 1 year, have the owner sign under seal.

title: District Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: District law sets these money limits for covered rental units, whatever the lease says. Security deposit (and any other payment held as security): no more than the first full month's rent, charged once. Late fee: no more than 5% of the rent due, only after more than 5 days (or a longer lease grace period), once per late payment, and only if the lease states the grace period and maximum. Application fee: $50 adjusted yearly for inflation, the only fee allowed before signing; a fee for a replacement tenant, assignment or sublet may not exceed the application-fee limit. No fee at all for services needed to keep the unit habitable, for professional cleaning or for ordinary wear and tear. Rent-stabilized units: annual increases capped at the inflation adjustment plus 2% (never over 10%), with lower limits for elderly tenants and tenants with a disability, and vacancy increases of 10% or 20%. Lock change requested by a victim of an intrafamily offense: the lock-change statute lets you recover your cost plus a fee no higher than you charge other tenants, but whether the 2026 ban on fees for services you must provide (which names locks) now bars that is unsettled, so the cautious course is not to charge. There is no cap on returned-payment fees, and a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney's fees or court costs.

title: Prescribed Wording and Agency Forms
bodyText: The District prescribes no lease form and no verbatim lease text. It does prescribe wording for some side documents and requires agency forms for others. Prescribed wording: the notice of intent to file for nonpayment of rent must use the statute's text or substantively similar language (amount owed, attached ledger, the $600 floor, right to defend, and the Office of the Tenant Advocate and legal-aid phone numbers). The day-of-eviction notice must include or attach the text of the statute's storage-and-access subsection. A real estate licensee's brokerage-relationship disclosure that substantially follows the statutory model complies. Agency forms you must use: the Rent Administrator's disclosure form at application (with the Tenant Bill of Rights published by the Office of the Tenant Advocate); the Rent Administrator's rent-history form with a new lease in a rent-stabilized unit; the Mayor's lead-paint disclosure form before a pre-1978 lease is signed; the Mayor's lead-rights notice at every lease signing or renewal and rent-increase notice; the Mayor's lead-plumbing disclosure form before any lease or renewal; and copies of the registration or exemption form. Notices to correct or vacate and the 21-day pre-eviction notice have required contents but no prescribed wording. Practical step: download the current agency forms when you use them, since agencies revise them; the 2026 revision of the Tenant Bill of Rights is an example.

title: No Duty to Disclose HIV/AIDS or Past Crimes or Deaths at the Property
bodyText: District law says certain facts that might bother a renter are not material facts you must disclose when leasing or subleasing, and failing to disclose them cannot be the basis of a lawsuit against the owner, broker, property manager or a tenant who sublets. The listed facts are: an occupant at any time had or was suspected of having HIV; an occupant had or was suspected of having AIDS or any other disease medically shown to be highly unlikely to spread through occupancy alone; and the property was, or was suspected to be, the site of a suicide, homicide or other felony. This covers every rental. Unlike some places, the District statute has no sentence telling you how to answer if a prospective tenant asks, and no District statute requires a landlord to disclose sex-offender registry information, before or after a question; registry information is published by the Metropolitan Police Department. Practical step: do not volunteer health information about past occupants, and if an applicant asks a direct question, do not answer falsely; whether a false answer is actionable under fraud or consumer-protection law is a question for case law.

title: Storage Space in District Leases
bodyText:
A District lease may assign a storage locker or area and limit what may be kept there (for example no hazardous, flammable or perishable items). Three limits apply.

First, as with parking, the lease may not exempt the owner from, or limit the owner's liability for, loss or damage caused by the negligence of the owner or the owner's agents or employees in operating or maintaining any facility on the property, so a blanket "landlord is not liable for items stored" clause should not be used.

Second, the District's self-service storage lien law covers real property used for renting individual storage spaces that occupants use on a self-storage basis, and its lien and sale remedy depends on a separate rental agreement stating the lien in bold type. No District statute or regulation settles whether it reaches a locker provided as part of a residential tenancy, so do not rely on it to sell a tenant's stored belongings; a tenant's property is handled through the eviction property rules and the landlord-lien rules instead.

Third, storage provided with a rent-stabilized unit is a related facility, so mandatory storage charges need approval and substantial reductions can lower the rent.

Practical step: use the District storage clause (no liability disclaimer).

title: Subletting and Assignment Rules
bodyText:
In the District you may prohibit subletting or assignment in your sole and absolute discretion only if the prohibition is written into the lease. If the lease is silent, or allows subletting with your reasonable consent, you may condition consent only on the proposed subtenant meeting your reasonable rental qualification guidelines, which you must give the tenant on request.

A bad-faith violation of this rule can cost treble damages. If you let a tenant find a replacement, assign or sublet, any fee you charge the outgoing tenant may not exceed the application-fee cap. In a rent-stabilized unit, a tenant may not sublet for more rent than the tenant pays you. A subtenant is a tenant under the Rental Housing Act and a tenant who sublets becomes a housing provider, so the subtenant gets the Act's protections.

A tenant generally cannot host short-term rentals: District law requires the property to be the host's primary residence eligible for the homestead deduction, and the regulations require that the host own it. Enforcing a sublet ban still requires the 30-day notice to correct or vacate. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Late Fee on the Subsidy Share
bodyText: When a housing voucher or other rent subsidy pays part of the rent, you may not charge the tenant a late fee for the late payment or nonpayment of any portion of the rent that the subsidy provider, rather than the tenant, is responsible for paying. A late fee can apply only to the tenant's own share, and then only under the general late-fee rules: the lease must set out the grace period and maximum fee, the tenant's share must be unpaid more than 5 days after the due date (or any longer grace period), and the fee may not exceed 5% of the rent due. This applies to every covered unit, rent-stabilized or exempt. Knowingly or willfully charging a prohibited late fee makes you liable for the unlawful amount (trebled for bad faith) plus a civil fine of $100 to $5,000 per fee. See the late-fee row for the full rules.

title: Surrender Follows End of Tenancy, Not End of Term
bodyText:
In the District, the end of the lease term does not by itself end the tenancy or require the tenant to move out. A tenant who keeps paying rent may stay, and the tenancy ends only when the tenant leaves (a month-to-month tenant on 30 days' written notice) or when a court orders possession on a just-cause ground. A surrender clause therefore must not make the expiration of the term, by itself, end the tenant's right to stay.

At move-out, a tenant's promise to leave the unit in good repair does not require substantial repairs, replacement of obsolete materials, or fixing defects the tenant did not cause through negligence or fault, and you may not charge for ordinary wear and tear or professional cleaning. When the tenancy ends you must ask for a forwarding mail or email address, and within 45 days send any notice of unpaid amounts (including the cost of removing items left behind) with photos and the tenant's dispute rights, separate from the deposit rules.

District law has no special procedure for belongings left after a voluntary move-out; the 7-day storage rules apply after a court eviction. Practical step: use the shared surrender clause, whose saving phrase ("unless applicable law entitles Tenant to remain") keeps the tenant's right to stay; the limits above apply even though the clause does not repeat them.

title: Cable Television Access for Tenants
bodyText: District cable law limits what a residential landlord may do about cable television. You may not interfere with the installation, operation, upgrade or maintenance of cable television facilities on your property, but you may set reasonable conditions and architectural controls to protect the property's safety, function and appearance and tenants' convenience, require the cable operator or tenant to bear the full cost, and require the operator to indemnify you for damage. You may not demand or accept payment from a tenant or a cable operator for allowing access or service, except as the cable office's rules allow, and you may not charge different rent, or otherwise treat tenants differently, depending on whether they subscribe. Cable operators may not make deals with you that limit a tenant's choice of video provider or antenna. A tenant or other person harmed can sue for damages, punitive damages and attorney's fees. Rooftop antennas must clear the roof by 8 feet and may not be attached to fire escapes. Practical step: do not sign exclusive cable deals or charge subscription-based rent differences.

title: Tenancy at Will: Old Statute Displaced by Just Cause
bodyText: An old District statute says a tenancy at will may be ended by 30 days' written notice from either landlord or tenant, and a tenancy by sufferance by written notice at any time (with rent prorated to the quit date). For residential rental units covered by the Rental Housing Act, which is essentially all of them, those landlord-side rules are displaced: a residential tenancy can be ended by a 30-day notice only from the tenant, and the landlord can recover possession only on a just-cause ground with the notice and waiting period the eviction statute requires, followed by a court case. The Act's definition of tenant includes anyone entitled to possession or occupancy of a rental unit, so an informal or oral tenancy with rent paid is protected the same way. Any notice to quit must be served in English and Spanish, personally, on a person of suitable age at the premises, or by posting plus first-class mail within 3 days; a notice cannot be withdrawn without the other side's consent. Practical step: treat an at-will or informal residential occupant who pays rent as a protected tenant, put the arrangement in writing, and use only the statutory eviction grounds and notices.

title: Tenant Bill of Rights at Application
bodyText: The District has an official tenant-rights statement: the Tenant Bill of Rights published by the Office of the Tenant Advocate. For every covered rental unit (rent-stabilized or exempt), you must give it to each prospective tenant when the tenant applies, together with the Rent Administrator's disclosure form and its attachments. If no application is used, give the disclosure package before the lease is signed or agreed to. This is a pre-signing duty, not a lease term. The OTA issued its first revision in September 2026 (FORM OTA 2026.09.25); applications must get a revised version starting 90 days after it is noticed in the D.C. Register, so use the current OTA version. Separately, at the start of every tenancy you must give the tenant a copy of the landlord-tenant chapter of the housing regulations and two enforcement sections (see the lease-copy row). No District statute or housing regulation requires the statement to be the lease's first page, or the tenant to sign or initial it. The sanction is not a bar on suing: you may not raise the rent if you willfully skip the disclosures, or fail to fix them within 10 business days after written notice. Practical step: have the tenant sign the receipt line on the OTA form anyway and keep it.

title: Tenant-Caused Damage: Duties, Deposit Rules and Void-Lease Exception
bodyText:
District housing rules make the tenant responsible for keeping the part of the unit the tenant controls clean and sanitary and for using fixtures and appliances properly, and bar the tenant and anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission from willfully or wantonly damaging the unit, its fixtures or equipment. Damage beyond ordinary wear and tear (deterioration from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, an immediate family member or a guest) may be charged to the tenant and deducted from the deposit with the required notices; age-related breakdown may not.

The District has no general fire or casualty statute letting a tenant end the lease. Instead, a lease becomes void if housing-code violations make the unit unsafe or unsanitary and are not corrected in time, but only if the violations did not result from the intentional acts or negligence of the tenant or the tenant's invitees, so tenant-caused damage does not void the lease.

If a government order displaces the tenant, rent is suspended though the tenancy continues. Your recovery of lost rent after tenant-caused damage is limited to actual damages you could not mitigate. A lease may not excuse your own negligence.

Practical step: document unit condition at move-in and move-out, and bill tenant-caused damage with photos and invoices.

title: Tenant Data: District Security and Breach-Notice Rules
bodyText: No District statute bars a landlord, as such, from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's information, or lists confidential tenant data that needs written consent to share. The District's general data-security law does reach landlords, because it applies to any person or entity that owns, licenses, maintains or possesses personal information of a District resident. Personal information means a name combined with, for example, a Social Security, taxpayer or government ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, medical, genetic, health-insurance or biometric information, or an e-mail login with password. Under that law you must keep reasonable security safeguards suited to the information and the size of your operation, require any service provider you give the data to (screening or payment vendors, for example) to do the same by written agreement, and take reasonable steps when destroying records. If a breach occurs you must notify affected District residents promptly, and notify the Attorney General if 50 or more residents are affected; a violation is an unfair trade practice. Other rules limit particular uses: sealed eviction records, a known address-confidentiality participant's address, and threats to disclose citizenship status when collecting debts. Practical step: collect only what screening needs, store it securely and shred it when no longer needed.

title: Tenant Early-Termination Rights: Intrafamily-Offense Release and Void Lease
bodyText: District law gives a tenant only a few ways to end a fixed-term lease early without liability, and none can be waived by the lease. A tenant who is a victim of an intrafamily offense (or the parent or guardian of a minor victim) is released from the lease on written notice with a copy of a civil protection order or signed documentation from a qualified third party such as a police officer, health professional or domestic-violence counselor. The request must come within 90 days of the incident; the release takes effect 14 days after you receive the notice and documentation, or earlier if a new tenancy begins. The tenant owes rent only through that date and no lease penalty. If you refuse or fail to respond within the 14 days, you are treated as having unlawfully demanded all remaining rent. If housing-code violations not caused by the tenant make the unit unsafe or unsanitary and are not corrected in time, the lease is void. Federal law also lets servicemembers end leases in some circumstances. No District statute lets a tenant end a lease because of a landlord's misrepresentation, job loss or a home purchase. A tenant who simply leaves owes your actual damages, which you must mitigate, and a month-to-month tenant may leave on 30 days' written notice.

title: Tenant Maintenance Duties Under the Housing Regulations
bodyText:
In the District the housing regulations set the tenant's maintenance duties directly. In the part of the premises under the tenant's exclusive control, the tenant must keep it as clean and sanitary as its condition permits, dispose of all rubbish, garbage and other organic or flammable waste safely, keep plumbing fixtures clean, properly use and operate electrical, gas, plumbing and heating fixtures and appliances, and supply and use proper garbage receptacles, carrying refuse to the common storage area unless you collect it.

The tenant must not willfully or wantonly damage or remove any part of the unit or its facilities, or let guests do so. Extermination falls on the occupant of a single-family home, or on the occupant of a multi-unit building when only that unit is infested, unless your building upkeep caused it. Everything else, including common areas and the facilities, utilities and services the regulations require, is your duty and cannot be shifted by a general maintenance clause.

A tenant's promise to keep or return the unit in good repair does not oblige the tenant to make substantial repairs or fix defects that are not the tenant's fault. No District rule found addresses well or septic maintenance in rentals. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Tenant Opportunity to Purchase (TOPA) Before Selling
bodyText: Before you sell a District rental building, or issue a notice to vacate for demolition or ending housing use, the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act generally requires a bona fide written offer of sale, sent to each tenant by certified mail, tracked delivery or hand delivery, with a copy and signed statement to the Mayor the same day. The offer must give the price and terms, the tenants' purchase rights, whether a third-party contract exists, and that building information is available on request. Timelines depend on size. 5 or more units: tenants have 45 days to register a tenant organization, then at least 120 days to negotiate and 120 days to settle. 2 to 4 units owned mainly by a business corporation: 15 days for a joint statement of interest (then 7 days individually), 90 days to negotiate plus 30, 90 days to settle. Other 2 to 4 unit buildings and single-family homes (including a single condo unit): no offer of sale, but written notice to tenants within 3 days of receiving or soliciting a written purchase offer, plus full rights for certain elderly or disabled tenants. Tenants also get a 15-day right of first refusal on a third-party contract. A lease cannot waive the right to receive an offer of sale. Willful violations carry fines up to $50,000.

title: Tenant Receivership for Serious Violations
bodyText: The District's Tenant Receivership law lets a court take rent collection and management away from an owner of a rental housing accommodation, of any size, that is cited for serious housing-code or property-maintenance violations the owner was properly notified of but did not timely fix, or that shows a 30-day pattern of neglect threatening tenants' health, safety or security. Serious threats include vermin, filth, inadequate heat, ventilation, light or sanitation, inoperative fire equipment, and inoperative door or window locks. The Attorney General may petition, and a majority of tenants may ask the Attorney General to petition and then file themselves if the Attorney General does not act within 5 business days. The court can appoint a receiver ex parte for up to 14 days in an emergency, can accept an owner's abatement plan instead, and can order the owner to contribute money beyond the rents, including rent refunds for past disrepair. While the receiver serves, you may not collect rent and may file a nonpayment eviction only with the receivership court's permission. Separately, the District may correct violations itself and bill the cost as a tax on the property.

title: Rent Ledgers, Unit Records and Data Security
bodyText: Rent records: keep a rent ledger for every tenancy. A nonpayment notice of intent to file must attach a ledger of rent charges and payments for the period of delinquency, and in any nonpayment case you must bring to every hearing, including mediation, all ledgers going back to the last zero balance (or, without a ledger, bank statements and receipts), and give them to the tenant on request. Every payment other than a personal check needs a written receipt. Unit records: for each rental unit covered by the Rental Housing Act you must keep a compilation of the unit's records (registration, license, rent and increase history, fees and deposit terms, recent housing-code violation notices, mold history, the Tenant Bill of Rights and more), make it available for inspection, update it within 30 days of a change, and give a tenant a free copy within 10 business days of a once-a-year request; willful noncompliance blocks rent increases. Applicant and tenant data: anyone holding District residents' Social Security, driver's license, account or similar numbers must keep reasonable security safeguards, bind service providers to them by contract, destroy records securely, and notify affected residents promptly after a breach (and the Attorney General if 50 or more residents are affected). Practical step: keep ledgers current and screening files locked or encrypted.

title: Tenant Remedies When Repairs Are Not Made
bodyText: District statutes and rules give tenants several remedies when you fail to repair, and a lease cannot waive the housing-code chapter they rest on. Every lease carries an implied warranty that the unit meets the housing regulations; if serious violations the tenant did not cause are not corrected in time, the lease is void. In a nonpayment eviction case the tenant may raise recoupment or setoff and a counterclaim based on rent paid or credits against rent, and housing-code violations can reduce the amount the court orders paid into its registry while the case is pending. The retaliation statute protects a tenant who lawfully withholds rent after giving written or witnessed oral notice of a code violation. Tenants can also seek a court-appointed receiver for serious unabated violations, recover treble damages for mold you fail to remediate in bad faith, and, in rent-stabilized units, petition for a rent reduction when services or facilities decrease. No District statute authorizes repair-and-deduct. Whether and how a tenant may withhold rent or self-help repair is governed by case law. Practical step: fix reported conditions promptly and document repairs.

title: Tenants Right to Organize
bodyText: District tenants have a statutory right to organize: to form, join and meet in tenant organizations, to meet and confer with the owner through representatives they choose, to act together for mutual aid and protection, and to refrain from these activities. In a multifamily building, neither the owner nor its agent may interfere with tenants or tenant organizers distributing literature in common areas and under doors, posting on building bulletin boards, holding meetings at reasonable times in units, community rooms, lobbies or other spaces tenants can use under their leases, or responding to rent increases, service changes or conversions. Owners and agents may not attend or record meetings unless the organization (or a majority present) allows it. Outside organizers who are not tenants get the same access as other outside parties; if the building has no consistently enforced written no-canvassing policy it is treated as allowing canvassing, and under such a policy a tenant must accompany the organizer. Knowing violations carry civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation (adjusted for inflation), injunctions, damages, license suspension with a rent freeze, and attorney's fees. Organizing activity is also protected from retaliation. Practical step: keep house rules on common rooms, flyers and solicitation consistent with these rights.

title: Tenant Screening: Notice, Limits and Adverse-Action Rules
bodyText: District tenant screening is regulated in detail for every covered rental. Before asking for any information or fee, give the applicant written notice (or post it) of: each fee or deposit and whether it is refundable; the information checked; automatic and other denial criteria; the credit agency and free-report right; expected availability; your response time; dispute rights; the right to a refund of an unused fee; and complaint rights. The application fee is capped (about $50, inflation-adjusted), only one fee applies to applications to several of your units within 30 days, and no other fee may be charged before lease signing. You may not ask about or rely on eviction cases that did not end in a judgment for you or were filed 3 or more years ago, or lease-breach allegations tied to domestic violence, crime victimization or disability, and you may not deny solely on a credit score. For subsidy holders, income level and pre-subsidy credit or rent history may not be used. If you deny, give written reasons, copies of third-party information, and dispute rights, and answer any dispute within 10 days. Criminal history has its own rules (see the next row).

title: Tenant Duties Set by the Housing Regulations
bodyText: District tenants have duties set by the housing regulations that apply whether or not the lease repeats them. In the part of the premises under their exclusive control they must keep it clean and sanitary, dispose of garbage properly, keep plumbing fixtures clean and properly use fixtures and appliances; they must not willfully or wantonly damage the unit or its facilities or let guests do so; they must not occupy or allow occupancy beyond what the regulations permit; and a tenant who alleges a housing code violation must give you access within 48 hours of your written request. A tenant who causes a code violation faces the same penalties as an owner. Breaches of these duties, being imposed by the housing regulations, can support eviction only through the 30-day notice to correct or vacate. See the tenant-maintenance and prohibited-acts rows for detail. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Tenant Property Insurance and Liability Disclaimers
bodyText:
A District lease may tell the tenant that the landlord's insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings and may require the tenant to carry renter's insurance. It may not go further and excuse the owner from liability: the housing regulations forbid any lease provision that exempts the owner, or limits the owner's liability, for injury to persons or property caused by the negligence of the owner or the owner's agents or employees in operating, caring for or maintaining the premises.

A blanket statement that the landlord is not liable for any loss of the tenant's property reaches that negligence and should not be used. No District statute specifically addresses sending landlord-responsible repairs to a tenant's renter's insurance, but the result is the same. The owner's duty to keep the premises in compliance with the housing regulations is part of every lease and cannot be waived, and the owner may not charge tenants for services needed to keep the unit habitable. Applies to all District rental units.

Practical step: use the District version of the insurance clause, which requires coverage without the liability disclaimer, and handle repairs yourself regardless of the tenant's insurance.

title: Changing Terms During a Tenancy
bodyText: District law has no procedure for a landlord to change a month-to-month tenant's terms by notice, and the usual route used elsewhere (ending the tenancy and offering a new one) is closed: a residential tenancy may be ended by notice only from the tenant, and the landlord may evict only on a statutory ground, so the end of a term or a refusal of new terms is not a ground. A change to non-rent terms therefore needs the tenant's agreement. Rent and fees: "rent" in the Rental Housing Act means everything the landlord demands as a condition of occupancy or for related services and facilities, so raising a recurring charge the lease already provides is treated like a rent increase. No rent increase takes effect until the first rent day more than 60 days after written notice, and longer notice may be needed if the lease requires a tenant move-out notice over 30 days. Rent-stabilized units add limits: increases must fit the program's caps and timing, mandatory fees need Rent Administrator approval, and substantially reducing services or facilities can lead the Rent Administrator to reduce the rent. Practical step: get signed amendments for term changes and give at least 60 days' written notice of any increase in rent or recurring charges.

title: Only the Tenant May End a Tenancy by Notice: 30 Days to the First of a Month
bodyText:
In the District only the tenant can end a residential tenancy by notice. A month-to-month tenant may end it by a written 30-day notice, which takes effect on the first day of the first month that begins at least 30 days after the notice is given. You cannot end any residential tenancy, fixed-term or periodic, by a notice to quit or by declining to renew; you may recover possession only on a just-cause ground with the specific notice and waiting period for that ground (for example 30 days to correct a lease violation or 90 days for owner occupancy).

Limits on the tenant's notice: a lease may not require more than 30 days' notice to vacate unless it also requires you to give written notice of any rent increase at least 30 days longer than that period, and a longer notice tied to the end of the initial term is void unless the lease says it expires with that term and that the tenant may then leave on 30 days' notice while month to month.

Once given, a notice cannot be withdrawn without the other party's consent. Practical step: use the District tenant-notice clause, which states the 30-day rule and that the end of the term does not end the tenancy.

title: Pre-Lease Notice That a New Building Is Excluded From TOPA
bodyText: Tenants in the District generally have a right to buy their building before the owner sells it (the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act, TOPA; see the TOPA notice row). Since December 31, 2025, sales of a new multifamily building within 15 years after its permanent certificate of occupancy are excluded from TOPA, on one condition the owner must meet at sale (a Notice of Transfer to tenants). Pre-lease duty: if your building is excluded under that new-construction rule, you must give each prospective tenant written notice of the exclusion before the tenant enters into the lease. Give it as a separate pre-signing notice (for example with the application disclosures), not only as a lease clause, and keep proof. Owners of buildings that became excluded on December 31, 2025 had to notify all existing tenants within 90 days. Missing the notice does not cancel the exclusion, but it is still a statutory duty. No other TOPA exclusion (family transfers, foreclosure, small-owner 2 to 4 unit buildings, single-family homes) carries a pre-lease notice duty; several exempt transfers instead require a Notice of Transfer to the Mayor and, by certified or tracked mail, to each tenant at the time of the transfer. The owner bears the burden of proving any exclusion.

title: Towing Vehicles from Rental Property
bodyText:
District law makes it a violation to park or store a motor vehicle on private property without the property owner's consent, or to keep an abandoned or dangerous vehicle there (unless it is fully enclosed or at a lawful repair or salvage business). The District, or a towing company acting at the Department of Public Works' direction, removes a vehicle parked without consent immediately after a notice of infraction is placed on it, removes a dangerous vehicle right away, and removes an abandoned vehicle 45 days after mailing a warning notice to the property owner.

A vehicle is abandoned on private property only after more than 30 days there and only if it is apparently inoperable, harbors pests, or lacks valid tags (expired tags count only once at least a year out of date). No one may remove a vehicle owned by another person unless they are its owner, someone the owner authorized in writing, a District employee on duty, or a tow operator with valid District authorization; the civil fine is up to $500.

Private tow-company licensing, signage, rates and storage rules sit in District regulations. Practical step: post clear parking limits, call the District's parking enforcement or a District-authorized tow operator for unauthorized vehicles, and never move a vehicle yourself.

title: Rental Housing Act Termination Date
bodyText: The Rental Housing Act of 1985 carries a dated termination clause: all of its subchapters except subchapter III and subchapter V (evictions and retaliation) and the inspection-access section terminate on December 31, 2030. The Council has moved that date forward several times (earlier versions set 2005 and 2010). The clause has no present effect. Today every part of the Act applies in full, including rent stabilization, registration, the late-fee limits, the entry, notice and subletting rules, and the screening and fee rules, and the lease library is written to that current law. Do not draft leases or plan rent increases on the assumption that any part of the Act will lapse. No other District landlord-tenant statute is on a dated repeal clock, apart from temporary and emergency acts, which by their nature last 225 or 90 days.

title: Notice Languages; No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: No District statute or housing regulation requires a private landlord to translate the lease itself, even when the tenancy was advertised or negotiated in another language, or sets a lease type-size or prescribed-text rule tied to translation. The District's Language Access Act binds District government agencies, not private landlords, unless a contract imposes it. Notices are different. Every notice to quit, notice to correct or vacate, nonpayment notice of intent to file and other eviction-grounds notice must be in English and Spanish, and also in the tenant's primary language if you know (or, for the regulation's notices, reasonably should know) that it is one of the languages the District designates under the Language Access Act; a court may dismiss a possession case if you skip a required language. A written lease or addendum you gave in a covered language is evidence you knew the tenant's language. Debt-collection notices about charged-off rent debt go in English and Spanish, or in English and the language principally used in the original contract. Practical step: if you lease in another language, plan to send eviction-related notices in that language too, and keep translated copies.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: District law reaches unconscionable lease terms in two ways. First, the housing regulations' landlord-tenant chapter says its listed rights, remedies and prohibited terms do not stop a court from finding other lease provisions, practices or acts contrary to public policy, unconscionable or otherwise unlawful. Second, the Consumer Protection Procedures Act makes it an unlawful trade practice to make or enforce unconscionable terms in sales, leases or other consumer contracts, and lists factors such as gross disparity between price and value, knowledge that the consumer cannot benefit, and taking advantage of the consumer's age, abilities, lack of knowledge, reading ability or difficulty understanding the agreement. A tenant who proves a violation may recover treble damages or $1,500 per violation, whichever is greater, plus fees. The debt-collection law separately bars unfair or unconscionable collection means. The District has no statute declaring any particular lease clause enforceable despite unconscionability arguments, and the commercial-code unconscionability sections apply to goods, not real property. How courts apply the doctrine to residential leases is case law. Practical step: avoid one-sided remedies, hidden fees and terms a tenant cannot reasonably understand, and explain unusual terms before signing.

title: Unlawful-Entry Law Lets the Person in Charge Remove Unauthorized Non-Tenants
bodyText: The District's unlawful-entry law covers private apartment buildings, condominiums, cooperatives and houses. It is a misdemeanor to enter any part of such property against the will of the lawful occupant or the person lawfully in charge, or, being there without lawful authority to remain, to refuse to leave on that person's demand. As the person in charge of common areas, a landlord or its manager can ask an unauthorized non-tenant to leave and call the police if the person refuses. A no-trespassing sign on vacant, boarded-up or secured property is prima facie evidence of unlawful entry. Limits: the statute reaches only people without lawful authority to be there. A tenant's invited guest generally enters on the tenant's authority, and in a multifamily building a tenant organizer has the access rights that District law grants (the same as other outside visitors, or as invited visitors when accompanied by a tenant). The statute says nothing about written bar notices for private buildings; the Housing Authority's bar-notice rules apply only to its own properties. Never use trespass enforcement against a tenant or household member in possession; removing a tenant requires a court eviction.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in the District)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that District property law does not use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise. The closest District interest is a life estate (for example, a person who holds a house for life while others own the remainder). The only District statute on a life tenant's lease deals with rent: if a life tenant who leased the property dies, the life tenant's executor or administrator may recover from the tenant the rent for the period up to death (all of it if death falls on the rent day). The statute speaks of a lease that ends on the life tenant's death, but District law also says a tenant of a covered rental unit may not be evicted, despite the end of a lease, except on the statutory grounds and notices, and a remainder owner who takes over and collects rent is a housing provider. How those rules fit together after a life estate ends is a question for case law. Practical step if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease and have the remainder owners sign it or agree in writing that the tenancy continues if the life estate ends.

title: Utilities Included in the Rent
bodyText:
District law lets you include some or all utilities in the rent, but once a utility is your responsibility or under your control you must furnish it in the quantities needed for normal occupancy, and where the tenant does not control heat or hot water you must meet the heat and hot-water standards. List the utilities you pay in the lease.

You may not add a separate fee for utilities you are required to provide, including administrative fees for third-party billing, and from January 1, 2027 you may not bill tenants separately for the utilities of common spaces or vacant units. In a rent-stabilized unit, utilities included in the rent are related services: you cannot later impose a mandatory utility fee unless it is approved through the rent stabilization program, and reducing them can support a rent reduction.

If you hold the account and fall behind, tenants of a master-metered building of 3 or more apartments may get service in their own names and deduct those payments from rent, and the utility or the tenants may have a receiver appointed to collect rents; see the landlord-held utility account row.

Practical step: budget for these utilities in the rent.

title: Who Pays for Utilities
bodyText:
A lease may make the tenant arrange and pay for utilities directly, but District law limits how far. You must provide adequate heating and water-heating facilities; where the heating or hot-water equipment is not under the tenant's control, you must supply heat (68 degrees from 6:30 a.m. to 11 p.m., 65 overnight) and a continuous supply of hot water; and any utility that is your responsibility or under your control must be furnished in the quantities normal occupancy needs.

Since August 14, 2026 you may not charge any fee for services you must provide to keep the unit habitable, including fees related to utilities, trash, locks or administrative fees for third-party billing. Beginning January 1, 2027, you may not bill tenants separately, other than through rent, for common-space or vacant-unit utilities, though a ratio utility billing system may still allocate master-metered charges.

You may not pass through more stormwater fee than the District charges. If you fall behind on a master-metered electric, gas or water account, tenants may take service in their own names and deduct what they pay from rent. In a rent-stabilized unit, cutting a utility service you provided can be challenged as a reduction in services. The same rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Ratio Utility Billing and the 2027 Limit
bodyText: District law expressly allows a ratio utility billing system: you may allocate master-metered water, sewer, electricity, oil or natural gas charges among tenants (and the property owner) by a formula such as square footage, occupancy or number of bedrooms. From January 1, 2027, neither you nor a billing company you hire may charge tenants separately, outside the monthly rent, for utilities used by common spaces (lobbies, leasing offices, business centers, pools, fitness centers and similar areas) or by vacant units, so the formula must exclude those shares. You may not charge tenants an administrative fee for third-party utility billing, now or later. In a rent-stabilized unit, a mandatory utility charge is a mandatory fee that must be approved through the rent stabilization program, so apportioned billing there is risky. District law sets no lease-disclosure form for apportioned billing, but put the method and the utilities covered in the lease. Practical step: if leases signed now run past January 1, 2027, make sure the allocation already excludes common areas and vacant units.

title: When the Landlord Holds the Utility Account
bodyText: If you hold the utility account and fall behind, District law protects your tenants and redirects your rent. Electric and gas: in an apartment house of 3 or more apartments billed to you, the utility may not cut service for your delinquent bill unless it gives tenants a practical chance to take service in their own names without liability for your arrears, and if that is not practical it may not cut service at all. Tenant payments count as rent and may be deducted from what they owe you. Water and sewer: for any rental property of 1 or more units, tenants may get service in their own names without liability for your arrears where the Mayor finds it practicable, again deducting payments from rent. In either case the utility or the tenants can have a court appoint a receiver to collect the rents and pay the bills; collecting rent from tenants after that order is contempt, and you may not file a nonpayment eviction without the receivership court's permission. You also may not ask an electric or gas company to cut service to such an apartment house without a Public Service Commission finding. Under a temporary law (expires March 27, 2027), DC Water posts disconnection notices at the building and, where practicable, at each unit.

title: Utility Shutoff Limits
bodyText: District utility shutoff law works mainly through weather limits and tenant protections rather than a winter season. The electric company may not disconnect residential electric service on the day before or the day of a National Weather Service forecast of 95 degrees F or above, or 32 degrees F or below, and when such a forecast precedes a holiday or weekend, on any day of that holiday or weekend. The gas company has the same rule for forecasts of 32 degrees F or below. DC Water may shut off water if charges are unpaid 30 days after the bill. No District statute adds a winter notice period. As a landlord, you may not use a shutoff against a tenant: utilities you control must be furnished in the quantities needed for normal occupancy, reducing services is listed retaliation, and you may not ask an electric or gas company to cut service to an apartment house of 3 or more units without a Public Service Commission finding. If your own unpaid bill threatens service, tenants have the protections in the landlord-held utility account row. Separately, evictions may not be carried out in extreme weather.

title: Utility Shutoff Notices: Tenant May Name You
bodyText: District law gives an owner no right to sign up, on its own, to be told when a tenant's utility service is about to be cut off for nonpayment. What exists is customer-driven: each District water, natural gas and electric utility must run a Third-Party Notification program under which a customer may designate another person or agency to receive copies of past-due and termination notices, and the enrollment form lets the customer keep its contact and account information confidential. So a tenant who holds the account in the tenant's own name may choose to name you as a third-party contact, but you cannot require it in a way that overrides the tenant's choice, and a third-party contact is not liable for the bill and cannot stop or delay the shutoff. Enrollment is mandatory only for assisted-living, community-residence and nursing facilities, which must name their oversight agency. Practical step: if you want notice, ask the tenant to enroll you with the utility; do not condition the tenancy on it without checking the Public Service Commission rules.

title: Give Applicants Code Violation Reports; Placarded Units and Reletting Certificates
bodyText: Yes, for every covered rental unit. At the time a prospective tenant applies, the Rent Administrator's disclosure form you provide must come with copies of all housing code and property maintenance code violation reports the Department of Buildings issued for the building or unit within the last 12 months, plus older reports for violations not yet abated. You must keep a compilation of these documents available to tenants, update it within 30 days of any change, and give a tenant a free copy once a year on written request. Willful noncompliance, or failure to cure within 10 business days of written notice, blocks rent increases. Unfit units: the District may placard a unit or building as unfit for human habitation; 30 days after placarding no one may occupy an affected apartment until the District removes the placard. A tenancy ended by a life-safety placard is not deemed terminated until the unit is offered back to the tenant, and while a tenant of a covered unit is displaced by an administrative order for unsafe premises, the tenant owes no rent. After a court finds a breach of the implied warranty or voids a lease, you must obtain a District certificate of code compliance before reletting. A lease of a unit that is unsafe or unsanitary at the start because of violations you knew or should have known about is void.

title: Hot Water: 120 Degree Minimum, No Maximum Setting Rule
bodyText: District housing regulations set a minimum, not a maximum, hot-water temperature. Every residential building must have a water heating facility, properly connected to the hot water lines of the required fixtures, that can supply enough hot water at not less than 120 degrees F at those fixtures to meet normal demand. Where the tenant does not control the water heater, you must provide and maintain a continuous supply of running hot water. In a rented single-family home where a housing violation notice was issued for a defective owner-controlled water heater that is separate from the heating system, you must have it inspected by a qualified person (including a check of flues, vents and dampers for carbon monoxide) between March 1 and September 1 after the notice, and file the inspection form. No District statute or housing regulation requires setting a unit's water heater to a maximum temperature at each new occupancy or limits scalding temperatures in rental housing (in those sources, the only maximum applies to assisted living residences). Practical step: check the water heater at turnover, keep delivery at or above 120 degrees F at the taps, and consider anti-scald valves where young children or older adults live.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Most notices that matter in a District tenancy must be in writing, and the lease cannot make oral notice enough. Landlord to tenant: every eviction ground requires a written notice meeting the statute (a nonpayment notice of intent to file, a 30-day notice to correct or vacate, and the longer notices for owner use, sale, renovation, demolition or discontinuance); entry needs written notice at least 48 hours ahead unless the tenant agrees in writing to less; rent increases take effect only after at least 60 days' notice; the deposit-withholding notice and the move-out unpaid-amounts notice are written; and the 21-day pre-eviction notice is written and delivered three ways. Tenant to landlord: a month-to-month tenancy ends on the tenant's 30-day written notice. A tenant's oral repair request witnessed by a third party still counts for retaliation protection. The old landlord-tenant chapter lets parties agree in writing to a different notice to quit or to waive it, but for units covered by the Rental Housing Act that agreement cannot displace the written eviction notices the Act requires. Applies to all District rental units. Practical step: put every notice in writing, keep a copy and proof of the delivery method, and follow each notice's own delivery rule.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: The District of Columbia follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (D.C. Code § 28:3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (D.C. Code § 28:1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: The District of Columbia's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (D.C. Code title 42, chs. 32 and 35 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how the District of Columbia's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a District Lease
bodyText: No District law makes a residential lease wait for a government officer's approval before it is valid, and the District has no communal, tribal or native land system. The District's real property title has no chapter on such land, and its landlord-tenant and rental housing laws contain no approval step for a private lease. What the District does require of a lease is form and process, not approval: a lease for longer than 1 year must be made by a deed signed and sealed by the lessor (D.C. Code § 42-306(b)), and the rental housing laws' registration and disclosure rules apply (see "Lease Length: Deed Formality and Recordation", "Prescribed Wording and Agency Forms").

title: Recording a Lease in the District
bodyText: No District law requires you to record an ordinary residential lease. Recording matters for longer leases. A lease for longer than 1 year can be created only by a deed signed and sealed by the lessor, in person or through a power of attorney (D.C. Code § 42-306(b)). A deed conveying an interest in District real property takes effect between the parties from delivery, but as to creditors and later good-faith buyers and mortgagees without notice of it, only from the time it is delivered to the Recorder of Deeds for record (D.C. Code § 42-401). Between two deeds to good-faith buyers for value without notice, the one recorded first is preferred (D.C. Code § 42-406). A lease or ground rent for a term of 30 years or more (counting renewals) is a 'deed' taxed at recordation; a shorter lease is not (D.C. Code §§ 42-1101(3)(B), 42-1103(a)(1)). Whatever the term, a tenant of a covered rental unit keeps the eviction protections of the Rental Housing Act whether or not the lease is recorded (see "Lease Length: Deed Formality and Recordation"). No District statute ties notice to a relative's lease the way Nebraska's does. Practical step: for a lease longer than 1 year, have the owner (or attorney-in-fact) sign under seal, and consider recording it if it gives the tenant a long term or a purchase option.

title: No Special District Statement Required
bodyText: No District law requires a lease to tell the tenant that the property lies in a special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges. The application-stage disclosure the Rental Housing Act requires (rent, surcharges, rent-control status, code violations, deposit terms, ownership information, the Tenant Bill of Rights and other items) doesn't include it (D.C. Code § 42-3502.22(b)(1)). The District's special districts are Business Improvement Districts (BIDs). A BID tax falls on 'taxable property', mainly commercial classes; residential property is taxable only in the Mount Vernon Triangle, NoMa, Navy Yard, Downtown and Golden Triangle BIDs, and even there buildings with fewer than 10 dwelling units, buildings where 20% or more of units have project-based Section 8 contracts, and certain senior buildings are excluded (D.C. Code § 2-1215.02(24)). BID taxes are billed and collected like real property taxes, and unpaid BID tax can lead to a tax sale of the property (D.C. Code § 2-1215.15(c), (g)). So the tax is the owner's; if your lease passes it through, state the charge in the lease.

title: Dormitories Are Outside the Rental Housing Act
bodyText: The District's student-housing rule is an exemption, not a duty. The Rental Housing Act, which holds the District's rent stabilization, registration and eviction-protection rules, doesn't apply to any dormitory (D.C. Code § 42-3502.05(e)(3)). A 'dormitory' is a structure or building owned by an institution of higher education or private boarding school in which at least 95% of the units are occupied by presently matriculated students of that institution (D.C. Code § 42-3501.03(11)). So the exemption reaches only school-owned buildings filled almost entirely with the school's own students. A privately owned house or apartment building rented to students, or a building a school leases from a private owner, is not a dormitory under that definition, and the Act applies to it in full, including its limits on evicting a tenant without a statutory ground. No District law found sets other rules for student leases, such as parental guarantees or academic-year terms.
